Which box-joining pairings accurately describe the synchronization primitives?

options.text: Box 1 -- (1) --> Mechanic A is correct (Interlocked executes atomic CPU instructions)
Box 2 -- (2) --> Mechanic B is correct (Monitor provides thread mutexes with thin-lock optimizations)
Box 3 -- (3) --> Mechanic C is correct (SemaphoreSlim supports async awaiting)
Box 4 -- (4) --> Mechanic D is correct (ReaderWriterLockSlim optimizes read-heavy shared state)
Box 1 -- (1) --> Mechanic C is correct (Interlocked provides async awaitable semaphores)

questions.explanation: Boxes 1 to 4 correctly pair each synchronization primitive with its operational model. Option e is false because Interlocked is purely synchronous CPU instructions.

questions.text: Which of the following statements are accurate regarding dependency injection lifetimes and captive dependencies in ASP.NET Core?

options.text: A Transient service creates a brand-new instance every time it is resolved from the service provider
A Scoped service is created once per HTTP request context and disposed at the request boundary
Injecting a Scoped DbContext into a Singleton background worker creates a dangerous Captive Dependency
Singletons are disposed and recreated on every incoming HTTP request

questions.explanation: Transient creates on demand; Scoped lives for the HTTP request; capturing a Scoped service in a Singleton prevents disposal and causes concurrency/memory bugs.

questions.text:
Review the following box-joining diagram connecting .NET Garbage Collection generations (Boxes 1-3) with dashes to their expected object lifecycles:
[Box 1: Generation 0] -- (dash) --> [Short-lived temporary objects, local variables, and string concatenations]
[Box 2: Generation 1] -- (dash) --> [Buffer generation separating short-lived objects from surviving long-lived objects]
[Box 3: Generation 2] -- (dash) --> [Long-lived objects, application singletons, static references, and cached pools]
Which of these GC generation connections are accurate?

options.text: Box 1 accurately describes short-lived temporary allocations in Gen 0
Box 2 accurately describes the buffer role of Gen 1
Box 3 accurately describes persistent long-lived objects in Gen 2
Box 1 holds 100 MB cached data structures by default

questions.explanation: Generational GC collects Gen 0 frequently for temporary objects, promotes survivors to Gen 1, and holds long-lived objects in Gen 2.

database-indexes.title: Database indexes
database-indexes.description: What an index buys, what it costs, and how to tell whether a query is using one.

questions.text: What does an index mainly speed up?

options.text: Inserts
Reads that filter or sort on the indexed columns
Table creation
Backups

questions.explanation: An index is an ordered structure the database can search instead of scanning the whole table.

questions.text: Adding more B-tree indexes to a table generally makes its inserts, updates and deletes slower.

options.text: True
False

questions.explanation: A write usually has to update each index that covers the changed row, so more indexes mean more work per write, and each index also takes space. The cost is real even though a few writes (for example a row that falls outside a partial index) skip some indexes.

questions.text: A composite index on (last_name, first_name) can efficiently serve which query?

options.text: WHERE first_name = 'Ada'
WHERE last_name = 'Lovelace'
WHERE first_name LIKE '%da'
None of them

questions.explanation: A composite index is ordered by its first column, then the second. A query must use a leftmost prefix of the columns to benefit.

questions.text: Which columns usually deserve an index? Select all that apply.

options.text: A foreign key used in frequent joins
A column in the WHERE clause of a hot query
A boolean column with a 50/50 split, filtered alone on a huge table
Every column, to be safe

questions.explanation: Index what queries actually filter and join on. Low-selectivity columns rarely help on their own, and indexing everything slows writes.

questions.text: EXPLAIN shows a sequential scan on a large table even though an index exists. What is a likely cause?

options.text: The table is too small
The query wraps the indexed column in a function, so the index cannot be used
Indexes only work for integers
The database is offline

questions.explanation: WHERE lower(email) = ... cannot use a plain index on email. Rewrite the predicate or create an index on the expression. Two other usual suspects are a filter that matches a large share of the rows, where a sequential scan really is cheaper, and stale statistics.

questions.text: In PostgreSQL, orders.customer_id is declared as a FOREIGN KEY to customers(id), and you often fetch all orders for one customer. What do you need to do about indexing orders.customer_id?

options.text: Nothing, because PostgreSQL creates an index for every foreign key automatically
Create the index yourself, because PostgreSQL indexes primary keys and unique constraints automatically but not the referencing side of a foreign key
Nothing, because the index on customers(id) already speeds up lookups on orders.customer_id
Nothing, because foreign keys are only indexed when ON DELETE CASCADE is set

questions.explanation: The primary key on customers(id) is indexed, but orders.customer_id is a separate column in a separate table, and PostgreSQL does not index it for you. Without your own index, finding one customer's orders (and checking the foreign key when a customer is deleted) scans the whole orders table.

questions.text: Which single index serves this query best? SELECT * FROM orders WHERE customer_id = 17 AND created_at >= '2026-01-01' ORDER BY created_at

options.text: (created_at, customer_id)
(customer_id, created_at)
(created_at) alone
(customer_id) alone

questions.explanation: Put the equality column first and the range or sort column second. The index then jumps straight to customer 17 and reads that customer's rows already sorted by created_at from the start date. With (created_at, customer_id) the database has to walk every entry since the start date, for all customers, and check customer_id as it goes. An index on customer_id alone finds the right rows but leaves the date filter and the sort to extra work.

database-transactions-and-isolation-leve.title: Database transactions and isolation levels
database-transactions-and-isolation-leve.description: ANSI SQL vs Snapshot Isolation anomalies: dirty reads, non-repeatable reads, phantom reads, and write skew.

questions.text: Which concurrency anomaly occurs when Transaction A reads uncommitted data written by Transaction B, which later rolls back?

options.text: Non-Repeatable Read
Dirty Read
Phantom Read
Write Skew

questions.explanation: A Dirty Read occurs when a transaction reads uncommitted changes from another concurrent transaction. Read Committed isolation prevents dirty reads.

questions.text: Under standard Snapshot Isolation (e.g. PostgreSQL Repeatable Read), which anomaly is NOT prevented?

options.text: Dirty Read
Non-Repeatable Read
Write Skew
Lost Update on a single row

questions.explanation: Snapshot Isolation prevents dirty reads, non-repeatable reads, phantom reads, and single-row lost updates (first-committer-wins). However, it allows Write Skew (where two concurrent transactions read overlapping disjoint sets and violate a shared cross-row invariant, such as doctor on-call shifts).

questions.text: How does Two-Phase Locking (2PL) differ from Two-Phase Commit (2PC)?

options.text: They are identical protocols used interchangeably
2PL is a concurrency control protocol to serialize local transactions; 2PC is an atomic commitment protocol across distributed nodes
2PL operates on replicas; 2PC operates on single instances
2PC acquires row locks; 2PL coordinates message queues

questions.explanation: 2PL (Growing phase acquiring locks, Shrinking phase releasing locks) ensures local transaction serializability. 2PC (Prepare phase, Commit/Abort phase) ensures all distributed nodes agree whether to commit or abort.

questions.text: How does Serializable Snapshot Isolation (SSI) in modern databases (like PostgreSQL) achieve true serializability without blocking read locks?

options.text: By executing all transactions sequentially on a single CPU core
By tracking rw-antidependencies (siREAD locks in memory) and aborting one transaction if a cycle of dependencies appears
By writing all reads to disk in a separate log file
By acquiring exclusive table locks on every SELECT query

questions.explanation: PostgreSQL SSI tracks read-write conflicts using non-blocking memory markers (SIREAD locks). It detects dangerous dependency structures (cycles in the serialization graph) and aborts one transaction with a serialization failure error.

questions.text: In PostgreSQL, a SELECT query inside a READ COMMITTED transaction takes a new snapshot at the start of each individual statement.

options.text: True
False

questions.explanation: True. In Read Committed mode, each statement within a transaction sees a new snapshot of committed data at the instant that statement begins. In Repeatable Read mode, the snapshot is taken once at the start of the first query and reused throughout the entire transaction.

design-patterns-creational-structural-be.title: GoF Design Patterns in Practice
design-patterns-creational-structural-be.description: Identify the exact design pattern needed to solve common software architecture and low-level design problems.

questions.text: You need to instantiate families of related UI widgets (e.g., WindowsButton + WindowsCheckbox vs MacButton + MacCheckbox) without hardcoding concrete classes in client code. Which pattern is best suited?

options.text: Factory Method
Abstract Factory
Builder
Prototype

questions.explanation: Abstract Factory provides an interface for creating families of related or dependent objects without specifying their concrete classes. Factory Method creates only one product at a time via inheritance, whereas Abstract Factory bundles multiple creation methods for an entire product family.

questions.text: A third-party billing library returns an incompatible interface from what your existing accounting domain expects. You want to bridge this gap without altering the vendor's source code. Which pattern should you use?

options.text: Adapter
Decorator
Proxy
Bridge

questions.explanation: Adapter converts the interface of a class into another interface that clients expect. It allows classes with incompatible interfaces to work together by wrapping the adaptee and translating calls between interfaces.

questions.text: You want to dynamically attach gzip compression, request logging, and rate limiting to an HTTP client without modifying the client or creating an explosion of subclasses. Which pattern is designed for this?

options.text: Composite
Decorator
Facade
Flyweight

questions.explanation: Decorator attaches additional responsibilities to an object dynamically. Decorators provide a flexible alternative to subclassing for extending functionality, sharing the exact same interface as the wrapped object and delegating calls through a chain of wrappers.

questions.text: What is the primary structural and intent difference between the Strategy pattern and the State pattern?

options.text: Strategy relies on multiple inheritance, whereas State uses single inheritance
Strategies are independent algorithms swapped by the client; States represent lifecycle phases where state objects trigger transitions to next states
State is a creational pattern, while Strategy is a structural pattern
There is no functional or architectural difference; they are exact duplicates

questions.explanation: While both Strategy and State share similar UML structures, their intent differs completely. In Strategy, algorithms are independent and the client selects which one to use; strategies rarely transition the context. In State, the context's behavior changes dynamically as its internal state changes, and state subclasses actively coordinate transitions to subsequent states.

questions.text: Which design pattern is used by web framework middleware pipelines (e.g., ASP.NET Core, Express) where an HTTP request is passed along a series of handlers that can each process or short-circuit the request?

options.text: Chain of Responsibility
Observer
Command
Mediator

questions.explanation: Chain of Responsibility passes a request along a chain of potential handlers. Upon receiving a request, each handler decides either to process the request and pass it to the next handler in the pipeline, or to short-circuit the chain and return a response immediately.

questions.text: Which of the following problems can be resolved or mitigated using the Command pattern?

options.text: Implementing multi-level Undo and Redo operations
Queueing and scheduling tasks for background execution
Logging operations to disk for transactional crash recovery
Eliminating virtual method table dispatch in the CPU cache

questions.explanation: The Command pattern encapsulates a request as a standalone object containing all information about the call. This makes it trivial to parameterize clients with different requests, queue or log requests, and support reversible undo/redo operations by storing execution history.

questions.text: A text editor needs to render 500,000 glyphs on screen without exhausting RAM. Most characters share the exact same font, size, and bitmap rendering data, differing only in line coordinates. Which pattern should be applied?

options.text: Flyweight
Prototype
Singleton
Proxy

questions.explanation: The Flyweight pattern minimizes memory usage by sharing as much common data as possible with other similar objects. It splits state into intrinsic state (shared, immutable font/bitmap data stored in the flyweight) and extrinsic state (context-dependent screen coordinates passed to methods).

questions.text: The Facade pattern alters the underlying interfaces of subsystem classes to enforce strict type checking on callers.

options.text: True
False

questions.explanation: False. A Facade provides a higher-level, simplified interface to an existing complex subsystem without modifying the subsystem's underlying classes or restricting direct access to them if advanced functionality is needed.

questions.text:
Examine the architectural box-joining diagram mapping GoF structural patterns (Boxes 1-4) with dashes `-- (dash) -->` to their runtime behaviors:
[Box 1: Decorator] -- (1) --> [Behavior A: Dynamically attaches responsibilities while keeping the exact same interface]
[Box 2: Adapter]   -- (2) --> [Behavior B: Translates one incompatible interface into an expected interface]
[Box 3: Proxy]     -- (3) --> [Behavior C: Controls lazy loading, access permissions, or remote network RPC]
[Box 4: Facade]    -- (4) --> [Behavior D: Provides a simplified high-level entryway over complex subsystem classes]
Which box-joining pairings correctly reflect the intent of the pattern?

options.text: Box 1 -- (1) --> Behavior A is correct (Decorator enhances behavior without changing the interface contract)
Box 2 -- (2) --> Behavior B is correct (Adapter bridges incompatible interfaces)
Box 3 -- (3) --> Behavior C is correct (Proxy controls and manages access to the real subject)
Box 4 -- (4) --> Behavior D is correct (Facade unifies and simplifies a complex subsystem)
Box 1 -- (1) --> Behavior B is correct (Decorator translates incompatible foreign APIs)

questions.explanation: Boxes 1, 2, 3, and 4 correctly describe Decorator, Adapter, Proxy, and Facade respectively. Option e is false because adapting incompatible APIs is the sole intent of the Adapter pattern.

questions.text: Fill in the blanks (denoted by dashes `___`): 'In the Singleton pattern, double-checked locking requires the instance field to be declared as _____ (volatile/final) to prevent CPU instruction _____, and a thread-safe DI container assigns the singleton a _____ lifetime.' Which statements are true regarding Singleton implementations?

options.text: Declaring the field volatile inserts a memory barrier, preventing out-of-order writes where another thread sees an allocated but uninitialized object
CPU instruction reordering can cause thread B to observe a non-null instance pointer before the constructor has finished executing
A DI container Singleton lives for the entire application process lifetime, avoiding manual double-checked locking boilerplate
Singletons make unit testing easier by sharing global state across all test runners

questions.explanation: Without `volatile`, instruction reordering can publish a pointer to allocated memory before constructor field initialization completes. DI containers manage thread-safe singletons cleanly without manual boilerplate. Singletons actually make unit testing harder due to shared state pollution.

questions.text: Which of the following statements correctly compare Factory Method, Abstract Factory, and Builder?

options.text: Factory Method delegates the creation of a single object to subclasses via inheritance
Abstract Factory creates entire families of related objects without specifying their concrete classes
Builder separates complex multi-step object construction and validation from its final representation
Abstract Factory is strictly used for asynchronous coroutines, while Builder is synchronous only

questions.explanation: Factory Method delegates instantiation of one product to subclasses. Abstract Factory creates families of related objects. Builder constructs complex objects step-by-step with parameter validation.

questions.text:
Review the following box-joining diagram connecting Behavioral patterns (Boxes 1-3) with dashes to their event dispatch models:
[Box 1: Observer]                -- (dash) --> [In-process, synchronous callback iteration across in-memory subscribers]
[Box 2: Publish-Subscribe]       -- (dash) --> [Decoupled, asynchronous event streaming through a central message broker]
[Box 3: Chain of Responsibility] -- (dash) --> [Sequential request propagation through a pipeline with short-circuiting]
Which of these connections are accurate?

options.text: Box 1 accurately describes synchronous in-memory subscriber dispatch
Box 2 accurately describes decoupled asynchronous broker streaming
Box 3 accurately describes sequential middleware pipelines
Box 1 accurately describes distributed Kafka topic consumers

questions.explanation: Observer is an in-memory synchronous pattern; Pub/Sub is distributed and asynchronous; Chain of Responsibility passes requests sequentially along a pipeline.

distributed-consensus-and-raft.title: Distributed consensus and the Raft protocol
distributed-consensus-and-raft.description: Leader elections, randomized timeouts, log matching invariants, quorums, and split-brain prevention in Raft.

questions.text: In Raft, why are election timeouts randomized across nodes (e.g. between 150ms and 300ms)?

options.text: To prevent split votes where multiple candidates simultaneously declare candidacy and split the majority quorum
To reduce network bandwidth consumption between follower heartbeats
To allow Byzantine faulty nodes to be detected and isolated
To balance CPU utilization evenly across the cluster

questions.explanation: Randomized election timeouts ensure that typically only one follower times out first, increments its term, and gathers a majority before others time out, preventing indefinite split-vote stalemates.

questions.text: What is the Raft Log Matching Invariant?

options.text: Every node must have the exact same number of uncommitted log entries at all times
If two entries in different logs have the same index and term, they store the same command and their logs are identical in all preceding entries
The leader only accepts writes if all follower logs match its log bit-for-bit
Follower logs must always be strictly longer than the candidate's log

questions.explanation: The Log Matching Invariant guarantees that if two logs agree on an entry at index `i` with term `t`, then all prior entries up to `i` are identical. AppendEntries consistency checks enforce this induction.

questions.text: A network partition splits a 5-node Raft cluster into a minority partition of 2 nodes (including the current leader L1) and a majority partition of 3 nodes. What happens when clients send writes to L1?

options.text: L1 commits the writes locally and acknowledges success to clients immediately
L1 crashes and shuts down immediately
L1 accepts the write into its uncommitted log but cannot commit it because it cannot reach a majority quorum (3 nodes), so it never acknowledges success
The minority partition promotes a second leader and splits the state machine permanently

questions.explanation: To commit an entry, a leader must replicate it to a strict majority ($\lfloor N/2 \rfloor + 1 = 3$ nodes). In the minority partition of 2 nodes, L1 cannot reach 3 acknowledgments, so writes remain uncommitted and safe.

questions.text: When a Raft follower receives a RequestVote RPC from candidate C, under which condition MUST the follower refuse to vote for C?

options.text: If candidate C's log is less up-to-date than the follower's own log (lower last term, or same term with fewer entries)
If candidate C has a higher node ID than the follower
If candidate C has sent more than 3 heartbeats in the current term
If candidate C's term number is greater than the follower's term

questions.explanation: Raft's Leader Completeness Property requires that any elected leader contains all committed entries. Followers reject candidate votes if the candidate's log is less up-to-date than their own.

questions.text: In Raft, a leader may directly commit an uncommitted log entry from a previous term once it is replicated on a majority of nodes.

options.text: True
False

questions.explanation: False (Raft Section 5.4.2). Raft never commits prior-term entries by simply counting replicas; doing so can lead to committed entries being overwritten after leader crashes. A leader only commits entries from its CURRENT term by counting replicas; prior entries are committed indirectly by the Log Matching Property.

distributed-tracing-and-observability.title: Distributed tracing and modern observability
distributed-tracing-and-observability.description: W3C Trace Context, OpenTelemetry, spans, context propagation, head vs tail sampling, and metric histograms.

questions.text: What are the two mandatory HTTP headers standardized by the W3C Trace Context specification for propagating distributed trace context across microservices?

options.text: X-B3-TraceId and X-B3-SpanId
traceparent and tracestate
X-Request-ID and X-Correlation-ID
OpenTelemetry-Context and OpenTelemetry-Span

questions.explanation: The W3C Trace Context standard defines `traceparent` (version, 16-byte trace-id, 8-byte parent-id, 1-byte trace-flags) and `tracestate` (opaque vendor-specific routing state). This replaces proprietary headers like Zipkin's X-B3.

questions.text: What is the primary difference between Head-Based Sampling and Tail-Based Sampling in distributed tracing systems?

options.text: Head sampling occurs in browser clients; tail sampling occurs on backend databases

Head sampling decides whether to record a trace at the root request ingress; Tail sampling buffers all spans of a trace and decides whether to keep it only after the entire request completes (e.g. keeping only errors or high-latency traces)
Head sampling samples HTTP traffic; tail sampling samples gRPC traffic
Head sampling is deterministic; tail sampling is random

questions.explanation: Head-based sampling makes an upfront decision at ingress, meaning rare 500 errors or P99 latency spikes might be dropped. Tail-based sampling buffers spans in an OpenTelemetry Collector collector tier and retains 100% of errors and slow traces while discarding uninteresting successful requests.

questions.text: In Prometheus metrics instrumentation, why is it dangerous to attach a high-cardinality label (such as `user_id` or `order_id`) to a metric counter or histogram?

options.text: Prometheus requires all labels to be integers
Each unique combination of label key-value pairs creates a brand new distinct time-series in memory, leading to severe memory exhaustion (cardinality explosion)
Prometheus does not support string labels
It prevents Grafana dashboards from rendering line charts

questions.explanation: Time-Series Databases (TSDB) store each unique metric name + label combination as an independent time-series. With 10 million users, adding `user_id` creates 10 million separate time-series, consuming gigabytes of TSDB index RAM and crashing Prometheus.

questions.text: In a distributed trace, what does a single 'Span' represent?

options.text: The entire lifecycle of a user session from login to logout
A single contiguous named unit of work (e.g. an HTTP handler, database query, or RPC call) with start time, end time, attributes, and events
The size of a TCP socket buffer in the kernel
A physical machine in a Kubernetes cluster

questions.explanation: A Span is the fundamental building block of a distributed trace. It represents a single operation (e.g. `SELECT * FROM users`), containing operation name, timestamps, status, key-value attributes, and parent span references.

questions.text: Context propagation in OpenTelemetry relies strictly on thread-local storage and cannot propagate across asynchronous thread pools, coroutines, or message queues without manual bridging.

options.text: True
False

questions.explanation: True. Thread-local storage does not automatically follow tasks dispatched across thread pool executors, reactive streams, or message queues (like Kafka). Developers or instrumentation agents must explicitly inject the context into message headers or carrier bags and extract it on the receiving thread.

docker-containers-and-ci-cd.title: Docker containers, cgroups, and CI/CD pipelines
docker-containers-and-ci-cd.description: Docker layer caching, multi-stage builds, Linux cgroups v2 resource limits, and CI/CD security.

questions.text: Why should 'COPY package*.json ./' and 'npm install' precede 'COPY . .' in a production Node.js Dockerfile?

options.text: To prevent npm from running as root
To leverage Docker layer caching: dependencies are only re-installed when package files change, speeding up CI builds when only application source code is modified
Because npm install requires an empty working directory
To minify JavaScript files automatically

questions.explanation: Docker caches intermediate layers. If `COPY . .` is executed first, any tiny change to a source file or README invalidates all subsequent layers, forcing an expensive and slow `npm install` on every single commit.

questions.text: What is the primary security advantage of Docker Multi-Stage builds for compiled or bundled languages (Go, Rust, Java, TypeScript)?

options.text: It encrypts container disk volumes at rest

It leaves compilers, build tools, package managers, and source code in the build stage, producing a minimal final runtime container (e.g. distroless or alpine) with a drastically reduced CVE attack surface
It enables GPU acceleration for backend microservices
It runs containers without Linux kernel namespaces

questions.explanation: Compilers (GCC, Rustc, Go SDK) and package managers contain thousands of utilities that attackers can abuse if a container is compromised. Multi-stage builds copy only the compiled static binary into a clean runtime base, reducing image size from 1GB to 25MB and eliminating vulnerable binaries.

questions.text: When a container in Kubernetes exceeds its configured 'resources.limits.memory', what action does the Linux kernel take?

options.text: It throttles container CPU cycles until memory usage subsides
The Linux cgroups Out-Of-Memory (OOM) Killer immediately sends SIGKILL (exit code 137) to terminate the primary container process
It automatically expands the node's physical RAM swap file
It writes active memory pages to disk without stopping execution

questions.explanation: Unlike CPU limits (which cause throttling via CFS bandwidth quotas), memory cannot be compressed. When a container exceeds its cgroup hard memory limit, the kernel OOM Killer immediately terminates it with `SIGKILL` (reported as `OOMKilled` / Exit Code 137 in Kubernetes).

questions.text: Why is running a containerized production backend as the default 'root' (UID 0) user considered a dangerous security antipattern?

options.text: Because root processes cannot open ports below 1024
Because container UID 0 is mapped directly to the host's UID 0; a container breakout vulnerability grants the attacker full root control over the underlying host node
Because Linux terminates root containers after 24 hours
Because root containers cannot read environment variables

questions.explanation: Unless user namespaces (userns-remap) are configured, root inside a container is root on the host machine. If an attacker exploits a remote code execution or container breakout flaw, they immediately gain kernel-level host access.

questions.text: In Linux cgroups v2, CPU limits do not kill the container; instead, the Completely Fair Scheduler (CFS) throttles CPU time slices within the enforcement period.

options.text: True
False

questions.explanation: True. If a container exceeds its CPU limit (e.g. 500m / 0.5 CPU cores), the CFS scheduler simply halts thread execution until the next 100ms quota period begins, causing latency spikes without process termination.

docker-images-containers-and-volumes.title: Docker images, containers, volumes and networks
docker-images-containers-and-volumes.description: Image layers, the writable container layer, what survives a stop or a remove, and how containers reach each other.

questions.text: When Docker creates a container from an image, what does it add on top of the image's read-only layers?

options.text: A full copy of every image layer, so the container can change them freely
One thin writable layer that belongs to that container
A new read-only layer for each process the container starts
A separate virtual disk that replaces the image's filesystem

questions.explanation: Image layers stay read-only and are shared; each container gets only a thin writable layer on top. Copying every layer (option a) is exactly what the layered design avoids, and it would multiply disk use per container.

questions.text: You already have an image built FROM python:3.12-slim and you pull a second image that uses the same base. Why is the second pull fast?

options.text: Docker compresses the second image more aggressively
Docker skips verifying the second image against the registry
The second image is automatically merged into the first one
Layers are content-addressed and shared, so only the layers you do not already have are downloaded

questions.explanation: Identical base layers are stored once and reused, so Docker downloads only the missing ones. The images stay separate; nothing is merged, and nothing is skipped on the verification side.

questions.text: A file written inside a container's filesystem is still there after docker stop followed by docker start on the same container.

options.text: True
False

questions.explanation: stop and start reuse the same container, including its writable layer. The file is lost only when the container is removed with docker rm and a new one is created.

questions.text: A database container must keep its data after the container is deleted with docker rm and replaced by a fresh docker run. What should you do?

options.text: Let it write to its writable layer and use docker stop instead of docker rm
Add EXPOSE for the data directory in the Dockerfile
Mount a named volume at the database's data directory
Publish the data directory with -p

questions.explanation: A named volume is storage Docker manages outside any container, so it outlives docker rm. The writable layer is deleted with the container, and EXPOSE and -p only deal with network ports, not files.

questions.text: Container svcB runs ping svcA and gets 'bad address'. Both containers were started with docker run and no --network flag. What is the most likely fix?

options.text: Create a user-defined bridge network and start both containers on it, so names resolve through Docker's DNS
Publish svcA with -p so svcB can find it by name
Restart svcB so that it re-reads the hosts file
Switch both containers to the host network and use localhost

questions.explanation: The default bridge network does not resolve container names; a user-defined bridge does. Publishing a port only opens it to the host, so it does nothing for name resolution between containers.

questions.text: Which statements about container networking are correct? Select all that apply.

options.text: A server listening on port 8000 in a container answers at localhost:8000 on the host even when -p was not used
localhost inside a container refers to that container's own loopback, not the host
Two containers on a user-defined network should call each other on the host-published port, for example web:8080 after -p 8080:8000
On a shared user-defined network, another container can reach the app as http://web:8000 using its name and container port

questions.explanation: Each container has its own network namespace, so localhost means itself, and peers on a user-defined network use the container name with the container port. The published host port only matters for traffic coming in from outside the container network, and without -p nothing is listening on the host's localhost:8000, so option a is wrong.

questions.text: You ran docker run -d --name broken webapp python -c "print('hi')" and the container shows Exited (0) almost at once, although the image normally starts a Flask server. Why?

options.text: The command after the image name replaced the image's CMD, and that short command finished immediately
The -d flag only works with the image's default command
Python is missing from the image, so the container could not start
The port was not published, so Docker stopped the container

questions.explanation: A container lives only as long as its main process. Overriding CMD with a one-shot command leaves nothing running, and exit code 0 shows it finished normally rather than crashing. Missing Python would give an error and a non-zero exit code.

questions.text: Installing a package inside a running container with docker exec changes the image that the container was started from.

options.text: True
False

questions.explanation: Images are read-only. The change lands in that container's writable layer only, so a container started later from the same image will not have the package; to keep it, add it to the Dockerfile and rebuild.

embeddings-and-vector-search.title: Embeddings and vector search
embeddings-and-vector-search.description: Comparing embeddings with cosine, dot product and L2, why high dimensions behave oddly, chunk sizes, and how pgvector's approximate indexes behave.

questions.text: All the stored vectors and the query are normalised to length 1. Which statement about ranking results is correct?

options.text: Cosine similarity and dot product rank documents differently, because dot product also rewards length
Only cosine similarity gives a stable ranking; L2 distance depends on the query's length
Cosine descending, dot product descending and L2 distance ascending all return the same documents in the same order
L1 (Manhattan) distance is also guaranteed to give the same ranking, because it is a function of the angle

questions.explanation: For unit vectors cosine equals the dot product, and squared L2 distance is 2 - 2*cos, so all three orderings agree. L1 is not a function of the angle and can rank differently even on unit vectors.

questions.text: In pgvector, what does `SELECT id FROM chunks ORDER BY embedding <#> $1 DESC LIMIT 5` return?

options.text: The five most similar chunks, as you would expect from DESC
The five least similar chunks, because <#> is the negative inner product and so already sorts most-similar-first in ascending order
The five chunks closest by cosine distance
An error, because <#> cannot be used in ORDER BY

questions.explanation: Postgres index scans only go ascending, so pgvector negates the inner product. Adding DESC flips it and puts the least similar rows first, and it would also stop an index from being used.

questions.text: A similarity cutoff of 0.8 tuned for cosine similarity can be reused unchanged as a cutoff on L2 distance, because both measure how alike two embeddings are.

options.text: True
False

questions.explanation: The orderings can agree on unit vectors, but the numbers differ. For unit vectors a cosine of 0.8 is an L2 distance of about 0.63, and the direction is reversed (higher cosine is better, lower distance is better). A threshold does not transfer between metrics.

questions.text: What happens to the distances between random points as the number of dimensions grows very large?

options.text: Nearest and farthest neighbours become further apart in relative terms, so search gets easier
Distances shrink toward zero for every pair of points
Distances become exactly equal, so ranking is impossible in principle
The nearest and farthest points end up at almost the same distance, so absolute scores bunch together and fixed thresholds become fragile

questions.explanation: Distance concentration: the relative spread of distances shrinks roughly like 1/sqrt(D). They do not become exactly equal and real embeddings still work because real data has low intrinsic dimension, but you should tune cutoffs on your own labelled queries.

questions.text: A migration creates a table and, in the same step, an IVFFlat index on its empty vector column. The data is loaded afterwards. What is the likely outcome?

options.text: The index works and returns rows without an error, but recall is poor because its clusters were built from no data
Postgres refuses to create the index
The index rebuilds itself automatically as rows arrive
Queries fall back to an exact scan, so results are perfect but slow

questions.explanation: IVFFlat runs k-means over the rows that exist when it is built. On an empty table there is nothing to cluster, so you get only a notice, not an error. Load the data first, then create the index. HNSW has no such training step.

questions.text: Adding an approximate vector index (HNSW or IVFFlat) to a table can change the results of an existing query, unlike a B-tree index.

options.text: True
False

questions.explanation: A B-tree only changes speed. An approximate index returns the probably-nearest rows, so recall can drop. This is why exact search is used as ground truth when measuring recall.

questions.text: A filtered vector query (WHERE category = 'x' ORDER BY embedding <=> $1 LIMIT 10) on an HNSW index often returns fewer than 10 rows, because the filter runs after the index scan. Which fixes does the lesson describe? Select all that apply.

options.text: Index the filter column, so Postgres can search the matching rows directly
Turn on iterative index scans, so the scan continues until enough rows are found
Lower hnsw.ef_search so the index returns fewer candidates
Put the category condition inside the ORDER BY expression

questions.explanation: The index returns about ef_search candidates and the filter then discards non-matching ones. Indexing the filter column or using iterative scans helps. A lower ef_search makes it worse, and extra expressions in ORDER BY stop the vector index being used at all.

questions.text: An embedding model has a 256-token input limit, but your chunker produces 384-token chunks. What happens?

options.text: The model automatically splits each chunk into two vectors
Every embedding call fails with an error in all cases
Many models silently truncate, so the vector describes only the first 256 tokens while the LLM would still be sent all 384
The vector is built from all 384 tokens, just less precisely

questions.explanation: Sentence-Transformers models truncate text past their max sequence length, so the end of each chunk is invisible to search (some hosted APIs reject over-long input instead). Size chunks in the embedding model's own tokens with a margin.

git-branching-merging-and-rebasing.title: Git branching, merging and rebasing
git-branching-merging-and-rebasing.description: How branches and HEAD work, how merge and rebase differ, and how to undo mistakes safely with revert, reset and the reflog.

questions.text: You are on main and run git switch -c fix, then make one commit. Which statement is true afterwards?

options.text: Both main and fix point to the new commit, because they started at the same place
Only fix moves to the new commit; HEAD follows it and main stays where it was
main moves to the new commit and fix stays put, because main was checked out first
Neither branch moves until the commit has been pushed to a remote

questions.explanation: A branch is just a movable pointer to a commit, and a new commit moves only the branch that HEAD currently follows. After git switch -c fix that branch is fix, so main stays on the older commit, and nothing needs to be pushed for any of this to happen.

questions.text: Nobody has committed to main since you created feature from it, and feature has two new commits. You are on main and run git merge feature. What happens?

options.text: Git fast-forwards main to feature's latest commit and creates no new commit
Git creates a merge commit with two parents, because every merge makes one
Git replays your two commits as brand-new commits on top of main
Git stops with a conflict, because both branches have changed since they split

questions.explanation: Because main is an ancestor of feature, Git has nothing to combine and just slides the main pointer forward. A merge commit with two parents appears only when both branches have new commits, or when you ask for one with --no-ff. Replaying commits as new ones is what rebase does, not merge.

questions.text: Your feature branch is already pushed and a teammate has started working on top of it. You are tempted to run git rebase main on it. What is the main danger?

options.text: It squashes all of your commits into a single one, which hides what each separate change was for
It always produces merge conflicts, even when the changes on the two branches do not overlap
It cannot be undone once it has started, so any mistake destroys your work for good, with no way back
It gives your commits new hashes, so pushing needs a force-push that can erase your teammate's work

questions.explanation: Rebase replays your commits as new ones with new hashes, so history your teammate already has is replaced, and the push needs a force-push that can overwrite what they based their work on. Rebase your own unpublished branches freely and merge shared ones. It can be aborted midway and undone through the reflog, and it keeps your commits and messages.

questions.text: Two branches each edited app.py, one near the top of the file and one near the bottom. What happens when you merge them?

options.text: Git always reports a conflict, because both branches changed the same file
Git keeps the version from the branch you are on and silently drops the other change
Git combines both edits automatically, because they touch different lines
Git refuses to merge until one branch has been rebased onto the other

questions.explanation: Git merges line by line against the common ancestor, so edits to different parts of a file combine cleanly. A conflict appears only when both sides changed the same lines differently; then Git marks them in the file, and you edit the result, git add it and commit, or run git merge --abort to back out.

questions.text: You committed too early and want to undo that commit but keep all of its changes staged, ready to commit again. Which command does that?

options.text: git reset --soft HEAD~1
git reset --mixed HEAD~1
git reset --hard HEAD~1
git revert HEAD

questions.explanation: --soft moves the branch back one commit but leaves both the staging area and the files as they were, so the changes stay staged. --mixed (the default) also unstages them, --hard throws the changes away, and git revert makes a new commit that undoes the old one instead of removing it.

questions.text: A bad commit has already been pushed to the shared main branch and other people have pulled it. What is the safest way to undo its effect?

options.text: Run git reset --hard on main and then force-push the result to the remote
Run git revert on the bad commit and push the new commit it creates
Delete main on the remote and push a fresh copy from your clone
Use git rebase -i to drop the commit, then force-push main to the remote

questions.explanation: git revert adds a new commit that reverses the bad one, so history only moves forward and everyone's copy stays consistent. Reset or an interactive rebase followed by a force-push rewrites commits that others already have, which breaks their clones and can erase their work.

questions.text: Which of these can you usually get back with the help of git reflog?

options.text: Edits you made to a file but never staged or committed, discarded by git reset --hard
Commits that a git reset --hard made unreachable from your branch
Commits that exist only in a teammate's clone and were never fetched
The tip of a local branch you deleted by mistake with git branch -D
The commits as they were before a rebase went wrong

questions.explanation: The reflog is a local log of where HEAD and your branch tips have been, so commits that a reset, a rebase or a branch deletion left unreachable can be found there (until Git eventually cleans them up) and restored with git reset or git branch. Changes that were never committed were never recorded, and commits in another person's clone never passed through your reflog.

questions.text: Which statements about everyday Git commands are true?

options.text: git stash saves your changes to tracked files and leaves a clean working tree; git stash pop brings them back
git stash also saves new untracked files by default, so nothing is left behind
git cherry-pick copies one commit's change onto the current branch as a new commit with its own hash
A tag, unlike a branch, keeps pointing at the same commit when new commits are made
Deleting a branch with git branch -d removes its commits from the repository straight away

questions.explanation: A stash records changes to tracked files (add -u to include untracked ones), cherry-pick re-applies one commit as a new commit, and a tag is a fixed label on one commit while a branch moves forward. Deleting a branch removes only the pointer, so its commits stay in the repository until garbage collection.

questions.text: A path in .gitignore only stops Git from picking up untracked files; a file that was already committed stays tracked until you remove it from the index, for example with git rm --cached.

options.text: True
False

questions.explanation: Ignore rules apply only to files Git is not tracking yet, so adding a committed file to .gitignore changes nothing about it. git rm --cached stops tracking the file while leaving it on disk, but earlier commits still contain it, so a leaked secret must be rotated rather than just ignored.

questions.text: Putting a bug fix, a rename and a formatting change into one commit is fine, because Git can revert or cherry-pick any one of those changes on its own.

options.text: True
False

questions.explanation: Git reverts, cherry-picks and bisects whole commits, so a mixed commit forces you to take or undo all three changes together and makes review harder. Keeping each commit to one logical change is what makes those tools useful.

http-caching.title: HTTP caching
http-caching.description: The headers that decide whether a browser or a CDN may reuse a response.

questions.text: Which pair of headers lets a client check cheaply whether its cached copy is still current?

options.text: Content-Length and Host
ETag and If-None-Match
Accept and Vary
Cookie and Set-Cookie

questions.explanation: The client sends the ETag it holds in If-None-Match. If it still matches, the server answers 304 Not Modified with no body.

questions.text: Cache-Control: no-store means the response may be cached but must be revalidated before reuse.

options.text: True
False

questions.explanation: That describes no-cache. no-store tells caches not to keep the response at all.

questions.text: Which header lets a shared cache such as a CDN keep a response for an hour?

options.text: Cache-Control: private, max-age=3600
Cache-Control: public, max-age=3600
Cache-Control: no-store
Pragma: no-cache

questions.explanation: max-age gives the lifetime in seconds, and public explicitly allows shared caches such as a CDN to store the response. private would keep it to the user's own browser, and no-store and Pragma: no-cache ask caches not to reuse it.

questions.text: Which responses should usually NOT be stored in a shared cache? Select all that apply.

options.text: A logged-in user's account page
A fingerprinted JavaScript bundle
A response that sets a session cookie with Set-Cookie
A public product image

questions.explanation: Personalised responses and anything that sets a session must not be served to another user. Static, versioned assets are the ideal thing to cache.

questions.text: A file is named app.3f9a1c.js, where the hash changes whenever the content does. Which caching fits?

options.text: no-store
A very long max-age with immutable
max-age=0
A short max-age of 5 seconds

questions.explanation: A new version gets a new name, so the old name can be cached for a year. That is the standard way to combine long caching with instant deploys.

questions.text: A response says Cache-Control: max-age=60. A cache holds a copy that is 20 seconds old and a client asks for it again. What should the cache do?

options.text: Serve its stored copy without contacting the server, because the copy is still fresh
Send If-None-Match to the server first, because every reuse must be validated
Fetch the full response again, because max-age only applies to the first request
Refuse to serve it, because 20 seconds is more than zero

questions.explanation: For 60 seconds after it was fetched the copy is fresh, so it is reused with no request to the server at all. After that it is stale and has to be revalidated or refetched. Validating on every reuse is what no-cache asks for, not max-age.

questions.text: Your endpoint returns gzip-compressed or plain bodies depending on the request's Accept-Encoding header, and a CDN sits in front of it. Which response header stops the CDN from serving a gzip body to a client that cannot decode it?

options.text: Vary: Accept-Encoding
Cache-Control: immutable
If-None-Match
Last-Modified

questions.explanation: Vary lists the request headers that change the response, so a shared cache stores one copy per distinct value and picks the right one. Without it the cache keys only on the URL and can hand the wrong representation to someone. If-None-Match is a request header, and Last-Modified and immutable say nothing about which representation was sent.

questions.text: GET /profile returns the logged-in user's email address and is sent with Cache-Control: public, max-age=3600. What is the problem, and the fix?

options.text: A CDN or proxy may store the response and serve it to the next person who asks for /profile; mark it private (and no-store if it should not be kept at all)
The browser will never cache it, so add an ETag
Nothing, because a shared cache always checks the login before serving a stored copy
The max-age is too short, so raise it to a year

questions.explanation: public lets shared caches keep the response for an hour, and they key it by URL, not by user, so one user's data can be handed to another. Per-user responses should be private, and often no-store as well. A shared cache does not know about your login system.

http-methods-status-codes-and-rest.title: HTTP methods, status codes and REST
http-methods-status-codes-and-rest.description: Which method and which status code to use, what safe and idempotent mean, and how to model an API around resources.

questions.text: Which methods are both safe and idempotent? Select all that apply.

options.text: GET
HEAD
PUT
POST

questions.explanation: GET and HEAD only read, so they change nothing and repeating them changes nothing. PUT is idempotent but not safe because it modifies state, and POST is neither.

questions.text: User 42 has a name and an email. A client sends PUT /users/42 with the body {"email": "new@example.com"} only. What does PUT semantics say should happen?

options.text: Only the email changes and the name is kept
The server must reject the request with 405
The resource is replaced by the body, so the omitted name is erased
A second user is created

questions.explanation: PUT replaces the whole resource at a known URL with the representation you send, so omitted fields are lost. Changing just one field is what PATCH is for.

questions.text: A POST /users request successfully creates a new user. What is the conventional response?

options.text: 200 OK with an empty body
202 Accepted with a Retry-After header
204 No Content
201 Created with a Location header pointing at the new user

questions.explanation: 201 says a new resource now exists and Location tells the client where. 202 is for work accepted but not yet done, and 204 means success with deliberately no body, the usual answer to a DELETE.

questions.text: A logged-in user who is not an admin calls DELETE /users/42. Which status code fits best?

options.text: 401 Unauthorized
403 Forbidden
400 Bad Request
500 Internal Server Error

questions.explanation: The server knows who the caller is but they are not allowed to do this, which is 403. 401 despite its name means unauthenticated, no valid credentials at all. (Some APIs answer 404 instead, to avoid revealing that the resource exists, but 403 is the standard answer for 'known caller, not allowed'.)

questions.text: Which responses suggest that sending the same request again later might succeed? Select all that apply.

options.text: 503 Service Unavailable
404 Not Found for a path that does not exist
400 Bad Request for malformed JSON
504 Gateway Timeout

questions.explanation: 5xx codes say the server or something behind it failed, so the request itself may be fine. 4xx codes blame the request, and repeating an unchanged malformed or misdirected request will fail the same way.

questions.text: It is fine for an API to return 200 OK with a body like {"error": "not found"}, because clients can read the body.

options.text: True
False

questions.explanation: Caches, retry logic, proxies and monitoring all act on the status code, so a smiling 200 hides failures and may even be cached. The status line is the contract; the body adds detail.

questions.text: Which design best fits REST for cancelling order 42?

options.text: PATCH /orders/42 with {"status": "cancelled"}
POST /cancelOrder with {"id": 42}
GET /orders/42/cancel
PUT /orders/42 with only {"status": "cancelled"} as the body

questions.explanation: REST models state changes as changes to a resource rather than verbs in the URL, and PATCH edits just the status. A GET that cancels violates safety, since crawlers and prefetchers issue GETs, and /cancelOrder is the RPC style REST avoids. PUT would replace the whole order, erasing every field you left out.

questions.text: A client tries to register with an email address that already belongs to another user. Which status code fits best?

options.text: 404 Not Found
304 Not Modified
409 Conflict
503 Service Unavailable

questions.explanation: 409 means the request clashes with the current state of the resource. 404 would say the thing does not exist, and 5xx codes would wrongly blame the server.

idempotency-and-retries.title: Idempotency and retries
idempotency-and-retries.description: What makes a request safe to send twice, and how a server remembers that it already did the work.

questions.text: A client times out on a payment request and sends it again. What makes the retry safe?

options.text: Sending it again faster
An idempotency key the server uses to return the first result instead of charging twice
Switching from POST to GET
Closing the connection before retrying

questions.explanation: The client cannot know whether the first request reached the server. A key that identifies the operation lets the server detect the repeat and answer with the stored result.

questions.text: PUT and DELETE are idempotent by the definition of HTTP semantics.

options.text: True
False

questions.explanation: Repeating a PUT leaves the resource in the same state, and repeating a DELETE leaves it deleted. (The response may differ: a second DELETE can answer 404.)

questions.text: Which of these can be retried without any extra protection? Select all that apply.

options.text: GET /users/42
POST /payments with no idempotency key
PUT /users/42 with the full document
DELETE /orders/7

questions.explanation: GET, PUT and DELETE are idempotent. A POST that creates something is not, unless the server is given a key to deduplicate on.

questions.text: Where should an idempotency key and the result of its first request be stored?

options.text: In the client only
In durable storage shared by every server, with the key under a unique constraint
In each server's memory
In the URL

questions.explanation: A retry may reach a different server, or the same one after a restart. Shared durable storage and a unique constraint also settle two retries arriving at once.

questions.text: It is fine to reuse the same idempotency key for a request with a different body.

options.text: True
False

questions.explanation: A key names one operation. The server should reject a reused key whose request differs, rather than return the first answer to an unrelated request.

questions.text: A message consumer receives the same "order 7 was paid" event twice because the queue delivers at least once. Which handler is naturally safe to run twice, with no extra bookkeeping?

options.text: UPDATE orders SET status = 'paid' WHERE id = 7
UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance + 50 WHERE id = 3
INSERT INTO ledger (account, delta) VALUES (3, 50) with an auto-increment id
Send the customer a receipt email

questions.explanation: Setting a value to its final state gives the same result however many times it runs. A relative change (balance + 50), an insert with a fresh id and an email each repeat their effect, so they need a stable event id and a record of what was processed.

jwt-oauth-and-oidc.title: JWT, OAuth 2.0 and OpenID Connect
jwt-oauth-and-oidc.description: What a JWT does and does not guarantee, how short-lived tokens limit damage, and how OAuth 2.0 and OpenID Connect hand out access and identity safely.

questions.text: Which statements about a signed JWT are true?

options.text: Its payload is only base64url encoded, so anyone who holds the token can read it
A valid signature shows that the header and payload have not been changed since signing
Signing also encrypts the token, so secrets in the payload stay hidden from anyone who intercepts it
A valid signature proves that the person presenting the token is the user it was issued to

questions.explanation: A signed JWT is three base64url parts, and the signature only detects tampering: it hides nothing, so never put passwords or other secrets in the payload. A bearer token works for whoever holds it, so a valid signature says nothing about who is presenting it.

questions.text: Your API accepts a JWT after checking only its signature, with no database lookup, so it cannot tell whether a token has been revoked. Which setup best limits the damage from a stolen access token?

options.text: A long expiry, so users have to sign in less often and the token is exposed less
A revoked flag inside the payload, which the server sets as soon as a user logs out
A short expiry, with a refresh token that the authorization server can revoke
A stronger signing algorithm, so that a stolen token cannot be used

questions.explanation: A short lifetime means a stolen access token stops working within minutes, while the longer-lived refresh token goes only to the authorization server, which can revoke it. A signed token cannot be edited after it is issued, so a flag inside it can never change, and a stronger algorithm prevents forgery, not the use of a genuine token that was stolen.

questions.text: A server should verify a JWT with whichever algorithm the token's own header names, because the token knows how it was signed.

options.text: True
False

questions.explanation: The header is written by whoever built the token, so trusting it lets an attacker choose alg none (no signature at all) or switch RS256 to HS256 and sign with your public key as if it were a shared secret. The server must fix the allowed algorithms and keys itself.

questions.text: A browser app has to keep a session token somewhere. What is the trade-off between an HttpOnly, Secure, SameSite cookie and localStorage?

options.text: The cookie hides the token from scripts but needs CSRF defences; localStorage exposes it to any script
localStorage is safer, because it is never sent automatically and an injected script cannot read it
The cookie is always safer, because modern browsers make forged cross-site requests impossible by default
They are equally safe, since the same-origin policy and HTTPS protect both in the same way

questions.explanation: An HttpOnly cookie cannot be read by page scripts, so an XSS bug cannot simply copy the token, but the browser attaches it to requests automatically, so you still need SameSite or CSRF tokens. localStorage is the reverse: nothing is sent automatically, yet any script on the page, including an injected one, can read it.

questions.text: A photo-printing website asks to read a user's photos from a cloud storage service. After the user approves, which party issues the access token?

options.text: The photo-printing website, since it is the application that will use the token
The user, since the user owns the photos and grants permission by approving the request
The storage API that holds the photos, since the app will call it with the token
The storage service's authorization server, once it has signed the user in

questions.explanation: The authorization server authenticates the user, records their consent and issues the tokens. The website is only the client, the storage API is the resource server that checks the tokens it is given, and the user is the resource owner who grants permission; none of those three mints tokens.

questions.text: In the authorization code flow with PKCE, why can someone who only intercepted the authorization code not exchange it for tokens?

options.text: The code can only be sent to the registered redirect URI, so a copy anywhere else is useless
The exchange also needs the code_verifier, which only the app that started the flow knows
The code is bound to the state value, which an attacker has no way of guessing in time
The app proves itself with a client secret compiled into its code, which cannot be extracted

questions.explanation: At the start the app sends a hash of a random secret (the code_challenge); to redeem the code it must present the original secret (the code_verifier), which the server checks against that hash. The state value only defends the callback against forged requests, a registered redirect URI does not help once the redirect itself is intercepted, and a secret compiled into a public app is not really secret.

questions.text: Current security guidance tells browser apps to use the authorization code flow with PKCE rather than the implicit flow. What is the main reason?

options.text: The implicit flow requires a client secret, and a browser app has no safe place to keep one
Access tokens from the implicit flow cannot be JWTs, so APIs have no way to validate them
The implicit flow puts the access token itself in the redirect URL, where it can leak
The implicit flow has no way to ask for scopes, so every token it issues has full access

questions.explanation: In the implicit flow the access token comes back in the browser's address bar, where history, extensions and injected scripts can reach it, and nothing proves it went to the app that asked for it. The code flow returns only a short-lived code that is swapped for tokens over a direct HTTPS call, protected by the PKCE verifier. The implicit flow never used a client secret at all.

questions.text: A user approves a calendar app for the scope calendar.read. The app then calls DELETE /events/42 with its access token. What should the API do?

options.text: Allow it, because the signed-in user is allowed to delete their own events
Reject it, because the scopes in the token do not cover deleting events
Allow it, because scopes only shape the consent screen and APIs do not enforce them
Ask the authorization server to add the missing scope, then carry on with the request

questions.explanation: A scope is what the user approved this client to do with this token, so it limits the app even though the user could delete the event themselves, and the API has to check it on every request. Claims such as sub or email are facts about the user or the token; they do not grant anything on their own.

questions.text: Which statements about the state and nonce values in an OpenID Connect login are correct?

options.text: The app creates a random state before the redirect and rejects any callback whose state does not match
The nonce comes back inside the ID token, so the app can tell the token answers its own login request
State and nonce are secret keys that the authorization server uses to sign the ID token
State is needed only for clients with no client secret, and nonce only for clients that have one

questions.explanation: State ties the callback to the browser session that started the login, so an attacker cannot push their own authorization code into your session. The nonce is carried inside the ID token and ties that token to the request, which defeats replay. Both are random, single-use values rather than keys, and they are worth using whether or not the client has a secret.

questions.text: An OpenID Connect ID token is the credential an app should send to its backend API to prove that the user may call it.

options.text: True
False

questions.explanation: The ID token is meant for the client app: it says who signed in, and its audience is that app. The API should receive the access token, whose audience is the API, and reject anything else. OAuth 2.0 alone does not tell an app who the user is; OpenID Connect adds that with the ID token.

kafka-streaming-internals.title: Apache Kafka and event streaming architecture
kafka-streaming-internals.description: In-Sync Replicas (ISR), High Watermark, KRaft consensus, idempotent producer deduplication, and sticky rebalances.

questions.text: In an Apache Kafka topic with replication factor 3 and min.insync.replicas=2, how does a producer with acks=all behave?

options.text: The write succeeds only if all 3 replicas acknowledge receipt
The write succeeds as long as at least 2 in-sync replicas (including the leader) acknowledge receipt; if only 1 replica is in-sync, writes are rejected with NotEnoughReplicasException
The write is acknowledged immediately by the leader without waiting for followers
The write is stored in OS page cache on the leader and flushed to disk asynchronously

questions.explanation: With `acks=all`, the leader waits for all current in-sync replicas to acknowledge. If follower crashes drop the ISR size below `min.insync.replicas` (2), the broker rejects further writes to guarantee durability against leader crashes.

questions.text: What is the difference between a partition's Log End Offset (LEO) and its High Watermark (HW)?

options.text: LEO is the offset of the next record to be written by the leader; High Watermark is the highest offset replicated across all in-sync replicas and visible to consumers
High Watermark is the next record written; LEO is the consumer offset
LEO is only tracked on followers; High Watermark is only tracked on the controller
There is no difference; they are aliases for the same offset integer

questions.explanation: LEO represents the end of the leader's local append-only log. The High Watermark (HW) lags behind LEO until followers catch up; consumers are strictly forbidden from reading past the High Watermark to prevent dirty reads if an un-replicated leader crashes.

questions.text: How does Kafka's Idempotent Producer guarantee exactly-once message delivery per partition without duplicate records?

options.text: By calculating an MD5 hash of the payload and storing it in Redis
The broker assigns a unique Producer ID (PID); each message carries a monotonically increasing Sequence Number that the broker deduplicates
By executing a Two-Phase Commit transaction with all active consumers
By delaying message acknowledgment by 5 seconds to detect duplicates

questions.explanation: With `enable.idempotence=true`, the broker assigns a 64-bit Producer ID (PID). For each partition, the producer tags records with consecutive sequence numbers ($0, 1, 2, \dots$). If a network retry occurs, the broker recognizes that sequence number $K$ was already committed and ignores the duplicate.

questions.text: What major architectural improvement does the KRaft (Kafka Raft) metadata mode introduce over the legacy ZooKeeper architecture?

options.text: It eliminates the external ZooKeeper cluster, running Raft-based metadata consensus directly inside Kafka brokers for instantaneous metadata failover and support for millions of partitions
It compresses message payloads with Zstandard by default
It removes consumer groups in favor of direct socket streaming
It mandates schema validation via JSON schema

questions.explanation: KRaft stores metadata in an event-sourced, append-only metadata log managed directly by controller quorum nodes running Raft. This removes the ZooKeeper synchronization bottleneck, enabling rapid controller elections and scaling to tens of millions of partitions.

questions.text: In Kafka consumer groups, the Cooperative Sticky Assignor avoids the 'stop-the-world' pause of eager rebalancing by revoking only the specific partitions being moved.

options.text: True
False

questions.explanation: True. Eager rebalancing forces all consumers to revoke all partitions and stop processing during rebalances. Cooperative Sticky rebalancing uses a phased approach: consumers continue processing untouched partitions while only reassigned partitions are migrated.

kubernetes-networking-and-operations.title: Kubernetes Networking, Pod Lifecycle, and Operations
kubernetes-networking-and-operations.description: Test your deep knowledge of Kubernetes cluster networking, CNI implementations, pod graceful shutdown sequences, and service routing mechanisms.

questions.text: Why do large Kubernetes clusters (thousands of services and pods) typically switch `kube-proxy` from `iptables` mode to `IPVS` mode?

options.text: IPVS enforces mutual TLS (mTLS) natively in kernel space without sidecar proxies
iptables evaluates routing rules linearly in O(n) time, whereas IPVS uses kernel hash tables providing O(1) packet lookup regardless of service count
iptables cannot support HTTP/2 and gRPC streams, while IPVS operates at Layer 7
IPVS eliminates the need for a CNI plugin by directly handling container network interfaces

questions.explanation: In clusters with tens of thousands of services, `iptables` rule evaluation degrades significantly because rules are organized as a sequential list ($O(n)$ packet traversal) and synchronized by re-generating the entire table. IPVS uses kernel IP set hash tables, offering $O(1)$ packet matching and negligible sync overhead under high churn.

questions.text: When a Kubernetes Pod is deleted, which sequence of events accurately describes the lifecycle of traffic termination and container shutdown?

options.text: The container receives SIGKILL immediately, then kube-proxy removes the IP from Service endpoints
Pod state becomes Terminating; endpoints controller asynchronously removes the Pod IP from endpoints while the container executes preStop hooks and receives SIGTERM concurrently
All active TCP connections are severed by the Linux kernel, then kubelet sends SIGTERM
kubelet waits until all inbound HTTP requests return status 200 before sending SIGTERM

questions.explanation: Pod deletion triggers two parallel workflows: the Endpoints/EndpointSlice controller detects deletion and propagates IP removal to kube-proxy/ingress, while kubelet executes the container's `preStop` hook and sends SIGTERM. Because endpoint propagation takes several seconds, applications typically add a short preStop sleep (e.g. 5-10s) to avoid receiving new connections after SIGTERM.

questions.text: What is the primary operational characteristic and use case of a Kubernetes 'Headless Service' (`clusterIP: None`)?

options.text: It bypasses kube-proxy VIP allocation; DNS queries for the service name return direct A/AAAA/SRV records for individual matching Pod IPs, enabling peer discovery for stateful distributed databases
It exposes pods directly to the public internet without an ingress controller or cloud load balancer
It prevents pods from making outbound internet requests to ensure PCI-DSS compliance
It runs the pod directly on the host network namespace without a container veth pair

questions.explanation: Headless services do not allocate a ClusterIP virtual IP and do not perform load balancing via kube-proxy. CoreDNS returns the set of actual Pod IPs associated with the selector, allowing stateful systems (e.g., Kafka, Cassandra, ZooKeeper) to directly discover and communicate with specific peers.

questions.text: What is the key performance trade-off between an overlay CNI (e.g., Flannel/Calico with VXLAN) and a cloud-native flat routed CNI (e.g., AWS VPC CNI, GKE Alias IPs)?

options.text: Overlay networks have zero MTU overhead, whereas flat networks encapsulate every packet in UDP

Overlay networks wrap inner packet headers with outer UDP/VXLAN headers causing MTU reduction and CPU encapsulation cost; flat routed networks assign native VPC IPs to Pods, avoiding encapsulation at the cost of IP address exhaustion
Flat networks cannot use NetworkPolicies, while overlay networks can only run in single-zone clusters
Overlay networks require dedicated hardware ASICs on every worker node

questions.explanation: Overlay networks encapsulate container traffic in VXLAN/Geneve UDP packets across nodes, adding ~50 bytes per packet and minor CPU overhead. Flat VPC CNIs assign real VPC subnet IPs directly to container interfaces, providing line-rate wire speed and native cloud routing, but can quickly exhaust VPC subnet IP quotas.

questions.text: Which architectural limitation of the traditional Kubernetes `Ingress` resource does the Kubernetes `Gateway API` resolve?

options.text: Ingress could only route HTTP traffic on port 80, whereas Gateway API only supports gRPC

Ingress is a monolithic resource that blends infrastructure provisioning and application routing, causing vendor-specific annotation sprawl; Gateway API splits concerns across GatewayClass (infra), Gateway (cluster ops), and HTTPRoute (app developer)
Ingress required recompiling the Linux kernel for each new routing rule
Gateway API removes the need for Envoy or NGINX proxies completely

questions.explanation: The traditional `Ingress` resource forced cluster operators and application developers into a single shared resource with non-standard vendor annotations (e.g., `nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/*`). Gateway API provides role-oriented, expressive CRDs (`GatewayClass`, `Gateway`, `HTTPRoute`, `GRPCRoute`) with standardized multi-tenant support.

kubernetes-pods-probes-and-services.title: Kubernetes pods, probes, deployments and services
kubernetes-pods-probes-and-services.description: What a Pod is, what each probe does when it fails, how a Deployment replaces Pods, and how a Service finds them.

questions.text: Two containers run in the same Pod. How can the main container call the sidecar?

options.text: Through the sidecar's own Pod IP, which is different from the main container's
Only through a Service that selects the Pod
On localhost and the sidecar's port, because the containers share one network namespace and IP
Only by writing to a shared volume, since Pods have no network between containers

questions.explanation: All containers in a Pod share one IP address and one localhost, so they reach each other like two processes on one machine. Separate per-container IPs are how plain docker run containers behave, not Pod containers.

questions.text: A container is running but still warming up its cache, and its readiness probe is failing. What does Kubernetes do?

options.text: Kills and restarts the container
Removes the Pod from the Service's endpoints so it receives no traffic, without restarting it
Deletes the Pod and lets the ReplicaSet create a new one
Marks the node unschedulable

questions.explanation: A failing readiness probe only stops traffic reaching the Pod; it keeps running and is added back once the probe passes. Restarting is what a failing liveness probe does, and using liveness for slow warm-up can put the container in a restart loop.

questions.text: An app takes about two minutes to boot, and its liveness probe keeps killing it before it is ready. Which change fits best?

options.text: Replace the liveness probe with a readiness probe
Raise the container's memory limit
Set restartPolicy to Never
Add a startup probe so liveness checks only begin after the app has booted

questions.explanation: A startup probe holds off the other probes and gives a slow starter time. Swapping to readiness alone would remove the safety net that restarts a hung container, and a memory limit has nothing to do with slow startup.

questions.text: You change the image tag in a Deployment's Pod template, and the Deployment uses its default (RollingUpdate) strategy. What happens?

options.text: The existing Pods are edited in place to use the new image
The Deployment creates a new ReplicaSet and gradually moves Pods from the old ReplicaSet to it
All old Pods are deleted at once and then new ones are created
Nothing happens until you delete the Pods by hand

questions.explanation: A changed Pod template creates a new ReplicaSet and a rolling update shifts Pods over within the maxUnavailable and maxSurge limits. A Deployment replaces Pods rather than editing them in place, and the gradual shift is why users do not see downtime.

questions.text: A Service exists, but kubectl get endpoints shows none for it and requests fail. The Deployment's Pods are Running and Ready. What is the most likely cause?

options.text: The Service type must be NodePort to have endpoints
CoreDNS is not running
The Service's selector does not match the Pods' labels
The Deployment has too few replicas

questions.explanation: A Service builds its endpoints from Pods whose labels match its selector, so a typo or mismatch leaves it with nothing to route to. DNS problems would make the name fail to resolve, but they would not change the endpoints list.

questions.text: Which statements about resource requests and limits are correct? Select all that apply.

options.text: A container that exceeds its memory limit is killed and shows OOMKilled
