Port 8080 is a privileged port; ls -l shows who owns the binary
The DNS TTL is too long; dig +trace shows the delay

questions.explanation: A socket bound to the loopback address is invisible to every other host, and ss -tlnp shows the address it is bound to. One listening port serves many clients, 8080 is not below 1024, and DNS is not involved when the address is already known.

questions.text: dig example.com returns the correct IP, but curl example.com connects to a different machine. What should you check first?

options.text: Whether the TCP three-way handshake is being retransmitted
Whether the server certificate has expired
Whether the DNS record is a CNAME or an A record
Whether /etc/hosts has an entry for that name

questions.explanation: Applications resolve names through the system resolver, which normally reads /etc/hosts before asking DNS, while dig always queries a DNS server. When dig and getent or curl disagree, a hosts-file override is the first suspect.

questions.text: Which statements about DNS are correct? Select all that apply.

options.text: A CNAME record maps a name to another name, which the resolver then looks up
An A record maps a name to an IPv6 address
Lowering a record's TTL before a planned change makes the change take effect sooner
A DNS TTL is a hop counter that routers decrement

questions.explanation: CNAME is an alias, and a short TTL means caches refetch sooner, so operators lower it ahead of a migration. IPv6 addresses live in AAAA records, and the hop counter is the unrelated TTL field in the IP header; a DNS TTL is a caching lifetime in seconds.

questions.text: A host is configured as 10.0.5.40/29. Which of these addresses is on the same local network?
questions.explanation: A /29 has 8 addresses, so blocks start at multiples of 8 and this one spans 10.0.5.40 to 10.0.5.47. 10.0.5.39 and 10.0.5.48 sit in the neighbouring blocks, and 10.0.6.41 is a different third octet entirely, so the host would send those to its gateway.

questions.text: A container on a private address behind NAT can usually open connections to the internet, but an outside host cannot start a connection to it unless a port forward is configured.

options.text: True
False

questions.explanation: NAT creates its translation entry when the inside host sends the first packet out, so replies can find their way back. With no entry and a non-routable private address, unsolicited inbound traffic has nowhere to go until a port forward (destination NAT) maps it.

questions.text: Which workloads fit UDP better than TCP? Select all that apply.

options.text: Transferring a file where every byte must arrive intact
A DNS query and its short response
A database client talking to its server
A live voice call where a late packet is useless

questions.explanation: UDP skips the handshake and retransmission, which suits small request/response exchanges and real-time media where timeliness beats completeness. Files and database traffic need TCP's reliable, ordered delivery.

testing-strategies-for-backends.title: Testing strategies for backends
testing-strategies-for-backends.description: The test pyramid, test doubles, real versus in-memory databases, flaky tests, contract tests, and what code coverage can and cannot tell you.

questions.text: A team's suite has 5 unit tests, 20 integration tests and 400 browser-driven end-to-end tests. It takes 90 minutes and a few tests fail at random on every run. What does the test pyramid suggest?

options.text: Add even more end-to-end tests, because only they show what real users will actually see and experience when they use it
Move checks down: many unit tests for the logic, fewer integration tests for the seams, a few end-to-end tests
Delete the integration tests, since the end-to-end tests already exercise everything they would check
Run the 400 end-to-end tests in parallel on bigger machines and accept the occasional random failure

questions.explanation: Unit tests (one piece in isolation) are fast and point straight at the failure, integration tests (several pieces with real dependencies such as a database) catch problems at the seams, and end-to-end tests (the whole system, as a user would use it) are slow, flaky and costly, so you keep few of them. A suite shaped like an upside-down pyramid is slow and flaky because the slowest tests carry most of the load, and more of them or bigger machines does not fix that.

questions.text: Which statements about test doubles are correct?

options.text: A stub returns canned answers so the code under test can run, for example a payment client that always says 'approved'
A mock also verifies how it was used, for example that charge() was called once with the right amount
A fake is a simplified but working implementation, for example an in-memory repository backed by a dictionary
A stub makes the test fail if the code under test never calls it
A fake is the real production dependency, started for the duration of the test

questions.explanation: A stub supplies inputs, a mock verifies interactions and a fake offers a working shortcut; all three replace real collaborators so the code under test can run in isolation. Failing when a call never happens is mock behaviour, not stub behaviour, and a fake is a stand-in rather than the real system.

questions.text: A test asserts that OrderService calls repo.save() exactly once with particular arguments. After a harmless refactor that batches several saves into one call, the test fails although the behaviour is unchanged. What does this show?

options.text: The refactor was a mistake, because a correct refactor can never make an existing test fail
The test needs more verifications, such as the order of every call, to catch problems sooner
Mocks should never be used for writes, because a mock cannot reliably record a call to save()
The test is tied to how the code works, not what it does; checking results would survive it

questions.explanation: Verifying exact calls ties a test to the implementation, so it fails on harmless refactors and its false alarms teach people to ignore red builds. Prefer asserting on observable results (the saved orders, the response) and use a fake collaborator, keeping interaction checks for effects that are the point, such as 'an email was sent'.

questions.text: Integration tests for a PostgreSQL-backed service could use an in-memory substitute such as SQLite, or a throwaway PostgreSQL container. Which are good reasons to prefer the real engine?

options.text: A query that relies on a PostgreSQL feature can pass or fail differently on the substitute than in production
Constraints, transaction isolation and locking behave as they do in production, so integrity and concurrency bugs show up
The real engine always starts faster than an in-memory database
With a real engine, unit tests are no longer needed
Migrations run on the engine production uses, so a broken migration fails the build instead of the release

questions.explanation: The database is exactly the seam an integration test exists to check, and engines differ in SQL dialect, types, constraints, locking and migration behaviour, so a substitute can hide real failures. A container is usually slower to start than an in-memory database, and integration tests complement unit tests rather than replacing them.

questions.text: A test creates an order and asserts that its created_at equals the current time. It passes most runs but fails now and then. What is the most robust fix?

options.text: Loosen the assertion to accept any time within a few seconds either side of the current time
Add a short sleep before the assertion, so that the clocks have time to settle first
Inject a clock the test controls, or freeze time, so the expected value is known exactly
Let the CI server re-run the failed test automatically until it eventually passes

questions.explanation: A test that reads the real clock (or unseeded random numbers, or an unspecified ordering) has an input it cannot control, so it is non-deterministic. Control the input: pass in a clock, freeze time, seed the generator, sort before comparing. Margins, sleeps and automatic re-runs only hide the flakiness, and they teach the team to ignore failures.

questions.text: An integration test passes when it runs alone but fails when the whole suite runs, because it finds rows that another test left behind in the shared database. Which fix addresses the cause?

options.text: Give each test a clean start, such as a transaction rolled back after every test, or tables reset first
Run the failing test first in the suite, so that it sees the database before any other test has touched it
Add a sleep at the start of the failing test so the earlier tests have time to finish
Mark the test as flaky in CI, so that its failures no longer block the build

questions.explanation: A test that depends on what earlier tests left behind is coupled to them through the shared state, so its result depends on the order. Make every test start from a known state and leave nothing behind: roll back a per-test transaction, truncate tables, or build a fresh schema. Reordering, sleeping and ignoring failures hide the coupling instead of removing it.

questions.text: Service A calls service B's API, and A's tests use a mocked copy of B's responses. B's team renames a response field; both teams' CI stays green, but the integration breaks in production. What closes this gap without deploying both services together for every change?

options.text: More unit tests in A, written against the same mocked responses as before, to cover more cases
A contract test: A records what it relies on, and B's build verifies its real responses against that
A load test of B before every release, to see how it behaves with many concurrent callers
A stricter coverage target for B, so that every line of its response-building code is exercised by tests

questions.explanation: Each team tested against its own idea of the contract, and nothing ever compared the two. A consumer-driven contract test (for example with Pact) turns A's expectations into a check that runs in B's pipeline, so renaming the field fails B's build before release; more mock-based tests in A can never notice, because the mocks are frozen.

questions.text: Your service calls a payment API and must give up after 2 seconds. How can you test that behaviour without making the test wait?

options.text: Skip it, because timeouts can only be verified properly on a live production system
Call the real payment API from the test and hope that it happens to be slow enough to trigger the timeout
Use a test double that fails with a timeout at once, and assert how the service responds
Mock the service under test itself, so that the test finishes quickly and never waits

questions.explanation: Failure paths such as timeouts, 500 replies and malformed responses are exactly what production will hit, and a double can produce them instantly and repeatably. Waiting on a real dependency makes tests slow and random, and mocking the code under test means the test checks nothing about it.

questions.text: If a test suite reaches 100% line coverage, you can be sure the tests would catch a bug in any line.

options.text: True
False

questions.explanation: Coverage only records which lines ran during the tests, not whether anything checked the results, so a test with no assertions still counts. It also cannot show code that is missing, such as validation nobody wrote, or inputs nobody tried; use it to find untested code, not as proof of quality.

questions.text: A property-based testing tool generates many inputs automatically and checks that a rule you state, such as decode(encode(x)) == x, holds for all of them, instead of relying on a few hand-picked examples.

options.text: True
False

questions.explanation: You describe a property that should always hold, and the tool tries hundreds of generated inputs, including awkward ones such as empty values, huge numbers and odd characters, then shrinks any failure to a small example. It complements example-based tests, which remain the clearest way to document specific behaviours.

tls-and-https-basics.title: TLS and HTTPS basics
tls-and-https-basics.description: What TLS does and does not protect, how certificates are checked, and where HTTPS ends in a real deployment.

questions.text: Which three guarantees does TLS give an HTTPS connection?

options.text: Compression, caching and load balancing
Encryption, integrity and server authentication
Authorization, rate limiting and logging
Anonymity, availability and data-at-rest protection

questions.explanation: TLS keeps the bytes unreadable to eavesdroppers, detects tampering, and proves the server is who its certificate says. It does not hide who you connected to and does not protect data once it is stored or after TLS ends.

questions.text: If a site presents a valid certificate and the browser shows a padlock, you can be sure the site is honest and safe.

options.text: True
False

questions.explanation: The padlock means the connection is encrypted and the server is who its certificate says it is. A scam site can have a perfectly valid certificate for its own domain.

questions.text: When a client verifies a server's certificate during the TLS handshake, which checks does it make? Select all that apply.

options.text: The chain of signatures leads up to a root CA in its trust store
The hostname it asked for is covered by the certificate
The website's content has been reviewed and is safe
The current date is inside the certificate's validity period

questions.explanation: Chain of trust, hostname match and validity dates are what the client can actually check. Nothing in the certificate says anything about whether the site's content is safe.

questions.text: All your API clients suddenly fail with "certificate has expired". Which command shows the certificate's validity dates for a host?

options.text: curl -k https://example.com/
dig example.com TXT
openssl s_client -connect example.com:443 -servername example.com, piped to openssl x509 -noout -dates
ss -tlnp on the client

questions.explanation: openssl s_client fetches the certificate and x509 -noout -dates prints notBefore and notAfter. curl -k would just skip verification and hide the problem, and the other commands inspect DNS or local sockets.

questions.text: A network observer between a client and an HTTPS site can typically still see which of these? Select all that apply.

options.text: The destination IP address
The value of the Authorization header
The JSON request body
The server name sent in the TLS handshake (SNI), in a typical setup

questions.explanation: TLS hides the HTTP content: headers, cookies, tokens and bodies. It does not hide the fact of the connection, so the IP address and normally the SNI hostname stay visible.

questions.text: TLS is terminated at your load balancer, and the app behind it sees plain http:// requests. How can the app learn that the client originally used HTTPS?

options.text: From an X-Forwarded-Proto header set by the proxy
From the port number on the app's own socket
From the TLS certificate in the request
It cannot be known, so apps must always redirect to HTTPS themselves

questions.explanation: The proxy adds the original scheme as X-Forwarded-Proto, which the app should trust only from a proxy it controls. The certificate and the original TLS session never reach the app once TLS has ended at the balancer.

questions.text: What does the header Strict-Transport-Security: max-age=31536000 tell a browser?

options.text: The certificate will be renewed automatically in a year
Cookies should be encrypted at rest for a year
Session tokens expire after a year
For the next year, only connect to this site over HTTPS, even if the user types http://

questions.explanation: HSTS makes the browser refuse plain HTTP for the site, which defeats SSL-stripping downgrade attacks. It has nothing to do with certificate renewal or token lifetimes, and it only makes sense once HTTPS works everywhere on the site.

questions.text: Turning off certificate verification (curl -k, or verify=False in an HTTP library) in production code is acceptable because the traffic is still encrypted.

options.text: True
False

questions.explanation: Without verification you no longer know who you are talking to, so a man-in-the-middle can present their own certificate and read everything. -k is for debugging a certificate problem only.

tokens-attention-transformers.title: Tokens, attention and transformers
tokens-attention-transformers.description: What a language model actually sees, and the attention mechanics inside a transformer: Q/K/V, scaling, masks and heads.

questions.text: What does a language model actually receive as input?

options.text: The raw characters of the text, one at a time
One ID per word, using a dictionary of every English word
Integer IDs of tokens, which are chunks of text from a fixed learned vocabulary
The text plus a separate list of its grammatical parts

questions.explanation: A tokenizer maps text to vocabulary entries, and the model only sees their integer IDs. A token can be a whole word, a word piece or a single character or byte, so it is not the same as a word.

questions.text: A sentence in Hindi or Japanese usually costs about the same number of tokens as the English sentence with the same meaning.

options.text: True
False

questions.explanation: Tokenizers trained mostly on English text split non-Latin scripts into more, smaller tokens. The exact ratio depends on the language and the tokenizer (2-3 times is common, and it can be higher), but it is rarely close to 1. That raises both cost and latency for the same content.

questions.text: Why are queries, keys and values computed with three separate learned projections instead of using the token vectors X directly for all three?

options.text: It makes the matrices smaller so attention runs faster
Using X as both query and key makes the score matrix symmetric and biases each token toward attending to itself, so the model cannot learn directional relations between tokens
Softmax only works if the inputs come from a linear projection
It is needed to make the output the same length as the input

questions.explanation: If Q = K = X, the scores are X times X-transpose: the score from token i to token j always equals the score from j to i, and a token's dot product with itself (its squared length) tends to dominate its row, so each token is biased toward attending to itself. Separate Wq and Wk give each token a 'what I look for' vector and a different 'what I offer' vector, which removes the symmetry and lets the model learn which other tokens matter.

questions.text: Why are attention scores divided by sqrt(d_k) before the softmax?

options.text: Dot products grow with the dimension, so large scores would saturate the softmax and leave almost no gradient to learn from
It makes the weights for each row sum to exactly 1
It hides future tokens from the current position
It reduces the number of parameters in the layer

questions.explanation: The spread of dot products between random vectors scales with sqrt(d), so unscaled scores make softmax nearly one-hot and its gradient tiny. Softmax already normalises each row to 1, so that is not the reason for the scaling.

questions.text: A teammate implements a causal mask by setting the scores of future positions to 0 before the softmax. What goes wrong?

options.text: The model crashes with a shape error
Nothing; 0 and -inf give identical weights
Future positions get zero weight, but so do all past positions
Softmax still gives future positions a non-zero weight, so the model quietly leaks information from the future

questions.explanation: A score of 0 is not neutral to softmax; it counts as moderately plausible. Only adding -inf makes exp(-inf) = 0 and gives masked positions exactly zero weight. The bug does not crash, which is why it is dangerous.

questions.text: Going from 1 attention head to 8 heads at the same d_model adds roughly eight times as many parameters.

options.text: True
False

questions.explanation: Wq, Wk, Wv and Wo stay d_model x d_model whatever the head count. The heads are made by splitting the projected vectors, so the parameter count is unchanged and each head just works in a smaller subspace with its own softmax.

questions.text: Which statements about sampling the next token are correct? Select all that apply.

options.text: Top-k keeps exactly k candidate tokens, whether the model is confident or torn
Top-p keeps fewer tokens when one token holds most of the probability mass
Temperature removes low-probability tokens from consideration
Greedy decoding samples tokens in proportion to their probabilities

questions.explanation: Top-k is a fixed count while top-p adapts to the shape of the distribution. Temperature only reshapes the probabilities and removes nothing, and greedy decoding always takes the single most likely token rather than sampling.

questions.text: A batch pads shorter sequences with [PAD] tokens so they fit in one tensor. Which are true of masking in this setup? Select all that apply.

options.text: A padding mask stops real tokens from attending to the padding
A padding mask and a causal mask are applied by different mechanisms, so they cannot be combined
Both kinds of mask work by adding -inf to scores before the softmax
A causal mask also hides padding that comes before the real tokens, so no padding mask is needed

questions.explanation: Padding masks and causal masks are the same additive -inf tool aimed at different problems: one hides non-content, the other hides the future. They are commonly combined additively before a single softmax. A causal mask hides only future positions: padding placed before the real tokens (left padding) is in their past and stays visible, and an encoder with bidirectional attention has no causal mask at all, so a padding mask is still needed.

transactions-and-isolation-levels.title: Transactions, isolation and locking
transactions-and-isolation-levels.description: Read anomalies, PostgreSQL's isolation levels, pessimistic and optimistic locking, and how to avoid deadlocks.

questions.text: What is PostgreSQL's default isolation level, and what does each statement see?

options.text: Serializable: every transaction runs as if alone
Repeatable Read: one snapshot for the whole transaction
Read Committed: each statement sees data committed before that statement began
Read Uncommitted: uncommitted changes are visible to everyone

questions.explanation: Read Committed prevents dirty reads but allows a later statement in the same transaction to see newly committed changes. The stronger levels must be requested explicitly.

questions.text: Inside one transaction you run SELECT ... WHERE status = 'open' twice. Between the runs another transaction inserts a matching row and commits, and your second run returns an extra row. Which anomaly is this?

options.text: Dirty read
Phantom read
Non-repeatable read
Lost update

questions.explanation: A phantom is a row appearing in (or vanishing from) a set matched by a predicate. A non-repeatable read is when an existing row you already read comes back with a different value. A dirty read involves uncommitted data.

questions.text: On PostgreSQL at Read Committed, an application that reads a balance, adds 10 in code and writes it back is safe from lost updates.

options.text: True
False

questions.explanation: Two transactions can both read 100 and both write back their own result, so the second write overwrites the first. You need row locking, an atomic UPDATE, a version check, or a stronger isolation level with retries.

questions.text: Under PostgreSQL's REPEATABLE READ, two transactions update the same row. The first commits. What happens to the second?

options.text: It fails with a serialization error and must be retried
It silently overwrites the first update
It merges both updates automatically
It keeps waiting until the first transaction rolls back

questions.explanation: The second update blocks until the first finishes, then fails with 'could not serialize access due to concurrent update' because its snapshot is stale. The application has to catch that error and retry the whole transaction.

questions.text: Which approaches prevent a lost update when many requests change the same account balance? Select all that apply.

options.text: SELECT ... FOR UPDATE before computing the new balance
An UPDATE ... WHERE id = ? AND version = ? that is retried when it affects 0 rows
A single atomic statement such as UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance + 10
A plain SELECT then UPDATE at Read Committed, with a short transaction

questions.explanation: Pessimistic locking, optimistic versioning and an atomic update each stop two writers from acting on the same stale value. A short transaction narrows the window but does not close it.

questions.text: Two code paths transfer money between accounts A and B. One locks A then B, the other locks B then A, and they occasionally deadlock. What is the most effective fix?

options.text: Raise deadlock_timeout so transactions wait longer
Switch both paths to Read Uncommitted
Add more connections to the pool
Have every code path lock the rows in the same order, such as lowest id first

questions.explanation: A deadlock needs a cycle of waits, and a consistent lock order makes a cycle impossible. A longer timeout only delays detection, and PostgreSQL has no real Read Uncommitted anyway.

questions.text: With optimistic locking, your UPDATE ... WHERE id = 'A' AND version = 7 reports 0 rows affected. What does that mean?

options.text: The row does not exist, so you should insert it
The database lost the update; you should restart the server
Someone else changed the row first, so re-read it and retry
The write succeeded but nothing needed changing

questions.explanation: The version no longer matches because another transaction bumped it. The application must detect the zero-row result, re-read the fresh row and retry (the re-read also shows if the row was deleted instead). This only pays off when conflicts are rare.

questions.text: Several workers poll a jobs table, and you want each worker to claim different rows without waiting on each other. Which clause fits?

options.text: SELECT ... FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED
SELECT ... FOR SHARE
SELECT ... FOR UPDATE with no other clause
SET TRANSACTION ISOLATION LEVEL SERIALIZABLE

questions.explanation: SKIP LOCKED passes over rows another transaction already locked, so workers pick different rows. Plain FOR UPDATE makes every worker queue behind the first, and Serializable would produce errors to retry instead.

web-security-owasp-top-10.title: Web security and the OWASP Top 10
web-security-owasp-top-10.description: The most common ways web backends get broken into, and the habits that stop them.

questions.text: A logged-in customer changes the number in GET /api/invoices/1042 to 1043 and sees another customer's invoice. What is the proper fix?

options.text: Replace the numeric ids with random UUIDs so nobody can guess another invoice
Remove the links to other invoices from the page so users cannot find them
Check on the server that the caller owns the invoice, on every request
Serve the endpoint over HTTPS so that the id in the URL cannot be changed

questions.explanation: This is broken access control, here as an insecure direct object reference: logging in proves who the caller is, but the server must also check that this caller may see this object. Random ids only make guessing harder, and hiding links or adding HTTPS does nothing to stop someone who edits the URL.

questions.text: Which of these are safe ways to handle user input that ends up in a SQL query or a shell command?

options.text: Bind the search term as a parameter of a prepared statement
Strip quotes and semicolons from the requested sort column, then paste it into the SQL
Start the external program with its arguments as a list, without going through a shell
Reject any input that contains words such as DROP or SELECT
Map the requested sort name to a column from a fixed allowlist and refuse anything else

questions.explanation: Parameters keep values out of the SQL text, and an argument list keeps them out of a shell command line, so the input is never parsed as code. Table and column names cannot be bound as parameters, which is why an allowlist is used for them. Stripping characters or blocking keywords can be bypassed in ways you did not think of.

questions.text: An endpoint fetches a URL supplied by the user, for example to build a link preview. What is the best defence against server-side request forgery (SSRF)?

options.text: Allow only approved destinations and block private addresses after resolving DNS
Insist that the URL starts with https:// and that the host name looks like a public site
Reject any URL that contains the text localhost or 127.0.0.1, in any letter case
Apply a short timeout and a maximum response size to every outbound fetch

questions.explanation: In SSRF the attacker uses your server to reach places they cannot, such as internal services or the cloud metadata address. An https:// prefix does not stop that, text filters miss other spellings of the same address and host names that resolve to private ones, and timeouts only limit the load, so allow-list destinations and check the address the name resolves to.

questions.text: A production API returns a full stack trace, with file paths and the database host name, whenever a request fails. Why is that a security problem, and what is the fix?

options.text: It makes error responses slower, so debug mode only needs to go if latency becomes a problem
It breaks cross-origin rules in browsers, so add CORS headers to the error responses
It matters only on plain HTTP, so moving the whole site to HTTPS removes the risk
It reveals internals to attackers, so return a generic error and keep the details in logs

questions.explanation: Security misconfiguration includes debug output, default accounts, unneeded features and open storage buckets. A stack trace tells an attacker about your framework, versions, paths and queries, so return a generic message and keep the detail in your logs. Error pages have nothing to do with CORS, and HTTPS protects the connection, not what the server chooses to say.

questions.text: If the code your own team wrote has no vulnerabilities, a known security hole in a library you depend on, even an indirect one, cannot affect your service.

options.text: True
False

questions.explanation: A library runs inside your process with your service's privileges, so a hole in it, even in a dependency of a dependency, is a hole in your service. Keep a lockfile or software bill of materials, scan dependencies in CI and update promptly.

questions.text: Your login endpoint receives thousands of attempts from many different IP addresses, each trying one account with a password that appeared in an unrelated breach. A few succeed. Which defence fits best?

options.text: A slower, memory-hard hash for the passwords that are stored in your database
MFA, limits per account as well as per IP, and a breached-password check
Parameterised queries for the login lookup, so that usernames cannot carry SQL code
Longer random session ids, plus a brand new session id issued after every login

questions.explanation: This is credential stuffing: attackers replay username and password pairs leaked elsewhere and count on people reusing passwords, often from many IPs so that per-IP limits alone miss it. MFA, per-account throttling and breached-password checks all blunt it. Hashing, parameterised queries and session ids protect other things, not the live login.

questions.text: A signup endpoint runs User.create(request.body). A client adds the field isAdmin set to true to the JSON and becomes an administrator. What is the right fix?

options.text: Accept only an allowlist of request fields, and set privileged fields on the server
Remove the isAdmin checkbox from the signup form so that users cannot tick it
Check that the password in the body is strong enough before creating the user
Send the signup as form fields instead of JSON, since a form cannot carry extra fields

questions.explanation: This is mass assignment: the framework binds every property in the request to the model, including ones the form never showed. Anyone can send a raw request, so hiding a field in the UI or changing the format does not help; the server must decide which fields a caller may set.

questions.text: Which practices make logs useful for spotting an attack without creating new risks?

options.text: Record failed logins and access-control denials with time, account and source, and alert on unusual bursts
Log complete request bodies so that nothing is missed, passwords and tokens included
Ship logs to a separate system that the application servers cannot edit or delete
Keep logs only on each application server so they stay close to the code

questions.explanation: Failed logins and denied requests are the early signs of an attack, and nobody sees them unless someone is alerted. Logs on a separate, append-only system survive a compromised server, while an attacker who owns the app server can erase local logs. Logging passwords and tokens turns the log store itself into a prize.

questions.text: A web service connects to its database with an account that can read, change and drop every table in every schema. What does the principle of least privilege suggest?

options.text: Keep the broad rights, so the service never fails because of a permission error
Share one admin account between all services, so there is only one secret to look after
Limit the account to the tables and operations the service really needs to use
Rely on application code alone to enforce permissions, because a database cannot do it

questions.explanation: Least privilege means every account, service and token gets only the access it needs. If a bug such as SQL injection or a leaked password is then exploited, the attacker reaches a small part of the data and cannot drop tables. Broad or shared admin accounts trade a little convenience for a much bigger blast radius.

questions.text: If you validate every field when it arrives, you do not need to encode output when you put that data into an HTML page.

options.text: True
False

questions.explanation: Validation checks that data has the expected shape, but many legitimate values, such as a name like O'Brien or a comment with a less-than sign, contain characters that matter in HTML, SQL or a shell. Encode for the place where the data is used, and use parameterised queries, as well as validating.

client-retries-with-backoff.title: Add retries with backoff to an API client
client-retries-with-backoff.brief:
Your service calls a partner's HTTP API to create shipping labels (`POST /labels`) and to look up their status (`GET /labels/{id}`). Today the client makes one attempt with a 60 second timeout. During busy hours the partner answers some calls with `429 Too Many Requests` (sometimes with a `Retry-After` header), occasionally with `502` or `503`, and a few requests just time out. The first quick fix someone proposed was "retry up to 10 times with no delay", which made an incident worse.

Design the retry behaviour of this client and write it down precisely enough that another engineer could implement it and test it. Pay attention to which calls are safe to repeat: a retried `POST /labels` after a timeout may create two labels if the first attempt actually succeeded. The partner supports an `Idempotency-Key` request header on `POST`.
deliverables: A table of failure types (connection error, timeout, 429, 500, 502, 503, 504, 400, 401, 404) and whether each is retried, with the reason
The backoff formula with a base delay, a multiplier, a cap and jitter, and which jitter variant you chose and why
How a Retry-After header is honoured and how it combines with your own backoff
The maximum attempts and a total time budget for one logical call, and how this fits inside your own caller's timeout
How you make POST /labels safe to retry (idempotency key: when it is generated, that it is reused across attempts)
Timeouts per attempt (connect and read), and why 60 seconds is too long
A retry budget or circuit breaker so that many clients do not multiply load on a struggling partner
The logging and metrics you would add, and three test cases (including a fake server that fails twice then succeeds)

debug-slow-query-with-explain.title: Debug a slow query with EXPLAIN
debug-slow-query-with-explain.brief:
The "my shipped orders" page of an online shop takes about three seconds and the database CPU spikes when many customers open it. The database is PostgreSQL.

**Schema**

```sql
CREATE TABLE customers (
  id         bigint PRIMARY KEY,
  email      text NOT NULL,
  created_at timestamptz NOT NULL
);
CREATE UNIQUE INDEX customers_email_key ON customers (email);

CREATE TABLE orders (
  id          bigint PRIMARY KEY,
  customer_id bigint NOT NULL REFERENCES customers (id),
  status      text   NOT NULL,           -- placed, paid, shipped, delivered, cancelled
  total_cents integer NOT NULL,
  created_at  timestamptz NOT NULL
);
-- orders has about 20 million rows; a typical customer has under 200 of them
```

**Query 1 (the page)**

```sql
SELECT * FROM orders
WHERE customer_id = 4242 AND status = 'shipped'
ORDER BY created_at DESC
LIMIT 20;
```

```
EXPLAIN (ANALYZE)
 Limit  (cost=397604.25..397604.30 rows=20 width=48) (actual time=2810.40..2810.45 rows=20 loops=1)
   ->  Sort  (cost=397604.25..397604.54 rows=118 width=48) (actual time=2810.39..2810.42 rows=20 loops=1)
         Sort Key: created_at DESC
         Sort Method: top-N heapsort  Memory: 28kB
         ->  Seq Scan on orders  (cost=0.00..397600.00 rows=118 width=48) (actual time=1.20..2790.10 rows=96 loops=1)
               Filter: ((customer_id = 4242) AND (status = 'shipped'::text))
               Rows Removed by Filter: 19999904
 Planning Time: 0.15 ms
 Execution Time: 2810.60 ms
```

**Query 2 (support tool, finding a customer by email, case-insensitive)**

```sql
SELECT * FROM customers WHERE lower(email) = 'ana@example.com';
```

```
 Seq Scan on customers  (cost=0.00..27500.00 rows=5000 width=64) (actual time=0.05..410.30 rows=1 loops=1)
   Filter: (lower(email) = 'ana@example.com'::text)
   Rows Removed by Filter: 999999
 Execution Time: 410.40 ms
```

Diagnose both queries from the plans, propose the fixes, and say how you would prove each fix worked. Assume you are allowed to add indexes, but the table is large and busy.
deliverables: For each query: what the plan shows, in your own words (node types, rows removed by filter, estimated versus actual rows)
The index you would create for query 1, with the column order and the reason for that order (and why the sort node disappears)
The fix for query 2 and why the existing unique index on email cannot be used, plus the trade-off of the fix
The exact CREATE INDEX statements, including how you build them without blocking writes on a busy table
What you expect the new plans to look like and how you would verify it with EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS)
Two things that would still make the first query slow after the index exists (for example SELECT * or a very low-selectivity filter) and what you would do about them
How you would check that the new indexes did not hurt write performance, and when ANALYZE matters

eda-and-leak-audit.title: Audit a messy production dataset for data leakage and distributional defects
eda-and-leak-audit.brief:
You are auditing a customer churn prediction dataset containing 250,000 subscriber accounts and 45 raw features before it is fed into an automated retraining pipeline. The existing model claimed a 99.4% ROC-AUC in cross-validation, but when deployed to production, churn intervention campaigns yielded zero actual impact.

Your task is to write a systematic data audit and exploratory data analysis specification in Python/Pandas that flags all forms of target leakage, train-test contamination, impossible values, and skewed distributions, detailing how each flaw must be remediated.
deliverables: A checklist of target leakage red flags (features populated only after the churn event occurs, such as cancellation_survey_score, refund_processed_date, or account_status='closed')
A key uniqueness and merge cardinality check to ensure user_id is unique and not creating hidden cartesian explosion during feature joins
A missingness audit distinguishing Missing Completely at Random (MCAR) from Missing Not at Random (MNAR), with appropriate imputation strategies
Outlier and anomaly detection rules for negative tenure, 9999 sentinel codes, and future timestamp lookahead errors
A clean split architecture (time-based cutoff vs random split) ensuring no temporal leakage from future customer actions into past predictions
Code snippets in Python/Pandas implementing automated validation assertions that fail CI/CD if leakage features or severe drift are detected

gradient-descent-from-scratch.title: Implement a modular gradient descent optimizer suite in pure NumPy
gradient-descent-from-scratch.brief:
In order to deeply understand optimizer mechanics before debugging large-scale distributed training runs, you are tasked with building a modular, object-oriented gradient descent optimizer framework in pure Python and NumPy from first principles.

Your library must support vanilla SGD, Polyak Heavy-Ball Momentum, RMSProp, Adam, and decoupled AdamW, along with gradient norm clipping and a cosine annealing learning rate scheduler.
deliverables: A clean BaseOptimizer abstract class with step(), zero_grad(), and parameter registration interfaces
Vectorized implementations of SGD with momentum (v_t = beta * v_{t-1} + lr * g_t)
Vectorized Adam optimizer with first and second moment moving averages, bias correction factors (1 - beta^t), and epsilon stability guards
Decoupled AdamW implementation demonstrating why direct weight decay differs from L2 gradient regularization in adaptive optimizers
A global gradient clipping utility that scales gradients down if the L2 norm exceeds a threshold (clip_grad_norm)
A benchmark script optimizing an ill-conditioned quadratic bowl and the 2D Rosenbrock banana valley, comparing convergence paths and step counts

idempotent-payment-endpoint.title: Make a payment endpoint idempotent
idempotent-payment-endpoint.brief: Your service has `POST /payments`. Mobile clients on poor networks retry when a request times out, and some customers have been charged twice. Design the change that makes the endpoint safe to retry.
deliverables: How the client names an operation (the header, who generates the key, how long it stays valid)
The table or record that stores keys and results, with its constraints
What the server does when the same key arrives twice in sequence, and twice at the same moment
What it does when the key is reused with a different body
The tests you would write to prove it

leak-free-sklearn-pipeline.title: Build an end-to-end leak-free Scikit-learn feature pipeline
leak-free-sklearn-pipeline.brief:
You are designing the feature preprocessing and cross-validation pipeline for a financial credit risk scoring service. The dataset contains continuous financial metrics (income, debt-to-income, credit utilization), high-cardinality categorical attributes (employment industry, merchant category), and missing values. The previous team normalized features before splitting and computed target statistics on the full dataset, creating severe data leakage.

Design a leak-free scikit-learn Pipeline architecture using ColumnTransformer, strict cross-validation, and calibrated linear classification that can safely serialize to production.
deliverables: A modular Scikit-learn Pipeline incorporating ColumnTransformer to route numeric features through StandardScaler and categoricals through OneHotEncoder/TargetEncoder with strict handle_unknown guards
Proper integration of SimpleImputer or KNNImputer inside the pipeline so statistics are fitted solely on training folds
A StratifiedKFold or TimeSeriesSplit cross-validation harness ensuring no test fold data is ever exposed to transformer fit methods
Probability calibration using CalibratedClassifierCV with Platt scaling to convert raw SVM or uncalibrated margins into honest posterior probabilities
Decision threshold tuning against an asymmetric business loss matrix ($50 false positive inquiry cost vs $1,000 false negative default cost)
Model serialization specification with version pinning and input validation schemas

micrograd-autograd-engine.title: Build a scalar autograd engine and multi-layer perceptron from scratch
micrograd-autograd-engine.brief:
Deep learning frameworks like PyTorch and JAX operate on automatic differentiation computation graphs. To demystify these abstractions and diagnose gradient bugs with confidence, build a lightweight scalar reverse-mode automatic differentiation engine from scratch in pure Python.

Your implementation must construct a dynamic computation graph on the fly, execute reverse topological sorting, support gradient accumulation across branching nodes, and train a Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP) on a non-linear dataset.
deliverables: A Value scalar class tracking data, grad, child references (_prev), operation name (_op), and backward closure (_backward)
Operator overloads for addition, subtraction, multiplication, division, power, negation, and activation functions (ReLU, Tanh)
A backward() method executing a depth-first search topological sort to ensure adjoint gradients propagate in exact reverse dependency order
Proper handling of multi-path graph branches using gradient accumulation (self.grad += out.grad * local_derivative) to prevent dropped gradients
Neuron, Layer, and MLP classes built on Value objects supporting parameter collection and zero_grad()
A verification test suite comparing computed gradients against PyTorch autograd tensors to within 1e-6 relative tolerance

orders-index-strategy.title: Plan the indexes of an orders table
orders-index-strategy.brief: The `orders` table (id, customer_id, status, total, created_at) has 50 million rows. The three hot queries are: a customer's recent orders, all orders in status "pending" older than an hour, and one order by id.
deliverables: The CREATE INDEX statements you would add, with the column order justified
Which query each index serves and how you would confirm it with EXPLAIN
What the indexes cost on writes, and one index you chose not to create and why

paginated-list-endpoint.title: Design a paginated, cache-friendly list endpoint
paginated-list-endpoint.brief:
A blog platform has an endpoint that returns articles:

```
GET /v1/articles?page=3&per_page=20&tag=python
```

It is implemented as `SELECT ... FROM articles WHERE tag = ? ORDER BY published_at DESC LIMIT 20 OFFSET 40`. The table has 30 million rows and new articles are published every few seconds. Symptoms reported by users and the on-call engineer:

- Deep pages (page 5000 and beyond) take several seconds and load the database.
- A reader scrolling the list sees the same article twice, or misses one, when something new is published between two requests.
- The response is never cached by the CDN because every client sends different query strings and no caching headers are set.
- The endpoint returns a `total` count, and the `COUNT(*)` behind it is the slowest part of the request.

Redesign the endpoint. Write a short design document (and, if you like, a sketch of the handler and the SQL) that fixes all four symptoms without breaking existing clients more than necessary.
deliverables: The new request and response shape, including the cursor parameter and a sample JSON response
What the cursor contains and how it is encoded; why a tie-break column is needed when many rows share the same published_at
The SQL for the first page and for the next page, and the index that makes it fast (column order matters)
What you do about the total count (drop it, estimate it, or return it only on request) and why
Cache-Control, ETag and Vary choices for the first page and for later pages, and what must be part of the cache key
How deletes and edits between two requests behave, and the maximum limit you enforce
A migration path for clients that still send page and per_page

rate-limit-login.title: Rate limit a login endpoint
rate-limit-login.brief: Attackers are trying thousands of passwords against `POST /login`. Add rate limiting without locking out the legitimate user who mistypes twice.
deliverables: What you count and by which key (IP address, account, both) and why
The algorithm (fixed window, sliding window or token bucket) and its numbers
The response when the limit is hit, including the headers a client can use
How a shared store keeps the count right across several servers
How you avoid letting an attacker lock a victim out on purpose

zero-downtime-column-migration.title: Plan a zero-downtime column migration
zero-downtime-column-migration.brief:
Your orders table stores the order total as a decimal in a column named `total` (for example `19.99`). It has about 300 million rows and takes writes all day. The team wants to store money as integer cents in a new column `total_cents` and eventually drop `total`.

Constraints:

- The service runs as 12 replicas behind a load balancer and is deployed with a rolling update, so for several minutes old and new versions of the code run at the same time.
- A nightly reporting job, owned by another team, reads `orders.total` directly from a read replica. It cannot change this quarter.
- No maintenance window is allowed. Writes must never fail and no request may see a wrong total.
- The database is PostgreSQL. A plain `ALTER TABLE ... ALTER COLUMN TYPE` on this table is not acceptable.

Write the migration plan as an ordered runbook. Each step must say whether it is a schema migration, an application deploy, or a data job, what it changes, and what happens if you stop or roll back at that point.
deliverables: The ordered steps using expand and contract: add column, dual-write deploy, backfill, switch reads, stop writing the old column (only once the reporting job no longer needs it, or if you keep it filled another way), drop it; for each, the type of step and the rollback
The exact SQL for adding the column and why it is safe on a large table (locks taken and for how long)
The backfill design: batch size, how it walks the table (by primary key range), how it throttles itself, and why it must be idempotent and restartable
How you guarantee rows written during the backfill are correct (the dual-write code, or a trigger as an alternative, and the trade-off between them)
How you verify that total and total_cents agree before switching reads (a query or a checksum, and what you do on a mismatch)
How the reporting job keeps working: when you could finally drop total, what you do if the other team is not ready, and a way to keep total populated for them in the meantime
How and when you add a NOT NULL constraint without a long lock
What you monitor during the migration (replica lag, lock waits, error rate, backfill progress)

aspnet-core-middleware-and-di.title: ASP.NET Core Middleware and Dependency Injection

questions.q: What is middleware in ASP.NET Core?
questions.a: Middleware is software assembled into an application's HTTP request pipeline to handle requests and responses. Each component can inspect incoming HTTP context, execute code before delegating to the next component via a `RequestDelegate next`, await `next(context)` to invoke subsequent pipeline stages, handle exceptions or responses on the way back up, or short-circuit the pipeline entirely.

questions.q: What is the difference between app.Use and app.Run in ASP.NET Core?
questions.a: `app.Use` inserts a middleware delegate that takes `HttpContext` and `Func<Task> next`, allowing it to perform operations and invoke `await next()` to continue the pipeline. `app.Run` registers a **terminal middleware** delegate that receives only `HttpContext` without a `next` parameter; it handles the request, generates a response, and permanently stops further pipeline execution.

questions.q: What do app.Map and app.MapWhen do in the middleware pipeline?
questions.a: `app.Map` branches the middleware pipeline based on a matching request URL path prefix (e.g. `app.Map("/api", apiApp => ...)`). `app.MapWhen` branches the pipeline conditionally based on an arbitrary predicate evaluated against the `HttpContext` (e.g. checking query strings, headers, or client IP). If the predicate matches, execution diverges into the branch.

questions.q: Why does the order of middleware matter in ASP.NET Core? Give the standard order.
questions.a: Order matters because middleware executes sequentially on the incoming request and in reverse order on the outgoing response. A typical order is: 1. Exception Handling / ProblemDetails (catches errors from all downstream stages), 2. HTTPS Redirection & HSTS, 3. Static Files (short-circuits assets quickly), 4. Routing, 5. CORS, 6. Authentication (establishes identity), 7. Authorization (enforces permissions), 8. Endpoint execution.

questions.q: How do you write custom middleware in ASP.NET Core?
questions.a: Two approaches exist: 1. **Convention-based middleware:** A class with a constructor accepting `RequestDelegate next` and a `public async Task InvokeAsync(HttpContext context, ...)` method where scoped dependencies can be injected directly into `InvokeAsync`. 2. **Factory-based middleware:** Implements `IMiddleware`, allowing the middleware instance itself to be registered with a scoped lifetime in DI.

questions.q: What is the difference between middleware and filters in ASP.NET Core?
questions.a: **Middleware** operates at the low-level HTTP pipeline level on raw `HttpContext`, before routing chooses an action, with zero awareness of MVC controllers or endpoint models. **Filters** run inside the MVC / routing execution pipeline with rich context (ActionArguments, ModelMetadata, ModelState, Controller instances), executing before and after specific controller actions.

questions.q: What is the difference between AddSingleton, AddScoped, and AddTransient lifetimes?
questions.a: `AddSingleton`: A single instance is created on first request and shared process-wide for the application lifetime. `AddScoped`: A fresh instance is created once per client HTTP request scope and shared across all dependencies within that request. `AddTransient`: A brand-new instance is created every single time the service is requested from the container.

questions.q: What is a captive dependency in ASP.NET Core, and how do you prevent it?
questions.a: A captive dependency occurs when a service with a longer lifetime consumes a service with a shorter lifetime (e.g. a `Singleton` injecting a `Scoped` service). The scoped service is kept alive on the singleton for the application's duration, causing stale state, threading bugs, and memory leaks. Prevent it by enabling scope validation (`ValidateScopes = true`, default in Development).

questions.q: How do you safely resolve a scoped service inside a singleton or background service?
questions.a: Inject `IServiceScopeFactory` into the singleton or `BackgroundService`. Inside the execution loop or method, create an explicit temporary scope: `using var scope = _scopeFactory.CreateScope();`, then resolve the scoped service from the scope's provider: `var db = scope.ServiceProvider.GetRequiredService<MyDbContext>();`. The scope and its instances are disposed when exiting the block.

questions.q: Which service lifetime should Entity Framework Core's DbContext have, and why?
questions.a: `DbContext` should be registered with a **Scoped** lifetime (the default in `AddDbContext`). `DbContext` is not thread-safe and tracks entity state in memory. A singleton `DbContext` would collide across concurrent HTTP request threads. A transient `DbContext` would prevent sharing unit-of-work changes and change-tracker state across multiple repositories within one request.

questions.q: What is the difference between IOptions, IOptionsSnapshot, and IOptionsMonitor?
questions.a: `IOptions<T>` is registered as a **Singleton**; values are read once at startup and do not reload when config changes. `IOptionsSnapshot<T>` is **Scoped**; values are re-read once per HTTP request, reflecting config updates without restarting. `IOptionsMonitor<T>` is a **Singleton** that provides real-time notifications via `OnChange` whenever underlying configuration files change.

questions.q: What does WebApplication.CreateBuilder do in Program.cs?
questions.a: `WebApplication.CreateBuilder(args)` initializes a `WebApplicationBuilder`, bootstrapping default configuration sources (appsettings.json, environment variables, command-line arguments), default logging providers (Console, Debug, EventSource), and Kestrel web server defaults, while exposing `builder.Services` for registering application dependencies.

questions.q: What is the difference between builder.Services and app in ASP.NET Core?
questions.a: `builder.Services` is an `IServiceCollection` used during application startup to declare and configure service dependencies and their lifetimes before the container is built. `app` is a `WebApplication` created after calling `builder.Build()`; it represents the runtime host and is used to configure the HTTP middleware pipeline (`app.Use...`, `app.Map...`).

questions.q: What is Kestrel, and why is it usually deployed behind a reverse proxy?
questions.a: Kestrel is the cross-platform, event-driven HTTP server for ASP.NET Core. In production, it is typically fronted by a reverse proxy (Nginx, Apache, IIS, or Cloudflare) for SSL termination, public internet hardening against slow client attacks (Slowloris), static file serving, compression, and load balancing across application worker instances.

questions.q: How does global exception handling work in ASP.NET Core with ProblemDetails?
questions.a: Global exception handling uses `app.UseExceptionHandler()`. In ASP.NET Core 8+, implement `IExceptionHandler` to intercept unhandled exceptions, log errors, and format standard RFC 7807/9457 `ProblemDetails` JSON responses (status, title, detail, instance URI) without leaking internal stack traces or database connection strings to API clients.

questions.q: What is the difference between authentication and authorization middleware?
questions.a: **Authentication** middleware (`app.UseAuthentication()`) verifies *who* the caller is by inspecting credentials (e.g. validating a JWT Bearer token or cookie) and establishing the `ClaimsPrincipal` on `HttpContext.User`. **Authorization** middleware (`app.UseAuthorization()`) verifies *what* that caller is permitted to do against policies and roles.

questions.q: What is the N+1 query problem in Entity Framework Core, and how do you prevent it?
questions.a: The **N+1 problem** occurs when querying a parent collection executes 1 query to fetch $N$ parent records, followed by $N$ separate queries executed in a loop to fetch related child records for each parent. This generates devastating network latency and database query load. Prevent it by using eager loading via `.Include(x => x.Children)` to join child data in a single SQL query.

questions.q: What does AsNoTracking() do in EF Core, and when should you use it?
questions.a: `.AsNoTracking()` tells EF Core not to snapshot or track entities in the `ChangeTracker` cache. It should be used for **read-only queries** (e.g. GET endpoints, reports). Disabling tracking reduces memory allocations, eliminates snapshot comparison overhead, and significantly boosts read throughput.

questions.q: What is the difference between eager loading, lazy loading, and explicit loading in EF Core?
questions.a: **Eager loading** (`.Include()`) loads related data from the database as part of the initial query using SQL JOINs. **Lazy loading** defers loading navigation properties until they are accessed in code via proxy instances (which risks hidden N+1 queries). **Explicit loading** (`context.Entry(order).Collection(o => o.Items).Load()`) loads related entities on-demand via an explicit query call.

questions.q: How does hierarchical configuration work in ASP.NET Core, and which provider wins by default?
questions.a: ASP.NET Core stacks configuration providers in order: 1. `appsettings.json`, 2. `appsettings.{Environment}.json`, 3. User Secrets (in Development), 4. Environment Variables (using `Section__Key` double-underscore syntax), 5. Command-line arguments. The **last registered provider always wins**, meaning environment variables or CLI flags cleanly override default JSON settings in production.

questions.q: How do you securely manage production secrets in ASP.NET Core without committing them to source control?
questions.a: Never commit secrets to `appsettings.json`. In local development, use the .NET Secret Manager (`dotnet user-secrets init/set`), which stores credentials in a local machine profile outside the git repository. In production, inject secrets via environment variables, Azure Key Vault, AWS Secrets Manager, or HashiCorp Vault using configuration provider extensions.

questions.q: What is structured logging in ASP.NET Core, and why is `logger.LogInformation("Order {OrderId}", id)` superior to string interpolation?
questions.a: Using message templates (`"Order {OrderId}"`) preserves parameter names and types as first-class JSON fields in centralized logging engines (Elasticsearch, Seq, Datadog), allowing indexing and querying (`OrderId == 104`). In contrast, string interpolation (`$"Order {id}"`) bakes parameters into a flat string, destroying queryable metadata and incurring upfront string allocation costs even if logging is disabled.

questions.q: What is the architectural difference between MVC Controllers and Minimal APIs in ASP.NET Core?
questions.a: **Controllers** rely on heavy reflection, dynamic model metadata binding, action filter pipelines, and instantiating a controller class per request. **Minimal APIs** route requests directly to lightweight delegate handlers, bypassing controller activation and the MVC filter pipeline. Minimal APIs cut per-request allocations and startup work and, with the request delegate source generator (.NET 8), work with Native AOT, which MVC controllers do not.

questions.q: What are the five categories of action filters in ASP.NET Core MVC, and what is their execution order?
questions.a: Filters execute in this order around an action: 1. **Authorization filters** (check access first), 2. **Resource filters** (wrap model binding and caching), 3. **Action filters** (execute immediately before and after the action method), 4. **Exception filters** (handle unhandled exceptions), 5. **Result filters** (wrap execution of the action result or JSON serialization).

questions.q: How does JWT Bearer authentication validate tokens in ASP.NET Core, and how do you handle token revocation?
questions.a: `JwtBearerHandler` validates token signatures, issuer, audience, and expiration mathematically using the public or symmetric key, without database round-trips. However, because JWTs are stateless, compromised tokens remain valid until expiration. To handle revocation, maintain a distributed token blacklist or user security stamp in Redis checked inside `OnTokenValidated` events.

questions.q: What is policy-based authorization in ASP.NET Core, and how do Requirements and AuthorizationHandlers interact?
questions.a: A policy defines one or more `IAuthorizationRequirement` rules (e.g. `MinimumAgeRequirement(21)`). You implement an `AuthorizationHandler<TRequirement>`, which receives `AuthorizationHandlerContext`. The handler evaluates user claims, database permissions, or resource ownership and calls `context.Succeed(requirement)`. If all requirements succeed, ASP.NET Core permits access.

questions.q: What is the Strategy pattern? Give an example.
questions.a: The Strategy pattern defines a family of interchangeable algorithms, encapsulates each one behind a common interface, and makes them swappable at runtime. For example, an e-commerce checkout accepts an `IShippingCalculator` strategy (`StandardShipping`, `ExpressShipping`, `OvernightShipping`). The order context delegates shipping fee calculation to the injected strategy without conditional branching.

questions.q: How does Strategy help with the Open/Closed Principle?
questions.a: Strategy eliminates rigid conditional statements (`if/else` or `switch` on types). When business requirements introduce a new calculation or discount rule, developers add a new class implementing the strategy interface. The consuming context remains closed for modification yet open for extension, requiring zero code changes to existing classes.

questions.q: What is the difference between Strategy and State?
questions.a: **Strategy** encapsulates *how* an action is performed; the client typically chooses the strategy from the outside and passes it in, and the strategy rarely changes during the object's life. **State** encapsulates *what* an object does based on its internal state; state transitions happen automatically from within the state objects or context as business operations execute.

questions.q: Can a strategy just be a function?
questions.a: Yes. In modern programming languages with first-class functions (such as `Func<T, TResult>` in C# or `Callable` in Python), a full class hierarchy is often unnecessary for simple algorithms. A strategy can be passed as a lambda expression or method reference directly, reducing boilerplate while achieving identical runtime polymorphism.

questions.q: What is the Observer pattern?
questions.a: The Observer pattern defines a one-to-many dependency between objects: when one subject changes state, all its registered observers are notified and updated automatically. It decouples the core domain subject from disparate subscribers, such as UI views, telemetry loggers, or email notification dispatchers.

questions.q: How do C# events implement the Observer pattern?
questions.a: In C#, `event EventHandler` implements the Observer pattern natively via multicast delegates. The publisher declares an event and raises it when state changes. Observers subscribe using `+=` and unsubscribe using `-=`. Under the hood, the compiler generates thread-safe `add` and `remove` accessor methods that maintain a delegate invocation list.

questions.q: How can an event handler cause a memory leak in .NET?
questions.a: When a short-lived subscriber attaches a method to an event on a long-lived publisher (`publisher.Changed += subscriber.OnChanged`), the publisher's delegate holds a strong reference to the subscriber. The Garbage Collector cannot collect the subscriber even if outside references to it are gone. To fix this, always unsubscribe via `-=` in `Dispose()`, or use weak event patterns.

questions.q: What is the difference between Observer and Pub/Sub?
questions.a: **Observer** is in-process and synchronous: the subject maintains direct references to observer interfaces in memory and calls them directly. **Pub/Sub** uses an independent message broker (e.g., RabbitMQ, Kafka, Azure Service Bus): publishers emit messages to channels or topics, and subscribers consume them asynchronously without publishers and subscribers ever knowing each other.

questions.q: What is the Command pattern?
questions.a: The Command pattern encapsulates a request as a standalone object containing the action, receiver, and all necessary parameters. This decoupling turns invocations into first-class citizens, enabling features like parameterizing method calls, queueing requests, scheduling background execution, logging audit trails, and implementing reversible undo/redo operations.

questions.q: How would you implement undo using the Command pattern?
questions.a: Each command implements an `Execute()` method and an `Undo()` (or `Unexecute()`) method. An `Invoker` maintains a history stack of executed commands. When an operation occurs, the command saves the previous state, runs `Execute()`, and is pushed onto the stack. Calling `Undo()` pops the top command and invokes its `Undo()` method to restore prior state.

questions.q: Where is the Command pattern used in real systems?
questions.a: Command is used in GUI frameworks (WPF `ICommand` binding buttons to actions), transactional sagas in distributed systems (compensating transactions for rollbacks), task queues and job processors (serializing jobs into Redis or Celery), and CQRS architectures where write commands mutate state separately from query models.

questions.q: What is the Template Method pattern?
questions.a: The Template Method pattern defines the skeleton of an algorithm in an abstract base class method, deferring specific steps to subclasses via abstract or virtual methods without changing the overall algorithm structure. It enforces a fixed sequence of execution (e.g., `Authenticate() -> Validate() -> Process() -> Log()`) while allowing customization of individual hooks.

questions.q: What is the difference between Template Method and Strategy?
questions.a: **Template Method** relies on inheritance and compile-time binding: the algorithm invariant lives in a base class, and subclasses override specific protected steps. **Strategy** relies on composition and runtime delegation: the context delegates the entire algorithm to an interchangeable strategy object implementing a common interface, which can be swapped at runtime.

questions.q: What is the State pattern?
questions.a: The State pattern allows an object to alter its behavior when its internal state changes, appearing to change its class. The context class holds a reference to a `State` object that implements state-specific behaviors. Method invocations on the context are forwarded to the current state object, which can transition the context to the next state.

questions.q: How would you model order status changes with the State pattern?
questions.a: Define an `OrderState` base class with operations like `Cancel()`, `Pay()`, and `Ship()`. Implement concrete states (`PendingPaymentState`, `PaidState`, `ShippedState`). In `PendingPaymentState`, `Cancel()` transitions the order to `CancelledState`. In `ShippedState`, calling `Cancel()` throws an invalid transition exception. The `Order` delegates actions to its `_currentState` without nested switch statements.

questions.q: What is the Chain of Responsibility pattern?
questions.a: The Chain of Responsibility pattern passes a request along a sequence of handler objects. Each handler in the chain decides either to process the request, perform pre- or post-processing, and optionally pass the request to the next handler, or short-circuit and terminate the pipeline entirely. Handlers are linked dynamically via a `next` pointer or delegate.

questions.q: How is ASP.NET Core middleware an example of Chain of Responsibility?
questions.a: ASP.NET Core HTTP middleware executes as a Chain of Responsibility. Each component receives `HttpContext` and a `RequestDelegate next`. A component can perform operations before `next(context)`, invoke `await next(context)` to delegate down the chain, handle responses on the way back up, or terminate the pipeline without calling `next` (short-circuiting, e.g. on auth failure).

questions.q: What is the Iterator pattern, and how does yield return relate to it?
questions.a: The Iterator pattern provides a way to access the elements of an aggregate collection sequentially without exposing its underlying representation (e.g., list, tree, hash map). In C#, `yield return` automatically generates a compiler-synthesized state machine that implements `IEnumerable` and `IEnumerator`, enabling deferred, on-demand evaluation.

questions.q: What is the Mediator pattern, and how does it differ from Observer?
questions.a: The Mediator pattern centralizes complex communications between disparate objects, preventing them from referring to each other directly. In **Observer**, subjects broadcast events to many subscribers (one-to-many). In **Mediator**, communication is orchestrated centrally (many-to-many), with components (colleagues) routing all commands and notifications through the mediator (e.g., `MediatR` in .NET).

questions.q: What is the Visitor pattern, and what is double dispatch?
questions.a: The **Visitor pattern** separates an algorithm from the object structure on which it operates, allowing new operations to be added to existing class hierarchies without modifying them. It relies on **double dispatch**: the client calls `element.Accept(visitor)`, and inside `Accept`, the element invokes `visitor.Visit(this)`, binding dispatch on both the element type and visitor type at runtime.

questions.q: What is the Memento pattern, and how does it preserve encapsulation during state capture?
questions.a: The **Memento pattern** captures and externalizes an object's internal state without violating encapsulation, allowing the object to be restored to this state later (undo mechanism). The **Originator** creates and consumes the memento. The **Caretaker** (e.g. undo manager) stores mementos but is given a narrow interface, preventing it from inspecting or tampering with internal saved state.

questions.q: What is the Null Object pattern, and how does it eliminate null-checking boilerplate?
questions.a: The **Null Object pattern** provides an object that implements an interface with neutral, no-op behavior (e.g. `NullLogger` doing nothing on `Log()`) instead of passing `null`. Clients invoke methods safely without repetitive `if (logger != null)` checks, keeping domain code cohesive, readable, and free from defensive guard clauses.

questions.q: What is the Specification pattern, and how does it support composite business rules?
questions.a: The **Specification pattern** encapsulates a domain business rule or query predicate into an object implementing an `IsSatisfiedBy(candidate)` method. Specifications can be combined using boolean combinators (`And`, `Or`, `Not`) to form composite business rules (e.g. `isEligible = isOver18.And(hasActiveSubscription.Not())`), separating validation logic from domain entities.

questions.q: How do you implement the Strategy pattern using modern C# delegates instead of defining multiple classes?
questions.a: Inject a `Func<T, TResult>` delegate instead of an interface: `public class DiscountEngine { private readonly Func<Order, decimal> _strategy; public DiscountEngine(Func<Order, decimal> strategy) => _strategy = strategy; public decimal Apply(Order o) => _strategy(o); }`. Callers pass pure lambdas (e.g. `order => order.Total * 0.15m`), keeping code concise while preserving Open/Closed substitutability.

questions.q: How would you model order state transitions using the State pattern to prevent shipping an unpaid order?
questions.a: Create an `IOrderState` interface with `Pay(Order o)` and `Ship(Order o)`. In `DraftState`, calling `Ship()` throws an `InvalidOperationException("Cannot ship an unpaid order")`, while `Pay()` transitions `o.SetState(new PaidState())`. In `PaidState`, `Ship()` prints a tracking manifest and transitions to `ShippedState()`. The `Order` delegates behavior to `_state`, eliminating nested conditionals.

questions.q: What is the Interpreter pattern, and when is it appropriate to build a custom domain DSL interpreter?
questions.a: The **Interpreter pattern** defines a grammar representation for a domain-specific language (DSL) along with an interpreter that uses the representation to evaluate sentences. Nodes implement `Interpret(Context ctx)`. It is appropriate for simple, static grammars: evaluating dynamic boolean user-segmentation rules (`Age > 21 AND Country == 'US'`), math expressions, or internal query-filtering DSLs.

questions.q: What is the difference between Repository and Unit of Work, and should you wrap EF Core in a generic repository?
questions.a: A **Repository** mediates between the domain and data mapping layers, presenting an in-memory collection interface (`Add`, `GetById`, `Find`). A **Unit of Work** maintains a list of affected business objects and coordinates atomic transactions (`Commit`). Wrapping EF Core in a generic repository is usually redundant because `DbContext` already implements Unit of Work and `DbSet<T>` already acts as a repository.

questions.q: What architectural problems arise from using a generic IRepository in enterprise systems?
questions.a: A generic `IRepository<T>` often leaks database abstractions if it exposes `IQueryable<T>`, causing business logic to trigger unoptimized SQL queries across domain boundaries. Furthermore, it treats every aggregate as a flat CRUD table, encouraging anemic domain models, disabling specialized database operations (bulk inserts, raw SQL), and obscuring domain intention behind generic `Update()` calls.

questions.q: How does MediatR implement the Mediator and Chain of Responsibility patterns in ASP.NET Core?
questions.a: `MediatR` implements the **Mediator pattern** via `IMediator.Send(command)`: requests are dispatched to a single `IRequestHandler<TRequest, TResponse>`, eliminating direct dependencies between API controllers and domain handlers. It implements the **Chain of Responsibility pattern** via pipeline behaviors (`IPipelineBehavior<TRequest, TResponse>`), wrapping execution in validation, logging, and metrics hooks.

questions.q: How do you implement a thread-safe Observer pattern in Python without risking race conditions during notification?
questions.a: Use a `threading.Lock` to synchronize `subscribe` and `unsubscribe`. Inside `notify()`, make a defensive snapshot copy of the subscriber collection under the lock before invoking callbacks: `with self._lock: observers = list(self._observers)`. Then loop over the copied list outside the lock. This prevents deadlocks and avoids `RuntimeError: Set changed size during iteration` if a callback unsubscribes.

questions.q: Explain cache-aside and when you would use it.
questions.a: The application checks the cache first, and on a miss reads the database and fills the cache. It is simple, tolerates cache failure, and suits read-heavy data that can be briefly stale.

questions.q: What is a cache stampede and how do you prevent it?
questions.a: When a popular entry expires, many requests miss at once and all hit the database. Prevent it with request coalescing (one rebuild, the rest wait), jittered expiry times, or refreshing early in the background.

questions.q: How do you invalidate a cache correctly?
questions.a: Prefer short TTLs plus explicit invalidation on write. Delete the key after the database write commits. Accept that some staleness is unavoidable and decide how much the data can tolerate.

questions.q: When is caching the wrong answer?
questions.a: When the data must always be current, when the hit rate would be low, or when the slow query should be fixed instead (an index, a better query). A cache hides a problem and adds a consistency problem.

questions.q: Two Sum: given a list of integers and a target, return the indices of the two numbers that add up to the target. How do you do better than checking every pair?
questions.a:
**Approach.** Checking every pair is O(n²). Instead, remember each number you have already seen in a hash map (value → index). For each number `x`, the partner you need is `target - x`: one dictionary lookup tells you whether it appeared earlier.

```python
def two_sum(nums, target):
    seen = {}                          # value -> index
    for i, x in enumerate(nums):
```
