For a fast `count`, keep a second dictionary from value to how many keys hold it, and update it in one place (a single helper that every `set`, `delete` and rollback goes through).
lld-kv-transactions.explanation:
**The idea.** There are two ways to support transactions. You can copy the whole store at `begin()` (simple, O(n) per transaction), or write changes straight into the store and remember how to *undo* them. This solution does the second, so `begin` is O(1) and a transaction costs only as much as it changes.

**The undo log.** Each open transaction has a dictionary `key -> value before this transaction first touched it` (with a marker for "did not exist"). `setdefault` is the important call: the *first* old value is the one to restore, even if the key is changed five times.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    S[set / delete] --> W[write to the main data]
    S --> L[record the old value in the top log, once per key]
    R[rollback] --> P[pop the top log]
    P --> U[write its old values back]
    C[commit] --> E[clear every log]
```

**One place that writes.** `count` needs a second index (value to number of keys). If `set`, `delete` and `rollback` each updated it by hand, one of them would eventually forget. A single `_put` helper makes the index correct by construction, and rollback reuses it.

**Complexity.** `set`, `get`, `delete`, `count`, `begin` are O(1); `rollback` is O(keys changed in that transaction); `commit` is O(1) amortised.

**Going further.** Real databases make `commit` close only the innermost transaction (a *savepoint*). What would you change so that `commit` merges the top log into its parent instead of discarding everything?

lld-leaderboard.title: Leaderboard
lld-leaderboard.description: Build a game leaderboard with accumulating scores, ties that share a rank, a top list and the players around you.
lld-leaderboard.statement:
Write a class `Leaderboard` of players with integer scores.

**Methods**

- `add(player, points)` adds `points` (an `int`, which may be negative) to the player's score; a new player starts at `0`. A `points` that is not an `int` (a `bool` is not) raises `ValueError("Points must be a whole number")`.
- `remove(player)` deletes a player. An unknown player raises `ValueError("Unknown player")`.
- `score(player)` is the player's score (`ValueError("Unknown player")` for an unknown one).
- `top(k)` returns the best `k` players as `(player, score)`, highest score first; players with equal scores are ordered by name. It returns fewer if there are not `k` players. A `k` below 1 raises `ValueError("k must be positive")`.
- `rank(player)` is the player's place, starting at `1`. Players with the **same score share a rank**, and the next rank skips the shared places (scores `90, 80, 80, 70` have ranks `1, 2, 2, 4`). Unknown player: `ValueError("Unknown player")`.
- `around(player, n)` returns the players from `n` places above to `n` places below the given player in the **`top` order** (clipped at both ends) as `(rank, player, score)` triples.

**Example**

```
board = Leaderboard()
for name, points in [("ann", 90), ("bob", 80), ("cy", 80), ("di", 70)]:
    board.add(name, points)
board.rank("cy")        # 2
board.rank("di")        # 4
board.top(2)            # [("ann", 90), ("bob", 80)]
```
tests: assert error_of(board.top, 0) == "ValueError: k must be positive"
assert error_of(board.add, "ann", 1.5) == "ValueError: Points must be a whole number"
assert error_of(board.add, "ann", True) == "ValueError: Points must be a whole number"

for name, points in [("di", 70), ("cy", 80), ("ann", 90), ("bob", 80)]:
    board.add(name, points)
hints: Store one dictionary from player to score. Everything else (`top`, `rank`, `around`) is computed from it, so it can never disagree with the scores.

The order is "score descending, then name ascending": sort with the key `(-score, name)`. The **rank** of a player is one plus the number of players with a *strictly higher* score; that gives ties the same rank and skips the places after them for free.
`around` is a slice of the sorted list from `index - n` to `index + n`, with the start clipped at 0 (a negative start would wrap around and return the wrong players).
lld-leaderboard.explanation:
**The idea.** The score table is the only fact; ranking is a *view* on it. That is why `rank` is "one plus how many are strictly better", not a stored number that every `add` must repair.

**Ranks with ties.** This is called *competition ranking* (1, 2, 2, 4). The other common scheme, *dense ranking*, gives 1, 2, 2, 3. A good interview answer asks which one the product wants before writing code, because the data structure does not change but the formula does.

**Deterministic order.** Sorting by score alone leaves ties in whatever order the dictionary happened to be in. Adding the name to the sort key makes `top` and `around` repeatable, which is what makes them testable (and what players expect to see on a screen).

**Slicing trap.** `ordered[index - n:...]` with `index - n < 0` starts from the *end* of the list. Clip the start with `max(0, ...)`.

**Complexity.** This version sorts per call: O(n log n) for `top` and `around`, O(n) for `rank`. That is fine for thousands of players. For millions you would keep a balanced tree or a skip list (this is how Redis sorted sets work) to get O(log n) for all three.

**Going further.** Sketch the sorted structure you would need for O(log n) `rank`. What does each node have to store besides its score?

lld-lfu-cache.title: LFU Cache With Tie-Breaking
lld-lfu-cache.description: Build a cache that evicts the least frequently used entry, breaking ties by recency, in O(1) per operation.
lld-lfu-cache.statement:
Write a class `LFUCache`: a fixed-capacity cache that, when full, evicts the entry used the **fewest times**; among entries with the same count, the one used **least recently**.

**Creating one:** `LFUCache(capacity)`; `capacity` must be an `int` of 1 or more (not a `bool`), else `ValueError("Capacity must be positive")`.

**Counting uses.** A new key starts with frequency **1**. Every `get` hit adds 1. A `put` on a key that already exists replaces its value and also adds 1. A missed `get` changes nothing.

**Methods**

- `get(key, default=None)` returns the value (adding a use) or `default`.
- `put(key, value)` stores the value. When a **new** key arrives and the cache is full, first evict the entry with the lowest frequency (ties: the least recently used of them) and return it as a `(key, value)` tuple; otherwise return `None`. A new key never competes with itself: it is inserted *after* the eviction.
- `frequency(key)` is the key's count, or `0` when it is not cached.
- `len(cache)` and `key in cache` (neither counts as a use).

**Speed.** Every operation must be O(1). The tests put 60,000 new keys through a cache of 5,000 and expect it to finish quickly.
tests: assert len(cache) == 0 and cache.frequency("x") == 0 and cache.get("x") is None
assert cache.put(1, "one") is None and cache.put(2, "two") is None
assert 2 not in cache and cache.get(2) is None and cache.get(2, "gone") == "gone" and cache.frequency(2) == 0
assert 1 not in cache and 3 in cache and 4 in cache and len(cache) == 2
assert other.put("a", 10) is None and other.frequency("a") == 2 and other.get("a") == 10

ties = LFUCache(3)
for key in "abc":
    ties.put(key, key.upper())
ties.get("a")
ties.get("b")
ties.get("c")
ties.get("a")
assert ("a" in ties) and ("c" in ties) and ("d" in ties)
assert ties.frequency("a") == 3 and ties.frequency("c") == 2 and ties.frequency("d") == 1
assert single.put("x", 1) is None and single.get("x") == 1 and single.put("y", 2) == ("x", 1) and single.frequency("y") == 1
assert holder.get("k", "d") is None and holder.frequency("k") == 2

big = LFUCache(5000)
started = time.time()
for number in range(60000):
    big.put(number, number)
    big.get(number)
hints: Keep three maps: key to value, key to count, and **count to the keys that have that count**, oldest first. The last one is what makes "least frequent, then least recent" a single O(1) lookup.

Also keep the lowest count currently in use. A use moves a key from bucket `n` to bucket `n + 1`; if bucket `n` just became empty and `n` was the lowest, the lowest is now `n + 1`. A brand new key always has count 1, so the lowest is 1 again.
Evict **before** inserting the new key, and only for a new key. If you insert first, the new key (count 1) may be the one chosen for eviction.
lld-lfu-cache.explanation:
**The idea.** LRU needs one ordered list. LFU needs *a list per frequency*: every bucket is an `OrderedDict` of the keys that share a count, oldest first. Eviction takes the oldest key of the lowest bucket; a use moves a key to the next bucket.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    A["count 1: d"] --> B["count 2: c"] --> C["count 3: a"]
    C -. "get d moves it up" .-> B
```

**The lowest count is a variable, not a search.** Scanning the buckets for the smallest count is O(number of distinct counts). Keeping `lowest` up to date costs two lines and makes every operation O(1): it only ever moves up by one when a bucket empties, or resets to 1 on an insert.

**Why a naive version fails the timing test.** `min(counts, key=...)` over 5,000 entries on every eviction is 5,000 steps times 60,000 puts: hundreds of millions of operations.

**Frequency is not forever.** A key that was popular a year ago keeps a huge count and is never evicted. Real LFU caches *decay* counts. That is a good follow-up in an interview.

**Complexity.** O(1) per operation; O(capacity) space.

**Going further.** Add `decay()` that halves every count (and merges buckets). What breaks in the `lowest` bookkeeping?

lld-library-1.title: Library Lending, Step 1
lld-library-1.description: Step 1 of 3: a lending desk with books and copies, members, a loan limit and fourteen-day loans.
lld-library-1.statement:
This is **step 1 of 3**. Steps 2 and 3 add fines, renewals and reservations to the class you write here, so keep it tidy.

Write a class `Library`. Days are whole numbers (`today` is a day number, `0` or more; anything else, including a `bool`, is `ValueError("Bad date")`).

**Books and members**

- `add_book(isbn, title, copies=1)` adds copies of a book. Checks in order: blank `isbn` (not a string or only spaces) `ValueError("ISBN required")`; blank `title` `ValueError("Title required")`; `copies` not an `int` of 1 or more (not a `bool`) `ValueError("Copies must be positive")`. The ISBN and title are stored **stripped**. Adding a known ISBN adds copies; with a **different title** it is `ValueError("ISBN has a different title")` and nothing changes.
- `join(member)` makes a member. A blank name is `ValueError("Member required")`; a repeated one `ValueError("Already a member")`.
- `title_of(isbn)` and `available(isbn)` (copies not currently on loan). An unknown ISBN is `ValueError("Unknown book")`.

**Lending.** A loan lasts **14 days**: `due = today + 14`. A member may hold at most **3** loans.

- `borrow(member, isbn, today)` returns the due day. Checks in this order: `"Bad date"`, `"Unknown member"`, `"Unknown book"`, `"Already borrowed"` (the member already holds this book), `"Loan limit reached"`, `"No copies available"`.
- `return_book(member, isbn, today)` returns the copy; it returns `None`. Checks: `"Bad date"`, `"Unknown member"`, `"Unknown book"`, `"Not borrowed"`.
- `loans_of(member)` is a **new list** of `(isbn, due)` tuples sorted by due day, then by ISBN. Unknown member `ValueError("Unknown member")`.
tests:
for bad in (0, -1, 1.5, True):
    assert error_of(lib.add_book, "i1", "Dune", bad) == "ValueError: Copies must be positive"
assert error_of(lib.add_book, "i1", "Other") == "ValueError: ISBN has a different title" and lib.available("i1") == 3
assert error_of(lib.available, "zzz") == "ValueError: Unknown book" and error_of(lib.title_of, "zzz") == "ValueError: Unknown book"

for bad in ("", "  ", None, 3):
    assert error_of(lib.join, bad) == "ValueError: Member required"
lib.join("ann")
lib.join("bob")

for bad in (-1, 1.5, True, None, "3"):
    assert error_of(lib.borrow, "nobody", "nope", bad) == "ValueError: Bad date"
assert error_of(lib.borrow, "ann", "i4", 12) == "ValueError: Loan limit reached" and error_of(lib.borrow, "ann", "nope", 12) == "ValueError: Unknown book"
assert error_of(lib.borrow, "bob", "i2", 12) == "ValueError: No copies available" and lib.available("i2") == 0

for bad in (-1, 1.5, True):
    assert error_of(lib.return_book, "nobody", "nope", bad) == "ValueError: Bad date"
assert lib.available("i1") == 1 and lib.borrow("dee", "i5", 41) == 55 and lib.borrow("dee", "i1", 41) == 55
assert lib.loans_of("dee").append("junk") is None and lib.loans_of("dee") == [("i1", 55), ("i5", 55)]
hints: Keep one dictionary of books (`title`, total `copies`) and one of members, each holding that member's loans as `{isbn: due}`. Copies on the shelf is never stored: it is `copies` minus the number of members holding the ISBN, so it cannot go out of step.

Write tiny helpers `_member(name)`, `_book(isbn)` and `_check_day(today)` that raise the right error. Every public method then starts with the same few lines, in the order the statement lists, and the error order takes care of itself.
Steps 2 and 3 will need *per-loan* data (was it renewed?) and *per-member* data (fines). Notice that "a member's loans" is where both will go, and keep that in one place.
lld-library-1.explanation:
**The idea.** A lending desk is two tables, books and members, and a handful of rules about moving a copy between them. The shelf count is **derived** (copies minus loans), never stored, so there is no second number to forget to update.

**The order of checks is the API.** Bad date, unknown member, unknown book, then the rules about *this* borrower and *this* book. Callers (and tests) depend on which error they see when several things are wrong.

**Step 2 and 3 preview.** Step 2 adds money (fines), a renewal and a new reason to refuse a loan. Step 3 adds a queue for books with no copy on the shelf. Code that keeps "what a member holds" in one place and "how many copies are out" in one derived number absorbs both changes with small edits.

**Complexity.** `available` scans the members, O(members); an `out` counter per book makes it O(1) at the price of one more number to keep in step.

**Going further.** Two copies of the same book cannot be told apart here. What would you need to add to record *which* copy a member holds (a barcode)?

lld-library-2.title: Library Lending, Step 2
lld-library-2.description: Step 2 of 3: late returns cost money, high fines block new loans, and a loan can be renewed once.
lld-library-2.statement:
This is **step 2 of 3**. The starting code is a working solution to step 1. Everything from step 1 still holds **except where this step changes it**.

**What changes**

- `return_book(member, isbn, today)` now **returns the fine in cents**: `25` for every day after the due day (`max(0, today - due) * 25`), `0` when on time. The fine is added to the member's balance.
- `borrow` has a **new check**: a member whose balance is **500 or more** may not borrow: `ValueError("Fines too high")`. The order is now: `"Bad date"`, `"Unknown member"`, `"Unknown book"`, **`"Fines too high"`**, `"Already borrowed"`, `"Loan limit reached"`, `"No copies available"`.

**What is new**

- `fines(member)` is the member's balance in cents (unknown member `ValueError("Unknown member")`).
- `pay(member, amount)` reduces the balance and returns the new balance. Checks in order: `"Unknown member"`; `amount` not an `int` of 1 or more (not a `bool`) `ValueError("Amount must be positive")`; more than the balance `ValueError("Amount exceeds fines")`.
- `renew(member, isbn, today)` extends a loan by **14 more days from its current due day** (not from today) and returns the new due day. A loan can be renewed **once**. Checks in order: `"Bad date"`, `"Unknown member"`, `"Unknown book"`, `"Not borrowed"`, `"Already renewed"`, then `ValueError("Overdue")` when `today` is **after** the due day (renewing *on* the due day is fine). A renewed loan that is returned late is fined from its **new** due day.

**Example**

```
lib.borrow("ann", "i1", 10)         # due 24
lib.return_book("ann", "i1", 27)    # 3 days late: returns 75
lib.fines("ann")                    # 75
```
tests: assert error_of(lib.join, "ann") == "ValueError: Already a member" and error_of(lib.add_book, "i1", "Other") == "ValueError: ISBN has a different title"
assert lib.borrow("ann", "i1", 10) == 24 and lib.borrow("ann", "i2", 11) == 25 and lib.borrow("ann", "i3", 5) == 19

assert error_of(lib.borrow, "ann", "i4", 12) == "ValueError: Loan limit reached" and error_of(lib.borrow, "ann", "nope", 12) == "ValueError: Unknown book" and error_of(lib.borrow, "ann", "i1", 12) == "ValueError: Already borrowed"
assert error_of(lib.borrow, "bob", "i2", 12) == "ValueError: No copies available" and lib.available("i2") == 0
assert error_of(lib.borrow, "zed", "i2", 12) == "ValueError: Unknown member" and error_of(lib.borrow, "bob", "zzz", 12) == "ValueError: Unknown book"
assert error_of(lib.borrow, "bob", "i2", -1) == "ValueError: Bad date" and error_of(lib.return_book, "bob", "i2", 12) == "ValueError: Not borrowed"
assert lib.available("i2") == 1 and lib.loans_of("ann") == [("i3", 19), ("i1", 24)] and lib.borrow("bob", "i2", 31) == 45
assert lib.title_of("i2") == "Emma" and error_of(lib.available, "zzz") == "ValueError: Unknown book" and error_of(lib.loans_of, "zed") == "ValueError: Unknown member"
assert fine_lib.fines("ann") == 0 and error_of(fine_lib.fines, "zed") == "ValueError: Unknown member"

for bad in (0, -5, 1.5, True, None):
    assert error_of(fine_lib.pay, "ann", bad) == "ValueError: Amount must be positive"
assert error_of(fine_lib.pay, "ann", 276) == "ValueError: Amount exceeds fines" and fine_lib.fines("ann") == 275

late = Library()
late.add_book("x", "X")
late.add_book("y", "Y")
late.join("m")
late.borrow("m", "x", 0)
late.renew("m", "x", 14)
assert late.fines("m") >= 500 and error_of(late.borrow, "m", "x", 131) == "ValueError: Fines too high"
hints: A member now has two things: loans and a balance. Change `self._loans[member]` from a plain dict into a record `{"loans": {...}, "fines": 0}`, and let each loan carry `{"due": ..., "renewed": False}`. Everything else reads through those.
Put the new check exactly where the statement puts it, between "unknown book" and "already borrowed". The order of the checks is part of the contract, and the tests pin it.
`renew` adds 14 to the **old due day**, so an early renewal does not waste the days left. Mark the loan as renewed and reject a second renewal; compare `today > due` (not `>=`) for "overdue".

lld-library-3.title: Library Lending, Step 3
lld-library-3.description: Step 3 of 3: members queue for books that are out, a returned copy is held for the first in line, and holds survive other rules.
lld-library-3.statement:
This is **step 3 of 3**. The starting code is a working solution to step 2. Everything holds **except where this step changes it**.

**New idea: reservations.** A member can queue for a book that has **no copy available**. When a copy comes back, it is **held** for the first member in the queue until they borrow it (or cancel).

**What changes**

- `available(isbn)` is now copies **minus loans minus holds**: a copy that is held for someone is not available to anybody else.
- `borrow` : a member who has a **hold** on the book borrows it **even though `available` is 0** (the hold is used up). Everyone else still needs `available >= 1`. All other checks and their order are unchanged (fines, already borrowed and the loan limit are checked **before** the hold is used, and a refused `borrow` keeps the hold).
- `return_book` and `add_book` (new copies) hand copies to the queue: while the queue is not empty and a copy is available, the **first** queued member gets a hold.

**What is new**

- `reserve(member, isbn)` puts the member at the end of the queue and returns their **position** (1 for the first). Checks in order: `"Unknown member"`, `"Unknown book"`, `"Already borrowed"` (they hold a loan of it), `"Already reserved"` (they are queued or hold a hold), then `ValueError("Copies available")` when `available(isbn) > 0` (they should simply borrow).
- `cancel_reservation(member, isbn)` leaves the queue or gives up a hold (the copy passes to the next in line, or becomes available). Checks: `"Unknown member"`, `"Unknown book"`, then `ValueError("No reservation")`.
- `queue(isbn)` is a **new list** of the members still waiting; `holds(isbn)` is a **new list** of the members holding a copy for them. Unknown ISBN `"Unknown book"`.

hints: Add two dictionaries: `queues[isbn]` (members waiting, oldest first) and `holds[isbn]` (members who have a copy put aside). `available` just subtracts `len(holds[isbn])` as well.

Write **one** helper, `_assign_holds(isbn)`: while the queue is not empty and `available(isbn) > 0`, move the first queued member into the holds. Call it from `return_book`, from `add_book` and from cancelling a hold: three events, one rule.

In `borrow`, run every existing refusal first (fines, already borrowed, loan limit). Only then, if the member is in `holds[isbn]`, remove the hold and go ahead; otherwise require `available >= 1`. A refused borrow must leave the hold in place.
lld-library-3.explanation:
**The idea.** A reservation queue changes one number (what "available" means) and adds two lists. The rest of the class is untouched; step 1's rules and step 2's money rules still hold, and the tests re-check them.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    R[copy returned or added] --> Q{queue empty?}
    Q -- yes --> A[copy is available]
    Q -- no --> H[first in queue gets a hold]
    H --> B[holder borrows: hold used up]
    H --> C[holder cancels: next in line or available]
```

**One helper keeps three events consistent.** A copy can become free in three ways: returned, newly added, or released by a cancelled hold. If each way assigned holds on its own, one of them would be forgotten. `_assign_holds` is the single place where "a free copy meets a waiting member".

**A hold is not a loan.** The copy sits on the shelf but nobody else can have it. That is why `available` subtracts holds, and why a refused `borrow` (fines too high, loan limit) must leave the hold alone: the member did not give it up.

**Looking back.** Three steps, one class, no rewrite. Each step touched the data in one place and the rules in a few; the order of the checks stayed a contract all the way.

**Complexity.** `available` is O(members); the queue operations are O(queue).

**Going further.** Holds that never get collected block the next person for ever. Add an expiry (a hold lasts 3 days). Which methods now need to know what day it is?

lld-logger-framework.title: Logger Framework
lld-logger-framework.description: Build a logging framework with levels, child loggers that propagate to their parents and handlers you can plug in.
lld-logger-framework.statement:
Write a small logging framework: a `Logger` class and two handlers.

**Levels**, lowest to highest: `"DEBUG"`, `"INFO"`, `"WARNING"`, `"ERROR"`.

**A handler** is any object with a method `emit(record)`. A **record** is a dict

```
{"level": "INFO", "logger": "app.db", "message": "connected", "fields": {"host": "x"}}
```

**The two handlers you write**

- `ListHandler()` keeps every record it receives in its `records` list.
- `FormattingHandler(formatter, sink)` calls `sink(formatter(record))` for each record (`formatter` turns a record into a string; `sink` takes a string).

**`Logger(name, level="INFO", parent=None)`**

- `debug(message, **fields)`, `info(...)`, `warning(...)` and `error(...)` log at that level. A message **below the logger's effective level** is dropped.
- `add_handler(handler)` attaches a handler to this logger.
- `set_level(level)` changes the level; a level that is not one of the four names raises `ValueError("Bad level")`. `set_level(None)` means "inherit".
- `effective_level` is the level name that applies: this logger's own, or else its parent's, and so on up to the first logger that has one.
- `child(name)` returns the child logger called `"<this name>.<name>"` whose parent is this logger. It has **no level of its own** (it inherits, and follows later changes of its parent), and asking for the same child name again returns the **same object**.

**Delivering a record.** After the level check (made on the logger the call was made on, and only there), the record goes to that logger's handlers and then to the handlers of **every ancestor**, nearest first. Each handler receives **its own copy** of the record (changing it does not affect the next handler), and a handler that **raises** an exception must not stop the others: swallow it and carry on.

**Your `Logger` is tested with handlers you have never seen.** The tests write their own classes with an `emit(record)` method and attach them.

**Example**

```
app = Logger("app")
mem = ListHandler()
app.add_handler(mem)
app.child("db").info("connected", host="x")
mem.records[0]["logger"]      # "app.db"
```
tests:
app.debug("hidden")
app.info("hello", user="asha", n=2)
app.warning("careful")
app.error("boom")

lines = []
fmt = Logger("svc")
fmt.add_handler(FormattingHandler(lambda r: r["level"] + ":" + r["message"], lines.append))
fmt.info("up")
fmt.debug("no")
fmt.error("down")

class Counter:
    def __init__(self):
        self.count = 0
    def emit(self, record):
        self.count += 1
counter = Counter()
custom = Logger("custom")
custom.add_handler(counter)
custom.info("a")
custom.child("x").info("b")
custom.child("x").debug("c")

class Broken:
    def emit(self, record):
        raise RuntimeError("disk full")
resilient = Logger("r")
good = ListHandler()
resilient.add_handler(Broken())
resilient.add_handler(good)
resilient.info("still delivered")
assert [r["message"] for r in good.records] == ["still delivered"]

class Vandal:
    def emit(self, record):
        record["message"] = "vandalised"
        record["fields"]["x"] = 1
safe = Logger("s")
after = ListHandler()
safe.add_handler(Vandal())
safe.add_handler(after)
safe.info("clean", y=2)

top = Logger("top", level="ERROR")
below = top.child("below")
below.set_level("DEBUG")
seen = ListHandler()
top.add_handler(seen)
below.debug("child level decides")
assert [r["message"] for r in seen.records] == ["child level decides"]
hints: A logger has a name, an optional own level, an optional parent and a list of handlers. `effective_level` walks up the parents until it finds a logger with a level of its own, so a child follows later changes of its parent automatically (do not copy the level when you create the child).

Delivering is a loop: for this logger and then each ancestor, hand every handler a **new** record dict (with a copied `fields`). Wrap each `emit` in `try/except Exception` so one broken handler cannot silence the rest.

Check the level only once, on the logger the call was made on: the ancestors' levels are not consulted, only their handlers are used. Cache children in a dictionary so `child("db")` returns the same object every time.
lld-logger-framework.explanation:
**The idea.** This is the shape of Python's own `logging`, Log4j and every other logging library: **loggers** form a tree (by dotted name), **handlers** do the output, and a record travels from a logger up through its ancestors. Splitting *what to say* (the logger and its level) from *where it goes* (handlers) is the **Observer** pattern: a logger announces a record and any number of handlers, which it knows only as "has `emit`", receive it.

```mermaid
classDiagram
    class Logger {
        +name
        +effective_level
        +child() Logger
        +add_handler()
        +info()
    }
    class Handler {
        <<interface>>
        +emit()
    }
    Logger "1" o-- "*" Handler
    Logger --> Logger : parent
    Handler <|.. ListHandler
    Handler <|.. FormattingHandler
    Handler <|.. YourFileHandler
```

**Three rules that make it robust.**

1. **A failing handler must not hurt the application.** Logging is the last place a program should crash from. The `try/except` per handler also keeps one bad sink from silencing the others.
2. **Each handler gets its own copy.** A handler that edits the record (the `Vandal` in the tests) would otherwise corrupt what the next handler sees. Copy what you hand to code you do not control.
3. **Levels inherit dynamically.** A child with no level of its own reads its parent's at log time, so `app.set_level("ERROR")` quiets the whole subtree in one call. Copying the level when the child is made would freeze it.

**The subtle bit.** The level filter is applied once, at the logger you called. The ancestors' *levels* are not consulted, only their handlers, which is why a child set to `DEBUG` under an `ERROR` parent still delivers its debug record to the parent's handler (the last test). That is how Python's `logging` behaves too.

**Extension.** The tests plug in `Counter`, `Broken` and `Vandal`, classes you have never seen: only the `emit` interface is used.

**Complexity.** O(depth of the tree + handlers) per message.

**Going further.** Real frameworks also let a *handler* have its own minimum level and a *filter* that can drop records. Where would those go, and would they change `Logger`?

lld-lru-cache.title: LRU Cache With Stats
lld-lru-cache.description: Build a fixed-size cache that evicts the least recently used entry, with O(1) get and put and hit/miss counters.
lld-lru-cache.statement:
Write a class `LRUCache`: a key-value cache with a fixed capacity that, when full, throws away the entry that was **used least recently**.

**Creating one:** `LRUCache(capacity)`; `capacity` must be an `int` of 1 or more (not a `bool`), else `ValueError("Capacity must be positive")`.

**Methods**

- `get(key, default=None)` returns the value and makes the key the **most recently used**. A missing key returns `default` and counts as a miss.
- `peek(key, default=None)` returns the value **without** changing recency and without touching the counters.
- `put(key, value)` stores the value and makes the key the most recently used. Updating an existing key never evicts. When a **new** key arrives and the cache is full, the least recently used entry is removed first and `put` returns it as a `(key, value)` tuple; otherwise `put` returns `None`.
- `delete(key)` removes a key and returns `True`, or returns `False` when it was not there.
- `keys()` is a list of the keys, **most recently used first**.
- `len(cache)`, `key in cache` (does **not** change recency), and `stats`: a `(hits, misses)` tuple counting `get` calls only.

**Speed.** `get` and `put` must be O(1). The tests run 200,000 operations on a cache of 1,000 entries and expect it to finish quickly.
tests: assert len(cache) == 0 and cache.keys() == [] and cache.stats == (0, 0)
assert cache.put("a", 1) is None and cache.put("b", 2) is None and cache.put("c", 3) is None
assert cache.keys() == ["d", "a", "c"] and "b" not in cache and "a" in cache
assert cache.get("b") is None and cache.get("b", "none") == "none"
assert cache.keys() == ["c", "d", "a"] and cache.get("c") == 30 and len(cache) == 3
assert cache.put("d", 40) is None and cache.keys() == ["d", "e", "c"]
assert cache.delete("e") is True and cache.delete("e") is False and cache.keys() == ["d", "c"] and len(cache) == 2
assert cache.put("x", 1) is None and cache.put("y", 2) == ("c", 30)
assert zero.put(1, "a") is None and zero.put(2, "b") == (1, "a") and zero.get(1) is None and zero.get(2) == "b"
assert "k" in nothing and nothing.get("k", "d") is None and nothing.stats == (1, 0)

big = LRUCache(1000)
started = time.time()
for number in range(200000):
    big.put(number, number)
    big.get(number - 500)
hints: You need two things at once: look a key up in O(1) and know which key is oldest in O(1). A hash map that also remembers insertion order does both: Python's `collections.OrderedDict` has `move_to_end` and `popitem(last=False)`.
Keep the least recently used entry at the **front** and the most recent at the **back**. `get` and `put` of an existing key both move the key to the back; eviction pops from the front.
An update to an existing key must never evict, even when the cache is full. And `peek`, `in` and `keys` must not move anything, otherwise merely looking at the cache changes what it evicts.
lld-lru-cache.explanation:
**The idea.** An LRU cache is a hash map and a recency list that stay in step. The classic solution joins a dictionary to a doubly linked list so both "find" and "move to front" are O(1). `OrderedDict` is exactly that pair, built in.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    A[oldest] --> B[b] --> C[c] --> D[newest a]
    D -. "get a moves it here" .-> D
    A -. "evict from here" .-> A
```

**Reads are writes.** The surprise of LRU is that a `get` changes state. Reading must update recency or "least recently used" would mean "least recently inserted". Everything that must not count as a use (`peek`, `in`, `keys`) is therefore a separate path.

**Update is not insert.** A full cache that receives a *known* key has nothing to evict. Checking `key in items` first is what avoids the off-by-one that throws away a healthy entry.

**Complexity.** `get`, `put`, `delete` are O(1) average. Space is O(capacity).

**Going further.** Thread safety: two threads both calling `get` mutate the order. What lock granularity would you pick, and what does a read-write lock buy you when every read writes?

lld-matrix.title: Matrix
lld-matrix.description: Build an immutable matrix with addition, scalar and matrix multiplication, transpose, powers and clear shape errors.
lld-matrix.statement:
Write an immutable class `Matrix` of numbers.

**Creating one:** `Matrix(rows)` where `rows` is a list of equal-length lists of numbers. The matrix keeps its **own copy**. Raise `ValueError` for: no rows or a row with no numbers `"Matrix cannot be empty"`, then rows of different lengths `"Rows must have equal length"`.

**Properties:** `rows` (a tuple of tuples), `shape` (`(row count, column count)`), and `T`, the **transpose** (a new matrix). `m[r, c]` is one cell. `Matrix.identity(n)` is the n by n identity (`ValueError("Size must be positive")` when `n` is not an `int` of 1 or more).

**Operators** (every one returns a **new** matrix)

- `a + b` and `a - b` need equal shapes, else `ValueError("Shapes do not match")`.
- `a * k` and `k * a` multiply every cell by a number `k` (an `int` or `float`). Multiplying two matrices with `*` is not supported (`TypeError`: return `NotImplemented`).
- `a @ b` is the matrix product; the columns of `a` must equal the rows of `b`, else `ValueError("Inner dimensions do not match")`.
- `a ** k` is `a` multiplied by itself `k` times, for an `int` `k` of 0 or more (`a ** 0` is the identity); the matrix must be square, else `ValueError("Matrix must be square")`. A negative or non-int `k` is a `TypeError`.
- `==` compares shape and cells; matrices are hashable.

`trace()` is the sum of the diagonal (square matrices only, same error). `str(m)` puts each row on its own line with the numbers separated by one space.
tests: assert m.rows == ((1, 2), (3, 4)) and m.shape == (2, 2) and m[1, 0] == 3 and m[0, 1] == 2
assert error_of(Matrix, []) == "ValueError: Matrix cannot be empty"
assert error_of(Matrix, [[]]) == "ValueError: Matrix cannot be empty"
assert error_of(Matrix, [[1, 2], [3]]) == "ValueError: Rows must have equal length"
assert m.T == Matrix([[1, 3], [2, 4]]) and Matrix([[1, 2, 3]]).T.shape == (3, 1) and m.T.T == m
assert error_of(Matrix.identity, 0) == "ValueError: Size must be positive"
assert error_of(Matrix.identity, 2.0) == "ValueError: Size must be positive"
assert error_of(Matrix.identity, True) == "ValueError: Size must be positive"
assert m + m == Matrix([[2, 4], [6, 8]]) and m - m == Matrix([[0, 0], [0, 0]])
assert error_of(lambda: m + Matrix([[1, 2, 3]])) == "ValueError: Shapes do not match"
assert error_of(lambda: m - Matrix([[1], [2]])) == "ValueError: Shapes do not match"
assert kind_of(lambda: m + 1) == "TypeError" and kind_of(lambda: m * m) == "TypeError" and kind_of(lambda: m * "a") == "TypeError"
assert (m @ Matrix.identity(2)) == m and (Matrix.identity(2) @ m) == m
assert error_of(lambda: m @ Matrix([[1, 2, 3]])) == "ValueError: Inner dimensions do not match"
assert fib ** 0 == Matrix.identity(2) and fib ** 1 == fib and fib ** 2 == Matrix([[2, 1], [1, 1]])
assert error_of(lambda: Matrix([[1, 2, 3]]) ** 2) == "ValueError: Matrix must be square"
assert error_of(lambda: Matrix([[1, 2, 3]]).trace()) == "ValueError: Matrix must be square"
assert kind_of(lambda: m ** -1) == "TypeError" and kind_of(lambda: m ** 1.5) == "TypeError" and kind_of(lambda: m ** True) == "TypeError"
assert hash(m) == hash(Matrix([[1, 2], [3, 4]])) and len({m, Matrix([[1, 2], [3, 4]])}) == 1
hints: Store the rows as a tuple of tuples, copied in the constructor. That alone gives you immutability of the data, a free `==` and a free `hash`.
For the product, each cell is a row of `a` dotted with a column of `b`. `zip(*b.rows)` gives you the columns, so a cell is `sum(x * y for x, y in zip(row, column))`.

A power does not need `k` multiplications: square the base and multiply it into the result whenever the lowest bit of `k` is set. The identity matrix is the starting result, which is also why `a ** 0` needs no special case.
lld-matrix.explanation:
**The idea.** A matrix is a value: the same cells mean the same matrix. Storing a tuple of tuples makes equality and hashing the tuple's own, and the constructor is the one place that checks the shape; every operator builds a new matrix through it.

**Shape errors are the contract.** Most matrix bugs are a silent wrong-shaped result. Raising a clear `ValueError` the moment shapes disagree is the whole value of wrapping a list of lists in a class.

**`*` versus `@`.** Python gives matrix product its own operator for a reason: `a * b` reads like cell-by-cell multiplication, which is a different thing. Refusing `*` between matrices (`NotImplemented`) removes the ambiguity.

**Fast powers.** Squaring and halving the exponent needs O(log k) multiplications. This is how Fibonacci's `F(10**18)` mod a number is computed: `[[1,1],[1,0]] ** n`.

**Complexity.** Product of an n by m and an m by p matrix is O(n*m*p). Power is O(n^3 log k).

**Going further.** Add `determinant()` (cofactor expansion for small sizes) and think about what `__eq__` should do with `1` and `1.0` cells.

lld-media-player-state.title: Media Player States
lld-media-player-state.description: Build a media player whose play, pause, stop and next buttons each do something different depending on the state it is in.
lld-media-player-state.statement:
Write a class `MediaPlayer` that plays a list of tracks. Each track is `(title, seconds)`.

**Creating one:** `MediaPlayer(tracks)`. It starts in the state `"stopped"` on the first track at position `0`.

**Reading**

- `state` is `"stopped"`, `"playing"` or `"paused"`.
- `track` is the title of the current track (the first one while stopped), or `None` when the list is empty.
- `position` is the seconds played in the current track.

**Actions.** Each returns the new `state`. What an action does depends on the state:

| action | stopped | playing | paused |
|---|---|---|---|
| `play()` | start playing | nothing | resume (keep the position) |
| `pause()` | `ValueError("Nothing is playing")` | pause | nothing |
| `stop()` | nothing | stop and reset to the **first** track at `0` | same as playing |
| `next_track()` | `ValueError("Nothing is playing")` | go to the next track at position `0`, keep playing | same, and it **plays** |

- `play()` on an **empty** list raises `ValueError("No tracks")`.
- `next_track()` on the **last** track stops the player (back to the first track at `0`).

**Time.** `tick(seconds)` moves time forward. It only has an effect while **playing**: the position grows by `seconds`; whenever it reaches or passes the **end of the track** the player goes to the next track, as if `next_track()` had been called, and the **leftover time carries into the new track** (it may even finish that one too). Reaching the end of the last track stops the player. It returns the state.

**Example**

```
player = MediaPlayer([("one", 10), ("two", 5)])
player.play()          # "playing"
player.tick(12)        # "playing"   track "two" at position 2
player.tick(3)         # "stopped"   the playlist ended
```
tests: assert player.stop() == "stopped" and player.tick(100) == "stopped" and player.position == 0
assert player.play() == "playing" and player.tick(0) == "playing" and player.position == 0
assert empty.track is None and empty.state == "stopped" and empty.position == 0
assert single.tick(2) == "playing" and single.tick(1) == "stopped" and single.position == 0
hints: Make one small class per state (`_Stopped`, `_Playing`, `_Paused`), each with all five methods. The player forwards every action to its current state object and the state object decides what happens, including switching to another state.
Put the shared work on the player (`_become(state)`, `_rewind()`), so a state only says *what* to do. The "stopped" and "paused" tick are the same one-liner: return the name without moving anything.

For `tick`, add the seconds, then loop while the position is at or past the end of the track: compute the leftover, move to the next track (or stop if it was the last), and put the leftover into the new position. A single tick can cross several short tracks.
lld-media-player-state.explanation:
**The idea.** When an object behaves differently in different situations, the usual code is a tangle of `if self.state == "paused" and ...`. The State pattern moves each situation's behaviour into its own class, so adding or changing one state touches one place.

```mermaid
stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> stopped
    stopped --> playing: play
    playing --> paused: pause
    paused --> playing: play
    playing --> stopped: stop or the playlist ends
    paused --> stopped: stop
    playing --> playing: next_track or the track ends
    paused --> playing: next_track
```

**The table is the specification.** The 3 x 4 table in the statement is exactly the set of methods on the three state classes. If you can fill a table like that, you can write the pattern. A cell that says "nothing" is a method that returns the state name; a cell that says "error" is one that raises.

**When the pattern is worth it.** Earlier, the vending machine derived its state from the money inserted, with no state classes at all. That was right: its states had little behaviour of their own. Here each state reacts differently to *every* action, so classes pay off; a flag plus `if` chains would grow with every new button.

**Context and states.** The player is the *context*: it holds the data (tracks, index, position) and delegates. States hold no data of their own, which is why a new state object can be created freely on each transition.

**Leftover time.** `tick(12)` on a 10-second track must put 2 seconds into the next one. Subtract the track length instead of resetting to 0, otherwise a long tick loses time and a very long one never skips short tracks.

**Going further.** Add a `repeat` setting to the context. Which state classes change, and which do not?

lld-meeting-room-booking.title: Meeting Room Booking
lld-meeting-room-booking.description: Book the smallest free meeting room that fits a group, with cancellations and back-to-back bookings.
lld-meeting-room-booking.statement:
Write a class `RoomBooking` for an office with meeting rooms.

**Creating one:** `RoomBooking(rooms)` where `rooms` maps a room name to its capacity, for example `{"Alpha": 10, "Beta": 4}`.

**Methods**

- `book(start, end, people)` books a room for the time `[start, end)` (whole numbers, like minutes since midnight) and returns `(booking_id, room_name)`.
  - Choose the room with the **smallest capacity that still holds `people`** and is **free for the whole time**. If two rooms have the same capacity, pick the one whose name comes first alphabetically.
  - If no room qualifies, return `None` and change nothing.
  - Booking ids are `1, 2, 3, ...` in the order of **successful** bookings; a failed attempt does not use up an id.
  - `end` is not included: a booking that ends at `10` does not clash with one that starts at `10`.
  - Raise `ValueError("Bad time range")` when `start >= end`, then `ValueError("Bad group size")` when `people < 1` (check them in that order, before looking at any room).
- `cancel(booking_id)` frees the booking and returns `True`; it returns `False` for an id that never existed or was already cancelled. The id is not reused.
- `schedule(room_name)` returns the room's current bookings as a list of `(start, end)` pairs, **sorted by start time**. An unknown room raises `ValueError("Unknown room")`.

**Example**

```
rb = RoomBooking({"Alpha": 10, "Beta": 4, "Gamma": 4})
rb.book(9, 10, 3)     # (1, "Beta")     smallest room that fits, "Beta" before "Gamma"
rb.book(9, 10, 3)     # (2, "Gamma")    Beta is busy at 9
rb.book(10, 11, 3)    # (3, "Beta")     back to back with booking 1 is fine
```
hints: Sort the rooms once, in `__init__`, by `(capacity, name)`. Then "smallest room that fits and is free" is just the first room in that order that passes two checks.
Two time ranges `[a, b)` and `[c, d)` overlap exactly when `a < d` and `c < b`. Because the end is excluded, that comparison is already right for back-to-back bookings: do not use `<=`.
Hand out an id only when a booking actually succeeds, and keep a map from id to room so `cancel` knows where to look and can tell "already cancelled" from "never existed".
lld-meeting-room-booking.explanation:
**The idea.** Most of the work is choosing the right data to keep. Two small structures do it: the rooms in a fixed order (smallest capacity first, then name), and for each room the list of bookings it holds. Booking is then a scan in that order for the first room that fits the group and has no overlapping booking.

**Overlap, once.** Two half-open ranges `[a, b)` and `[c, d)` overlap when `a < d and c < b`. Memorise that; it is the building block of every scheduling problem. Because the end is excluded there is no special case for back-to-back bookings, and it also handles one range containing the other.

**Best fit, not first fit.** Always offering the biggest free room would work but wastes it: a group of two should not take the 20-person room while a four-seat room is free. The tests check this with four rooms that fill up in order.

**Ids.** Handing out ids from a counter that only moves on success is what the statement asks. Two common slips: incrementing before you know the booking will succeed, and reusing an id after a cancel.

**Complexity.** `book` is O(rooms × bookings per room) here, because it scans each room's list. That is fine for an office; at scale you would keep each room's bookings sorted and binary-search for the neighbour, or use an interval tree, to get O(log n) per room.

**Going further.** Recurring bookings ("every Monday at 9") break the "list of ranges" idea. What would you store instead, and how would overlap checking change?

lld-menu-composite.title: Menu Tree (Composite)
lld-menu-composite.description: Model a menu of items and nested sections that answer total, count, search and printing the same way (Composite).
lld-menu-composite.statement:
Write two classes, `Item` and `Section`, that share one interface: the *Composite* pattern. A menu is a tree; callers treat a single dish and a whole section of dishes alike.

**Common to both**

- `name` (stripped; blank is `ValueError("Name required")`) and `parent` (the `Section` it is in, or `None`).
- `total`: the sum of the prices of every item below (an item's own price for an `Item`).
- `count`: how many items are below (`1` for an `Item`).
- `find(name)`: the first node with that name, searching this node first and then each child's subtree in order (depth first); `None` if there is none.
- `path(name)`: the list of names from this node down to the node called `name` (this node's own name first), or `None`.
- `lines()`: the menu as a list of text lines. An `Item` is one line, `"<name> <price>"`, with the price in cents shown as `12.50` (`1250`) or `0.05` (`5`). A `Section` is the line `"<name>:"` followed by its children's lines, **each indented by two spaces**.

**Item.** `Item(name, price)`; `price` must be an `int` of 0 or more (not a `bool`), else `ValueError("Price must be a non-negative integer")`. Check the name first.

**Section.** `Section(name)`.

- `children` is a **tuple** of the children in order.
- `add(*children)` appends nodes and returns the section. Checks in this order, **before anything is added**: a child that is not an `Item` or `Section` `ValueError("Not a menu node")`; a child that is this section or one of its ancestors `ValueError("Cycle")`; a child that already has a parent (or appears twice in this call) `ValueError("Already in a section")`.
- `remove(child)` detaches a child (its `parent` becomes `None`); a node that is not a child of this section is `ValueError("Not in this section")`.
tests: assert soup.name == "Soup" and soup.total == 450 and soup.count == 1 and soup.parent is None
assert soup.lines() == ["Soup 4.50"] and Item("Gum", 5).lines() == ["Gum 0.05"] and Item("Free", 0).lines() == ["Free 0.00"] and Item("Big", 123456).lines() == ["Big 1234.56"]
assert soup.find("Soup") is soup and soup.find("x") is None and soup.path("Soup") == ["Soup"] and soup.path("x") is None

menu = Section("Menu")
starters = Section("Starters")
mains = Section("Mains")
pasta = Section("Pasta")
salad = Item("Salad", 600)
assert menu.add(starters, mains) is menu and menu.children == (starters, mains)
assert starters.add(soup, salad) is starters and mains.add(pasta, Item("Steak", 2400)) is mains
assert menu.total == 450 + 600 + 2400 + 1200 + 999 and menu.count == 5 and starters.total == 1050 and pasta.count == 2
assert soup.parent is starters and starters.parent is menu and menu.parent is None

assert menu.lines() == [
    "Menu:",
    "  Starters:",
    "    Soup 4.50",
    "    Salad 6.00",
    "  Mains:",
    "    Pasta:",
    "      Penne 12.00",
    "      Soup 9.99",
    "    Steak 24.00",
]
assert Section("Empty").lines() == ["Empty:"] and Section("Empty").total == 0 and Section("Empty").count == 0
assert menu.find("Soup") is soup and menu.find("Pasta") is pasta and menu.find("Menu") is menu and menu.find("Nothing") is None
assert menu.find("Soup").parent is starters and mains.find("Soup").name == "Soup"
assert menu.path("Penne") == ["Menu", "Mains", "Pasta", "Penne"] and menu.path("Menu") == ["Menu"] and menu.path("Soup") == ["Menu", "Starters", "Soup"]
assert mains.path("Penne") == ["Mains", "Pasta", "Penne"] and mains.path("Salad") is None and menu.path("zzz") is None
assert error_of(menu.add, "not a node") == "ValueError: Not a menu node"
assert error_of(menu.add, Item("Z", 1), 5) == "ValueError: Not a menu node"
assert error_of(mains.add, soup) == "ValueError: Already in a section"
assert error_of(menu.add, pasta) == "ValueError: Already in a section"
assert error_of(menu.add, fresh, fresh) == "ValueError: Already in a section"
assert error_of(menu.add, fresh, soup) == "ValueError: Already in a section"
assert len(menu.children) == before and fresh.parent is None
assert error_of(menu.add, fresh, "x") == "ValueError: Not a menu node" and fresh.parent is None
assert error_of(menu.add, fresh, menu) == "ValueError: Cycle" and fresh.parent is None
assert fresh.parent is menu and menu.children == (starters, mains, fresh)
assert error_of(starters.remove, fresh) == "ValueError: Not in this section"
assert error_of(starters.remove, "x") == "ValueError: Not in this section"
assert soup.parent is None and starters.children == (salad,) and menu.total == 600 + 2400 + 1200 + 999 + 100
hints: Give `Item` and `Section` the same methods, and let a `Section` answer each one by asking its children and combining: `total` is the sum of the children's totals, `lines` is its own heading plus the children's lines with two spaces added. The caller never asks "is this a leaf?".
Share what is identical (the name check, `parent`, `find`, `path`) in a small base class. `find` and `path` only differ in what "children" means: none for an item, the list for a section.

`add` must be all-or-nothing: validate every child first (type, then cycle, then "already has a parent or appears twice") and only then attach them. For the cycle check, walk from the section up through its parents; if you meet the child on the way, the child is an ancestor.
lld-menu-composite.explanation:
**The idea.** Composite makes *one thing* and *a group of things* look the same to the caller. `menu.total` works whether `menu` is a single dish or a menu of menus, because every node answers the same questions and a group answers by asking its members.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    M[Menu] --> S[Starters]
    M --> P[Mains]
    S --> a[Soup]
    S --> b[Salad]
    P --> c[Pasta]
    c --> d[Penne]
```

**One parent per node.** A tree node with two parents is a graph, and a graph can contain cycles. Refusing "already in a section" keeps it a tree; the ancestor walk prevents the node being added under its own descendant.

**Validate, then attach.** `add(a, b, bad)` must not leave `a` and `b` attached when `bad` is refused. Two passes (check all, attach all) are simpler than undoing.

**The cost of recursion.** Every operation visits the whole subtree. For a menu that is nothing; for a filesystem with millions of files you cache totals and invalidate on change.

**Complexity.** `total`, `count`, `lines`: O(nodes below). `find`, `path`: O(nodes) worst case. `add`: O(depth).

**Going further.** Cache `total` in each section. Which operations must now tell the parent chain that something changed, and what do you do about an item whose price can change?

lld-micro-batcher.title: Micro-Batcher
lld-micro-batcher.description: Collect items and send them in batches by size or age, keep a failed batch for retry and handle items added while flushing.
lld-micro-batcher.statement:
Sending one item at a time is slow; sending every hour is late. A **micro-batcher** collects items and sends them together when the batch is **full** or **old enough**. Write a class `MicroBatcher`.

**Creating one:** `MicroBatcher(flush, max_size, max_age, clock)`. Check in this order: `flush` is not callable `ValueError("Flush must be callable")`; `max_size` is not an `int` of 1 or more (not a `bool`) `ValueError("Max size must be positive")`; `max_age` is not a number above 0 (not a `bool`) `ValueError("Max age must be positive")`. `clock()` returns the time in seconds; call it **once** in every call to `add`, `tick` and `flush_now`.

**Methods**

- `add(item)` puts the item in the batch. The batch's **age starts when its first item was added**. When the batch reaches `max_size` items it is flushed at once and `add` returns `True`; otherwise `False`.
- `tick()` is called regularly by a timer: when the batch is not empty and `clock() - first_added >= max_age` it is flushed and `tick` returns `True`; otherwise `False`.
- `flush_now()` flushes a non-empty batch immediately (`True`), or does nothing (`False`).
- `pending` is the number of items waiting; `batches_sent` the number of successful flushes.

**Flushing.** `flush(batch)` is called with a **new list** of the items, oldest first. The batcher empties its buffer **before** calling it, so items added *during* the call (by `flush` itself) go into the **next** batch, and their age starts then. If `flush` **raises**, the exception propagates and the batch is **put back in front** of anything added in the meantime, keeping its **original** start time; `batches_sent` does not change. A successful flush increments `batches_sent`.
tests: assert error_of(MicroBatcher, "x", 3, 10, clock) == "ValueError: Flush must be callable" and error_of(MicroBatcher, None, 0, 0, clock) == "ValueError: Flush must be callable"
assert error_of(MicroBatcher, sent.append, 0, 0, clock) == "ValueError: Max size must be positive"
assert batcher.pending == 0 and batcher.batches_sent == 0 and batcher.tick() is False and batcher.flush_now() is False and sent == []
assert batcher.add("a") is False and batcher.add("b") is False and batcher.pending == 2 and sent == []
assert batcher.add("c") is True and sent == [["a", "b", "c"]] and batcher.pending == 0 and batcher.batches_sent == 1
assert batcher.tick() is False and sent == [["a", "b", "c"]]
assert batcher.tick() is True and sent[-1] == ["d"] and batcher.pending == 0 and batcher.batches_sent == 2
assert batcher.tick() is True and sent[-1] == ["e", "f"]
assert batcher.flush_now() is True and sent[-1] == ["h"] and batcher.batches_sent == 5

passed = []
check = MicroBatcher(passed.append, 2, 10, clock)
check.add(1)
check.add(2)
passed[0].append("junk")
check.add(3)
check.add(4)
assert error_of(retry.add, "b") == "OSError: network down" and attempts == [["a", "b"]] and retry.pending == 2 and retry.batches_sent == 0
assert error_of(retry.add, "c") == "OSError: network down" and attempts[-1] == ["a", "b", "c"] and retry.pending == 3
assert retry.tick() is True and attempts[-1] == ["a", "b", "c"] and retry.pending == 0 and retry.batches_sent == 1

clock3 = Clock(0)
age = MicroBatcher(flaky, 10, 10, clock3)
state["fail"] = True
age.add("x")
clock3.now = 10
assert error_of(age.tick) == "OSError: network down" and age.pending == 1
assert age.tick() is True and attempts[-1] == ["x"]

reentrant_sent = []
def spawning(batch):
    reentrant_sent.append(list(batch))
    if len(reentrant_sent) == 1:
        again.add("late")
clock4 = Clock(0)
again = MicroBatcher(spawning, 2, 10, clock4)
again.add("a")
clock4.now = 3
assert again.add("b") is True and reentrant_sent == [["a", "b"]] and again.pending == 1 and again.batches_sent == 1
assert again.tick() is True and reentrant_sent[-1] == ["late"]

clock5 = Clock(50)
mid_state = {"fail": True}
mid_batches = []
def failing_adder(batch):
    if mid_state["fail"]:
        mid.add("during")
        raise RuntimeError("boom")
    mid_batches.append(list(batch))
mid = MicroBatcher(failing_adder, 2, 10, clock5)
mid.add("a")
clock5.now = 55
assert mid.flush_now() is True and mid_batches == [["a", "b", "during"]]

def eater(batch):
    batch.clear()
    raise OSError("eaten")
eat = MicroBatcher(eater, 2, 10, Clock(0))
eat.add("a")

big_sent = []
big = MicroBatcher(lambda batch: big_sent.append(len(batch)), 1000, 10, Clock(0))
for number in range(10500):
    big.add(number)
assert big_sent == [1000] * 10 and big.pending == 500 and big.batches_sent == 10
hints: State: the list of items, the time the **first** item of this batch was added, and a counter. `add` records the time only when the list is empty, and flushes when the size is reached; `tick` flushes when the first item is old enough.

To make "items added while flushing go to the next batch" work, **take the batch out and empty the buffer first**, then call `flush` with a copy. That is also why a failed flush needs a repair step: put the batch back **in front of** whatever arrived meanwhile, and restore the original start time.
Read the clock once per public call, even in `flush_now` (which does not use the value): the statement counts the reads, so a test can detect a version that reads it twice or not at all.
lld-micro-batcher.explanation:
**The idea.** Batching trades a little latency for a lot of throughput: one request with 100 items costs far less than 100 requests. Two triggers bound the trade: **size** (do not grow without limit) and **age** (do not wait for ever when traffic is slow).

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A[add item] --> B{first item?}
    B -- yes --> C[start the age clock]
    A --> D{size reached?}
    D -- yes --> E[flush]
    T[timer tick] --> F{oldest item old enough?}
    F -- yes --> E
    E --> G{flush raised?}
    G -- yes --> H[put the batch back, keep its age]
    G -- no --> I[batches_sent + 1]
```

**Empty the buffer before calling out.** The flush function is somebody else's code: it may be slow, may add items, may fail. If the batcher cleared its buffer *after* the call, items added during it would be lost or sent twice. Taking the batch out first gives each item exactly one home.

**A failed batch keeps its age.** Restarting the clock on failure would let a broken downstream delay data indefinitely; keeping the original time means the next `tick` retries at once. The repaired buffer puts the failed items **first**, so order is preserved.

**Copy on the way out.** The flush callback receives a copy: if it keeps or changes the list, the batcher's own state is untouched.

**Complexity.** `add` and `tick` are O(1) apart from the flush itself (O(batch)).

**Going further.** Retrying forever with the same batch can wedge a pipeline (a poison item). Add a retry limit and a dead-letter list; which of the counters in this class would change?

lld-money-value-object.title: Money as a Value Object
lld-money-value-object.description: Build an immutable Money class with equality, hashing, arithmetic, ordering and a fair way to split an amount.
lld-money-value-object.statement:
Write a class `Money` that holds an amount in **whole cents** and a currency. It is a **value object**: two `Money` with the same cents and currency are interchangeable.

**Creating one:** `Money(cents, currency)`.

- `cents` must be an `int` (not a `bool`, not a float): otherwise `ValueError("Cents must be a whole number")`. It may be negative.
- `currency` must be a string of exactly three upper-case ASCII letters (`"USD"`): otherwise `ValueError("Bad currency")`.
- Read them as `money.cents` and `money.currency`.
- A `Money` is **immutable**: assigning to any attribute (including `cents`) raises `AttributeError`.

**Equality and hashing.** Equal when cents and currency are equal. The same objects must work as set members and dictionary keys. Comparing with something that is not a `Money` (`money == 1050`) is simply `False`, not an error.

**Arithmetic** (every result is a new `Money`)

- `a + b` and `a - b` need the same currency: otherwise `ValueError("Currency mismatch")`.
- `a * n` and `n * a` for an `int` `n`.
- `-a`.
- `<`, `<=`, `>`, `>=` between two `Money` of the same currency (otherwise the same `ValueError`), so `sorted(...)` works.
- `Money.zero(currency)` is a class method returning `Money(0, currency)`, so `sum(list_of_money, Money.zero("USD"))` works.

**Splitting.** `money.allocate(parts)` returns a list of `parts` `Money` that add up to **exactly** the original: every part gets `abs(cents) // parts` cents (with the original's sign) and the leftover cents are handed out **one each to the first parts**. So `Money(100, "USD").allocate(3)` is `[34, 33, 33]` cents, and `Money(-100, "USD").allocate(3)` is `[-34, -33, -33]`. `parts` below 1 raises `ValueError("Parts must be at least 1")`.

**Printing.** `str(Money(1050, "USD"))` is `"USD 10.50"` and `str(Money(-5, "EUR"))` is `"EUR -0.05"`. `repr` is `"Money(1050, 'USD')"`.

**Example**

```
price = Money(1999, "USD")
price * 3                   # Money(5997, 'USD')
Money(100, "USD").allocate(3)   # [Money(34, 'USD'), Money(33, 'USD'), Money(33, 'USD')]
```
tests: assert (usd == 1050, usd == "USD 10.50", usd == None) == (False, False, False)
assert error_of(lambda: Money(1, "USD") + Money(1, "EUR")) == "ValueError: Currency mismatch"
assert error_of(lambda: Money(1, "USD") - Money(1, "EUR")) == "ValueError: Currency mismatch"
assert error_of(lambda: Money(1, "USD") < Money(1, "EUR")) == "ValueError: Currency mismatch"
assert (Money(1, "USD") < Money(2, "USD"), Money(2, "USD") <= Money(2, "USD"), Money(3, "USD") > Money(2, "USD"), Money(1, "USD") >= Money(2, "USD")) == (True, True, True, False)
assert sorted([Money(30, "USD"), Money(-5, "USD"), Money(10, "USD")]) == [Money(-5, "USD"), Money(10, "USD"), Money(30, "USD")]
assert sum([Money(1, "USD"), Money(2, "USD"), Money(3, "USD")], Money.zero("USD")) == Money(6, "USD")
assert error_of(Money, 1.5, "USD") == "ValueError: Cents must be a whole number"
assert error_of(Money, True, "USD") == "ValueError: Cents must be a whole number"
assert error_of(Money(5, "USD").allocate, 0) == "ValueError: Parts must be at least 1"
hints: A value object is defined by its contents, not its identity. Store the two fields, make them read-only, and write `__eq__` and `__hash__` **together**: if two objects are equal their hashes must be equal, or sets and dictionaries break.

Keep money as integer cents so `0.1 + 0.2` can never happen. For `+`, `-` and ordering, check the currency first and raise `ValueError("Currency mismatch")`; return `NotImplemented` (not an error) when the other side is not a `Money`, so Python can try the other operand.

To split fairly, divide `abs(cents)` with `divmod(cents, parts)`: every part gets the quotient, and the first `remainder` parts get one more cent. Put the sign back at the end so negative amounts also add up exactly.
lld-money-value-object.explanation:
**The idea.** A **value object** is a small immutable object whose identity *is* its contents: `Money(100, "USD")` is the same thing as another `Money(100, "USD")`. Dates, points, colours and versions are value objects too. Making them immutable removes a whole class of bugs: nothing can change the price you stored in a dictionary.

```mermaid
classDiagram
    class Money {
        +cents int
        +currency str
        +allocate() list
        +zero()$ Money
    }
    Money ..> Money : + - * -x return new
```

**The three-way rule.** If you define `__eq__` you must define `__hash__` consistently; Python sets `__hash__` to `None` when you only write `__eq__`, so the object silently stops being usable as a dictionary key. Equal objects must hash equal: here both use `(cents, currency)`.

**Return `NotImplemented`, do not raise.** For `Money(1) + 5`, returning `NotImplemented` lets Python try `int.__radd__` and then raise a clean `TypeError`. Raising from inside `__add__` would stop that handshake. Raise a real error only for a case that is wrong *between two Money*: a currency mismatch.

**Why cents.** Floating-point amounts cannot represent most decimals exactly. Money is the textbook case for integers.

**The allocation puzzle.** Splitting `1.00` three ways cannot give three equal amounts; one cent has to go somewhere. Handing the leftover cents to the first parts guarantees `sum(parts) == original`, the invariant that matters: money is never created or lost. This is Fowler's *Money* pattern.

**Complexity.** All operations are O(1) except `allocate`, which is O(parts).

**Going further.** Real systems also carry a rounding mode and sometimes a currency's number of decimal places (JPY has none). Where would that information live?

lld-movie-ticket-booking.title: Movie Tickets With Expiring Holds
lld-movie-ticket-booking.description: Build a theater seat map where seats are held for a few minutes, then confirmed, released or lost when the hold expires.
lld-movie-ticket-booking.statement:
Write a class `Theater` for one screening.

**Creating one:** `Theater(rows, seats_per_row, clock, hold_seconds=300)`.

- Seats are named by row letter and number: with `rows=2, seats_per_row=3` they are `A1 A2 A3 B1 B2 B3`.
- `clock` is a function that returns the current time in seconds. **Never read the real time**: call `clock()` whenever you need "now".
- A hold made at time `t` is **active** while `clock() < t + hold_seconds` and **expired** from `t + hold_seconds` on.

**Methods**

- `available()` returns the seats that are neither booked nor in an **active** hold, sorted.
- `hold(user, seats)` reserves all of `seats` for `user` and returns a hold id (`"H1"`, `"H2"`, ... in the order holds are made). It is **all or nothing**.
- `confirm(hold_id, user)` turns an active hold into bookings and returns the seats, sorted. The hold id stops existing.
- `release(hold_id, user)` gives the seats back. Releasing an **expired** hold is allowed and does nothing. The hold id stops existing.
- `bookings(user)` returns the user's confirmed seats, sorted.

**What is refused.** Raise `ValueError` with exactly this message, change nothing, and check in this order.

`hold`: no seats (empty list): `"No seats"`; more than 6 seats: `"Too many seats"`; a seat that does not exist: `"Unknown seat"`; a seat that is booked or held by an active hold: `"Seat unavailable"`. (The same seat listed twice is `"Seat unavailable"` too.)

`confirm` and `release`: unknown hold id: `"Unknown hold"`; someone else's hold: `"Not your hold"`; and, for `confirm` only, an expired hold: `"Hold expired"` (the hold stays on record, so asking again says the same).

**Example**

```
now = [0]
theater = Theater(2, 3, lambda: now[0])
hold = theater.hold("ann", ["A1", "A2"])     # "H1"
now[0] = 299
theater.confirm(hold, "ann")                 # ["A1", "A2"]
```
tests: assert error_of(theater.confirm, first, "bob") == "ValueError: Not your hold"
assert error_of(theater.release, first, "bob") == "ValueError: Not your hold"
assert error_of(theater.confirm, second, "cy") == "ValueError: Not your hold"
hints: Store each hold as `(user, seats, expires_at)` under its id. "Active" is only `clock() < expires_at`: nothing needs to remove an expired hold, so you never need a timer.
Compute the blocked seats on demand: everything booked plus the seats of every active hold. Then `available`, and the "seat unavailable" check in `hold`, are one line each.
Validate everything before you change anything (that is what makes `hold` all-or-nothing), and allocate the hold id only after the checks pass, so a refused hold does not use up `H1`.
lld-movie-ticket-booking.explanation:
**The idea.** Ticketing has a middle state that simple booking does not: *held*. A seat is free, held for a short while, then booked, or free again.

```mermaid
stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> free
    free --> held: hold
    held --> booked: confirm
    held --> free: release
    held --> free: time passes
```

**Expiry without a timer.** The last transition has no method call: it happens because time passes. Rather than starting a background job that frees seats (hard to test, racy), each hold stores *when it expires* and every question is answered by comparing with `clock()`. The expired hold is simply ignored. That is called **lazy expiry**, and it is what makes the whole class testable with a fake clock.

**Inject the clock.** `clock` is a constructor argument, not a `time.time()` call inside the methods. A test moves a variable from 299 to 300 and checks the exact boundary; with the real clock it would have to sleep five minutes.

**All or nothing.** `hold` validates the whole request (count, existence, availability) before it records anything. A partial hold that fails halfway would block seats nobody owns.

**Real systems.** The same pattern is how a payment page keeps your seat for ten minutes. With many servers the "check then hold" would need a database transaction or an atomic compare-and-set; here one process makes it simple.

**Going further.** Add `extend(hold_id, user)` that gives a hold more time once. What should happen to an expired hold?

lld-music-player.title: Playlist Player
lld-music-player.description: Build a music player with next, previous, three repeat modes and non-destructive iteration over what is left to play.
lld-music-player.statement:
Write a class `Player` that plays a list of songs (strings) in order.

**Creating one:** `Player(songs, repeat="off")`. It keeps **its own copy** of the list. `repeat` is `"off"`, `"all"` or `"one"`; anything else raises `ValueError("Bad repeat mode")`. When there are songs, the first one is the current song.

**Reading**

- `current` is the song now playing, or `None` when the playlist is empty or has **ended**.
- `repeat` can be read and **assigned** (the same validation applies).

**Moving.** Both return the new `current`.

- `next()`:
  - `"one"`: stays on the same song.
  - `"all"`: goes to the next song, wrapping from the last to the first.
  - `"off"`: goes to the next song; after the last one the player has **ended** (`current` is `None`) and `next()` keeps returning `None`.
  - an empty playlist always returns `None`.
- `previous()` goes to the song before the current one. At the first song it **wraps to the last** in `"all"` mode and otherwise **stays** on the first. From the ended state it goes to the **last** song (in any mode).

**Queue.**

- `enqueue(song)` adds a song at the **end** of the playlist. If the player had ended, the new song becomes current again; the current song never changes otherwise.
- `play_next(song)` inserts a song **right after the current one**. If the playlist is empty or has ended there is no current song, so the new song is added at the end and becomes current.

**Looking ahead.** `iter(player)` yields the songs from the current one to the end, **without moving the player**; every call gives a fresh, independent iterator. (It does not wrap, whatever the repeat mode.)

**Example**

```
p = Player(["a", "b", "c"])
p.next(), p.next(), p.next(), p.next()    # "b", "c", None, None
p.previous()                              # "c"
list(p)                                   # ["c"]
```
tests: assert list(p) == ["c"] and list(p) == ["c"] and p.current == "c"
assert p.next() is None and p.current is None and p.next() is None
assert p.previous() == "c" and p.previous() == "b" and p.previous() == "a" and p.previous() == "a"
assert q.previous() == "c" and q.next() == "a" and q.next() == "b" and q.next() == "c" and q.next() == "a"
assert r.next() == "a" and r.next() == "a" and r.previous() == "a"
assert r.next() == "b" and r.next() is None
assert error_of(setattr, r, "repeat", "x") == "ValueError: Bad repeat mode"
assert e.current is None and e.next() is None and e.previous() is None and list(e) == []

while s.next() is not None:
    pass

t = Player(["a", "b"])
first, second = iter(t), iter(t)
assert next(first) == "a" and next(first) == "b" and next(second) == "a"
hints: Keep a list and an index. "Ended" is simply `index == len(songs)`; `current` is `None` whenever the index is outside the list.

When the player has ended, the cursor already points one past the last song, which is exactly where an appended song lands, so `enqueue` and `play_next` need no special case for it. `__iter__` can return `iter(self._songs[self._index:])`: a slice is a copy, so each call is independent and the player never moves.
Write the three `next()` modes as separate, small branches, then do the same for `previous()` (first song wraps only in "all"). Most bugs come from the ended state: test it explicitly.
lld-music-player.explanation:
**The idea.** A player is a list plus a cursor. All the behaviour is in how the cursor moves at the edges, and the edges are where the three repeat modes differ.

```mermaid
stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> playing
    playing --> playing: next / previous
    playing --> ended: next past the last song (off)
    ended --> playing: previous / enqueue / play_next
```

**A state worth naming.** "Ended" is not a separate flag: it is the cursor pointing one past the last song. Encoding it in the existing index avoids a second variable that could disagree with it.

**Why `__iter__` returns a fresh iterator.** If `Player` were its own iterator (`__next__` plus `return self`), two `for` loops over the same player would fight over one cursor. Returning `iter(copy)` gives every loop its own position, and looking ahead does not play anything.

**Complexity.** `next` and `previous` are O(1); `__iter__` copies the rest of the list, O(n).

**Going further.** Add shuffle by giving the player an injected `random.Random` so tests can seed it; how would shuffle interact with `previous()`?

lld-notification-factory.title: Notification Channel Factory
lld-notification-factory.description: Build a registry that creates senders by name, so a new channel is registered, not hard-coded (Factory).
lld-notification-factory.statement:
Write a `NotificationService` that creates message **senders** for named channels, and three senders to start with.

**A sender** is any object with a method `send(to, message)` that returns a string describing what was sent.

**The three senders you write**

| Class | Created with | `send(to, message)` returns |
|---|---|---|
| `EmailSender` | `EmailSender(from_addr)` | `"email from <from_addr> to <to>: <message>"` |
| `SmsSender` | `SmsSender(sender_id)` | `"sms <sender_id>-><to>: <message>"`, with the message cut to its first **160** characters |
| `PushSender` | `PushSender()` | `"push to <to>: <message>"` |

**`NotificationService()`** starts with the channels `"email"`, `"sms"` and `"push"` already registered. Each service has its **own** registry: registering a channel on one never shows up on another.

- `register(channel, factory, replace=False)` adds a channel. `factory` is any callable that takes keyword arguments and returns a sender. A name that is already registered raises `ValueError("Channel already registered")` unless `replace=True`.
- `create(channel, **config)` calls the channel's factory with `config` and returns a **new** sender each time. An unknown channel raises `ValueError("Unknown channel: <name>")`.
- The three built-in channels need their setting, passed as `from_addr=` for `"email"` and `sender_id=` for `"sms"`; `"push"` needs none. A missing one raises `ValueError("Missing config: from_addr")` (or `sender_id`).
- `channels()` returns the sorted channel names.
- `send(channel, to, message, **config)` creates the sender and returns what its `send` returns.

**Your `NotificationService` is tested with channels you have never seen.** The tests register their own factories (a `"slack"` channel, a class used as a factory) and send through them.

**Example**

```
service = NotificationService()
service.send("email", "asha@example.com", "Hi", from_addr="no-reply@x.io")
# "email from no-reply@x.io to asha@example.com: Hi"
```
tests: assert EmailSender("a@x.io").send("b@x.io", "Hi") == "email from a@x.io to b@x.io: Hi"
assert service.send("email", "asha@example.com", "Hi", from_addr="no-reply@x.io") == "email from no-reply@x.io to asha@example.com: Hi"
assert isinstance(sender, EmailSender) and sender.send("b", "m") == "email from a@x.io to b: m"
assert service.create("email", from_addr="a@x.io") is not sender
assert service.send("slack", "asha", "Deploy done", webhook="hooks/1") == "slack hooks/1 @asha: Deploy done"
assert error_of(service.register, "slack", Pager) == "ValueError: Channel already registered"
assert error_of(service.register, "email", Pager) == "ValueError: Channel already registered"
assert service.send("slack", "x", "now a pager") == "page ops: now a pager"
assert other.send("email", "b", "m", from_addr="a") == "email from a to b: m"
hints: Keep a dictionary from channel name to **factory** (any callable that builds a sender). `create` is a lookup and a call; it must not know which channels exist.
Build the registry in `__init__` (an instance attribute), never as a class attribute or a default argument, or every service shares one registry and the "other service" test fails.

The three built-in channels are registered the *same way* a new one is: small factory functions that check their settings and build the sender. Nothing about `"email"` should be special inside `create`.
lld-notification-factory.explanation:
**The idea.** A **factory** hides *which class* gets built behind a name. The caller says `create("slack", webhook=...)` and does not import `SlackSender`. A **registry** makes the factory open: a new channel is one `register` call, with no edit to the service.

```mermaid
classDiagram
```
