```mermaid
    class NotificationService {
        -factories dict
        +register()
        +create() Sender
        +send()
    }
    class Sender {
        <<interface>>
        +send()
    }
    NotificationService ..> Sender : creates
    Sender <|.. EmailSender
    Sender <|.. SmsSender
    Sender <|.. PushSender
    Sender <|.. YourSlackSender
```

**The wrong version.** `create` full of `if channel == "email": ... elif channel == "sms": ...`. Every new channel edits `NotificationService`, which is the **Open/Closed** violation; a registry turns the `if` chain into a dictionary lookup. The test that registers `"slack"` and a `Pager` *class* (a class is a callable that returns an instance, so it works as a factory unchanged) passes only if `create` treats all channels alike.

**Built-ins are just registrations.** The three starting channels go in the same dictionary through the same door. That is the sign of a good extension point: the framework uses it too.

**Per-instance state.** The registry lives on the instance. A class-level dictionary would make a channel registered in one test appear in every other service for the rest of the run, the kind of bug that only shows up in test order.

**Refusing duplicates.** Silently replacing `"email"` by accident would reroute every email; `replace=True` makes the intent explicit.

**Complexity.** O(1) per create.

**Going further.** Plug-in systems often register by decorator (`@service.channel("slack")`) or by scanning installed packages (entry points). Both end in the same `register` call.

lld-object-pool.title: Object Pool
lld-object-pool.description: Reuse expensive objects through a bounded pool: lazy creation, reuse, reset on release, exhaustion and a lease helper.
lld-object-pool.statement:
Write a class `Pool` that hands out a limited number of reusable objects (database connections, buffers) so they are not created again and again.

**Creating one:** `Pool(factory, size, reset=None)`. `factory()` builds a new object; `size` is the most objects the pool will ever have in existence, an `int` of 1 or more (not a `bool`), else `ValueError("Size must be positive")`. `reset(obj)`, if given, is called to clean an object when it is released.

**Methods**

- `acquire()` returns an object. Use an **idle** object if there is one (the one **released most recently** first); otherwise, if fewer than `size` objects exist, call `factory()` to build a new one (the factory is called **lazily**, never in advance); otherwise raise `ValueError("Pool exhausted")`. If `factory` raises, the error propagates and nothing is counted.
- `release(obj)` returns an object to the pool: first `reset(obj)` is called (if there is a `reset`), then the object becomes idle. Checks: an object that is idle already `ValueError("Already released")`; one this pool never handed out (or has discarded) `ValueError("Not from this pool")`; compare by **identity** (`is`), not equality. If `reset` **raises**, the object is **discarded** (the pool forgets it, so a new one may be built later) and the error propagates.
- `lease()` is a context manager: `with pool.lease() as obj:` acquires on entry and **always** releases on exit, even if the body raised.

**Questions:** `created` (objects that exist now, busy plus idle), `in_use` and `idle`.
tests: assert Conn.made == 0 and pool.created == 0 and pool.in_use == 0 and pool.idle == 0
assert Conn.made == 1 and pool.created == 1 and pool.in_use == 1 and pool.idle == 0
assert first is not second and Conn.made == 2 and pool.created == 2 and pool.in_use == 2
assert error_of(pool.acquire) == "ValueError: Pool exhausted" and Conn.made == 2
assert first.dirty is False and first.cleaned == 1 and pool.idle == 1 and pool.in_use == 1 and pool.created == 2
assert pool.acquire() is first and Conn.made == 2 and pool.in_use == 2 and pool.idle == 0
assert pool.acquire() is first and pool.acquire() is second
assert pool.acquire() is second and pool.acquire() is first
assert error_of(pool.release, Conn()) == "ValueError: Not from this pool"
assert error_of(pool.release, "text") == "ValueError: Not from this pool"
assert error_of(pool.release, None) == "ValueError: Not from this pool"
assert pool.created == 2 and pool.idle == 2 and pool.in_use == 0 and first.cleaned == 4

with pool.lease() as leased:
    assert pool.in_use == 1 and leased is second
    leased.dirty = True
assert pool.in_use == 0 and pool.idle == 2 and leased.dirty is False

with pool.lease() as one:
    with pool.lease() as two:
        assert one is not two and pool.in_use == 2
        assert error_of(pool.acquire) == "ValueError: Pool exhausted"
    assert pool.in_use == 1
assert shaky.created == 0 and shaky.in_use == 0 and shaky.idle == 0
assert error_of(shaky.release, bad_one) == "ValueError: Not from this pool"
assert fresh is not bad_one and fresh.id == 2 and shaky.created == 1
assert shaky.idle == 1 and shaky.acquire() is fresh
assert error_of(fp.acquire) == "RuntimeError: no connection" and fp.created == 0 and fp.in_use == 0
assert fp.created == 1 and fp.in_use == 1 and got is not None

plain = Pool(list, 1)
item = plain.acquire()
item.append(1)
plain.release(item)
hints: Keep two collections: a list of idle objects (use `pop()` so the most recently released comes back first) and a dict of busy objects keyed by `id(obj)`. `created` is just the two sizes added together.
Compare with identity, never `==`: a pooled object may define `__eq__` loosely. Look an object up with `id(obj)` and then confirm `is`, and look for "already released" with `any(item is obj ...)`.
In `release`, remove the object from the busy dict **before** calling `reset`. If `reset` raises, the object is then already forgotten (discarded), and the exception simply propagates.
lld-object-pool.explanation:
**The idea.** Some objects are expensive to make (a database connection, a TLS session) and cheap to clean. A pool makes a few, lends them out, and takes them back, so the expensive step happens at most `size` times.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    A[acquire] --> B{idle object?}
    B -- yes --> C[reuse it]
    B -- no --> D{created < size?}
    D -- yes --> E[factory builds one]
    D -- no --> F[Pool exhausted]
    G[release] --> H[reset then idle]
```

**Lazy, not eager.** Building all `size` objects at start-up wastes time when traffic is low and makes start-up slow when the factory is. The test counts factory calls to prove it.

**Reset on the way back.** The next borrower must never see the previous borrower's state. A reset that fails means the object is in an unknown state, so the safe move is to throw it away and let the pool build a new one later.

**LIFO reuse.** Handing out the most recently released object keeps a few objects "warm" (caches, open sockets) and lets rarely used ones time out. A queue would spread use evenly instead.

**`lease` makes release automatic.** Forgetting `release` leaks an object for ever. A context manager with `finally` makes the correct use the easy one.

**Complexity.** `acquire`, `release`: O(1) apart from the "already released" scan, O(idle).

**Going further.** In a threaded program `acquire` must *wait* when the pool is empty instead of failing. What primitive would you use, and what happens to waiters when an object is discarded?

lld-optimistic-versioning.title: Optimistic Versioning
lld-optimistic-versioning.description: Use version numbers and compare-and-set to avoid lost updates, with a retrying update helper and a hook that simulates a rival writer.
lld-optimistic-versioning.statement:
Write a class `VersionedStore`, a key-value store that stops two writers from overwriting each other without any locks: *optimistic concurrency control*. Every key has a **version**: `0` when it does not exist, then `1, 2, 3, ...` with each successful write.

**Methods**

- `get(key)` returns `(value, version)`; a missing key is `(None, 0)`. `version(key)` is the version alone, and `keys()` the sorted list of keys that exist.
- `put(key, value, expected_version)` writes the value **only if** the key's current version equals `expected_version`, and returns the new version. `expected_version` must be an `int` of 0 or more (not a `bool`), else `ValueError("Bad version")` (checked first). A mismatch is `ValueError("Version conflict: expected <expected> but found <current>")` and nothing changes.
- `update(key, fn, retries=3, before_write=None)` is *read, compute, compare-and-set*, repeated until it works:
  1. read `(value, version)`; compute `new = fn(value)` (`fn` gets `None` for a missing key; if `fn` raises, the error propagates and nothing is written);
  2. if `before_write` is given, call `before_write(attempt)` with the attempt number (1, 2, ...): this is where a test makes a **rival writer** change the key between your read and your write;
  3. if the key's version is **still** the one you read, write `new` with that version and **return `new`**; otherwise start again from step 1 (so `fn` sees the rival's value).

  At most `retries + 1` attempts are made; after the last conflict raise `ValueError("Too many conflicts for <key>")`. `retries` must be an `int` of 0 or more (not a `bool`), else `ValueError("Retries must be 0 or more")` (checked before anything runs).
tests: assert store.get("k") == (None, 0) and store.version("k") == 0 and store.keys() == []
assert store.put("k", "a", 0) == 1 and store.get("k") == ("a", 1) and store.version("k") == 1 and store.keys() == ["k"]
assert error_of(store.put, "k", "b", 0) == "ValueError: Version conflict: expected 0 but found 1" and store.get("k") == ("a", 1)
assert error_of(store.put, "k", "b", 5) == "ValueError: Version conflict: expected 5 but found 1"
assert error_of(store.put, "new", "b", 1) == "ValueError: Version conflict: expected 1 but found 0" and store.keys() == ["k"]

for bad in (-1, 1.5, True, None, "1"):
    assert error_of(store.put, "k", "x", bad) == "ValueError: Bad version"
assert store.put("z", None, 0) == 1 and store.get("z") == (None, 1) and store.keys() == ["k", "z"]

store.put("n", 10, 0)
seen = []
def double(value):
    seen.append(value)
    return value * 2
assert store.update("n", lambda v: v + 1) == 11 and store.get("n") == (11, 2)
assert store.update("fresh", lambda v: (v or 0) + 1) == 1 and store.get("fresh") == (1, 1)
assert seen == [11, 111, 211] and attempts == [1, 2, 3] and store.get("n") == (422, 5)
assert error_of(store.update, "n", lambda v: -1, retries=1, before_write=always) == "ValueError: Too many conflicts for n"
assert error_of(store.update, "n", lambda v: -1, retries=0, before_write=always) == "ValueError: Too many conflicts for n"
assert error_of(store.update, "n", lambda v: v, before_write=count) == "ValueError: Too many conflicts for n" and calls == [1, 2, 3, 4]
assert error_of(store.update, "n", lambda v: v, retries=2, before_write=count) == "ValueError: Too many conflicts for n" and calls == [1, 2, 3, 4, 1, 2, 3]
assert error_of(store.update, "n", boom, before_write=hooked.append) == "RuntimeError: boom" and hooked == [] and store.get("n") == snapshot
assert store.update("n", lambda v: "done", retries=0) == "done" and store.get("n") == ("done", snapshot[1] + 1)
assert store.update("q", lambda v: (v or "none") + "!", before_write=once) == "rival!" and store.get("q") == ("rival!", 2) and ran == [1, 2]
assert other.update("a", lambda v: v + 10) == 11 and other.get("b") == (2, 1) and other.keys() == ["a", "b"]

tally = VersionedStore()
tally.put("count", 0, 0)
for step in range(50):
    tally.update("count", lambda v: v + 1)
hints: Store `(value, version)` per key, and treat a missing key as `(None, 0)`. Then "create" and "update" are the same operation: write with the version you read.

`put` is the whole safety mechanism: compare the version you *read* with the version that is there *now*, and write only if they are equal. Raise the conflict error with both numbers and change nothing otherwise.

In `update`, the loop must **read again** on every attempt (so `fn` sees the rival's value), call the hook between the read and the write, and make at most `retries + 1` attempts. Validate `retries` before the loop starts.
lld-optimistic-versioning.explanation:
**The idea.** Two clients read the same account balance, each adds 10 and writes back: one update is lost. A lock would prevent it by making them take turns. **Optimistic** concurrency lets both proceed and checks at write time: "is this still the version I read?". If not, the write is refused and the client reads again.

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant A as Client A
    participant S as Store
    participant B as Client B
    A->>S: get n (value 11, version 2)
    B->>S: get n (value 11, version 2)
    B->>S: put n=21, expected 2
    S-->>B: version 3
    A->>S: put n=21, expected 2
    S-->>A: conflict: found 3
    A->>S: get n (value 21, version 3), retry
```

**The hook makes the race testable.** Real races depend on timing. `before_write(attempt)` runs exactly between the read and the write, so a test can play the rival deterministically: the second attempt sees the rival's value (the test lists `[11, 111, 211]`).

**When retrying is wrong.** Retrying is safe because `fn` is a pure function of the value. Side effects in `fn` (sending an email) would run once per attempt. That is why the contract says what `fn` may do.

**Bounded retries.** Under heavy contention an optimistic client can starve. A limit turns "spin for ever" into an error the caller can handle (back off, or switch to a lock).

**Complexity.** `put` is O(1); `update` is O(attempts).

**Going further.** HTTP's `ETag` and `If-Match` headers are exactly this protocol. What status code means "your version is stale"?

lld-order-book.title: Order Book
lld-order-book.description: Build the matching engine of an exchange: limit orders, price-time priority, partial fills, cancellation and market depth.
lld-order-book.statement:
Write a class `OrderBook` for one instrument. Prices and quantities are positive integers.

**Method**

- `submit(side, price, quantity)` places a **limit order** and returns `(order_id, trades)`.
  - `side` is `"buy"` or `"sell"`. Order ids are `1, 2, 3, ...` in the order orders are submitted.
  - A **buy** matches against resting **sells** priced **at or below** its limit, cheapest first. A **sell** matches against resting **buys** priced **at or above** its limit, highest first. At the same price the **older order goes first** (price-time priority).
  - Each match is a trade `(price, quantity, resting_order_id)` and happens at the **resting order's price**. Trades are listed in the order they happen.
  - What is not filled **rests** in the book at its limit price.
- `cancel(order_id)` removes the unfilled part of a resting order and returns `True`. It returns `False` when the order is already filled, already cancelled, or never existed.
- `remaining(order_id)` is the unfilled quantity (`0` once filled or cancelled). An unknown id raises `ValueError("Unknown order")`.
- `best_bid` and `best_ask` are the best resting buy and sell prices, or `None`.
- `depth()` returns `{"bids": [...], "asks": [...]}`, each a list of `(price, total_quantity)`: bids from the **highest** price down, asks from the **lowest** price up. Prices with nothing resting are left out.

**What `submit` refuses.** `ValueError("Bad side")` for any other side, then `ValueError("Bad price or quantity")` for a price or quantity that is not an `int` of at least 1 (a `bool` is not). A refused order does **not** use up an id.

**Example**

```
book = OrderBook()
book.submit("sell", 101, 5)       # (1, [])
book.submit("sell", 100, 3)       # (2, [])
book.submit("buy", 101, 4)        # (3, [(100, 3, 2), (101, 1, 1)])
book.depth()                      # {"bids": [], "asks": [(101, 4)]}
```
tests: assert book.best_bid is None and book.best_ask is None and book.depth() == {"bids": [], "asks": []}
assert error_of(book.submit, "buy", 0, 1) == "ValueError: Bad price or quantity"
assert error_of(book.submit, "buy", 10, 0) == "ValueError: Bad price or quantity"
assert error_of(book.submit, "buy", 10.5, 1) == "ValueError: Bad price or quantity"
assert error_of(book.submit, "buy", True, 1) == "ValueError: Bad price or quantity"
assert book.remaining(1) == 4 and book.remaining(2) == 0 and book.remaining(5) == 0
assert book.best_bid == 105 and book.best_ask is None
assert book.remaining(8) == 3 and book.best_ask == 99 and book.best_bid is None
assert book.cancel(8) is True and book.remaining(8) == 0 and book.depth() == {"bids": [], "asks": []}
assert book.cancel(8) is False and book.cancel(1) is False and book.cancel(99) is False
hints: Keep two lists of resting orders (buys and sells). An order is a small record with its side, price and unfilled quantity; "resting" means unfilled quantity above zero.

To match a buy, pick the cheapest resting sell at or below the limit, breaking ties by the lower order id (older first). Trade at the **resting** order's price, then loop until the incoming order is filled or nothing matches.

Cancelling is just setting the unfilled quantity to 0: every other method already ignores orders with nothing left. Allocate the order id only after validation, so a refused order does not use one up.
lld-order-book.explanation:
**The idea.** An exchange keeps two queues: buyers who want the lowest price and sellers who want the highest. A new order is first matched against the opposite side; whatever is left waits its turn.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A[new order] --> B{opposite side has a price that crosses?}
    B -- yes --> C[trade at the resting order's price]
    C --> D{order fully filled?}
    D -- no --> B
    D -- yes --> F[done]
    B -- no --> E[rest in the book]
    E --> F
```

**Price-time priority.** Best price first; among equal prices, whoever arrived first. Using the order id as the tiebreaker works because ids grow with time.

**Trade at the resting price.** The order that was already waiting set the price; the newcomer accepts it. That is why a buy at 101 against a sell at 100 trades at 100: the buyer gets a better deal than asked.

**Cancel as a flag, not a delete.** Setting the remaining quantity to zero keeps every list valid and every id lookup working. Real engines delete lazily too.

**Complexity.** This version rescans the book on every match (O(n) per trade), which is fine to learn the rules. A production book uses a heap or a sorted map per side, with a queue per price level, for O(log n) per order.

**Going further.** Replace the lists with `heapq` keyed by `(price, id)`. What makes lazy deletion of cancelled orders tricky in a heap?

lld-order-state-machine.title: Order State Machine
lld-order-state-machine.description: Model an order lifecycle as a table of allowed transitions, so a different workflow is data, not new code (State).
lld-order-state-machine.statement:
Write an `Order` whose life is a set of **states** and the **actions** that move it between them, and an exception for illegal moves.

**The default workflow**

| from | action | to |
|---|---|---|
| `created` | `pay` | `paid` |
| `created` | `cancel` | `cancelled` |
| `paid` | `ship` | `shipped` |
| `paid` | `cancel` | `cancelled` |
| `shipped` | `deliver` | `delivered` |

`delivered` and `cancelled` are final: no action leaves them.

**`IllegalTransition`** is an exception class (a subclass of `Exception`) that you define.

**`Order(order_id, transitions=None, initial="created")`**

- `transitions` is a dict `{(state, action): new_state}`. With `None` the default workflow above is used. The order keeps **its own copy** of the table: changing the dictionary afterwards must not change the order.
- `state` is the current state.
- `do(action)` performs the action and returns the new state. If the current state does not allow it, raise `IllegalTransition("Cannot <action> an order that is <state>")` (for example `"Cannot ship an order that is created"`) and change nothing.
- `pay()`, `ship()`, `deliver()`, `cancel()` are shortcuts for `do("pay")` and so on.
- `can(action)` says whether the action is allowed now.
- `available_actions()` is the sorted list of actions allowed now (`[]` in a final state).
- `history` is a list of `(from_state, action, to_state)` for every successful action, oldest first. It must be a **copy**: changing it does not change the order.

**Your `Order` is tested with workflows you have never seen**, passed in as a `transitions` table (a document that goes draft, review, published). The class must not hard-code the default states.

**Example**

```
order = Order("o1")
order.pay()                    # "paid"
order.available_actions()      # ["cancel", "ship"]
order.deliver()                # raises IllegalTransition("Cannot deliver an order that is paid")
```
tests: assert error_of(order.ship) == "IllegalTransition: Cannot ship an order that is created"
assert error_of(order.do, "teleport") == "IllegalTransition: Cannot teleport an order that is created"
assert error_of(order.deliver) == "IllegalTransition: Cannot deliver an order that is paid"
assert error_of(order.pay) == "IllegalTransition: Cannot pay an order that is paid"
assert error_of(order.cancel) == "IllegalTransition: Cannot cancel an order that is shipped"
assert error_of(order.pay) == "IllegalTransition: Cannot pay an order that is delivered"
assert (early.available_actions(), error_of(early.pay)) == ([], "IllegalTransition: Cannot pay an order that is cancelled")
assert error_of(page.pay) == "IllegalTransition: Cannot pay an order that is published"
assert error_of(page.do, "submit") == "IllegalTransition: Cannot submit an order that is published"
assert Order("d3", doc, initial="draft").can("delete") is True
hints: Keep the workflow as **data**: a dictionary from `(state, action)` to the next state. `do` is then three lines: look the pair up, refuse if it is missing, otherwise record and move. There is no `if state == "paid"` anywhere.
Copy the table in the constructor (`dict(table)`), and return a copy of the history from the property. Otherwise a caller who edits the dictionary they passed in changes an order that already exists.
Check first, change after: build the error from the *current* state before you touch the state or the history, so a refused action leaves no trace.
lld-order-state-machine.explanation:
**The idea.** An order is in exactly one **state**, and what you may do next depends on that state. The textbook **State** pattern gives every state its own class; for most business workflows there is a lighter, better way: put the states and moves in a **table** and have one small engine read it.

```mermaid
stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> created
    created --> paid: pay
    created --> cancelled: cancel
    paid --> shipped: ship
    paid --> cancelled: cancel
    shipped --> delivered: deliver
    delivered --> [*]
    cancelled --> [*]
```

**Why data beats classes here.** The test passes a *document* workflow (draft, review, published, archived) to the same `Order`. A solution built from `if self.state == "paid"` blocks cannot do that; a table-driven one does it for free. When the rule changes (add a "refund" step), you edit a dictionary, not the engine, and the next workflow is a configuration file, not a deploy.

**Fail loudly and leave no trace.** An illegal action raises a specific exception (`IllegalTransition`) and changes nothing: not the state, not the history. Callers can catch that one type without swallowing real bugs.

**Defensive copies.** The constructor copies the table and `history` returns a copy; the last tests change the original dictionary after the order exists and check that it does not notice.

**When to use real State classes.** If each state has *behaviour* of its own (a `Paid` state that knows how to compute a refund, with its own methods), classes earn their keep. When states differ only in which moves are allowed, a table is simpler and easier to review: product owners can read it.

**Complexity.** `do` and `can` are O(1); `available_actions` is O(number of transitions).

**Going further.** Real workflows need *guards* ("ship only if the address is complete") and *side effects* ("send an email on pay"). Where would you hook them in without turning the table back into code?

lld-parking-lot-1.title: Parking Lot, Step 1: Spots and Fees
lld-parking-lot-1.description: Step 1 of 3: build a parking lot that fits vehicles into spots and charges by the hour, with a clock you can control.
lld-parking-lot-1.statement:
This is **step 1 of 3** on one parking lot. In step 2 and step 3 the owner asks for changes, and the code you write here is what changes.

Write a class `ParkingLot` for a lot with three sizes of spot.

**Creating one:** `ParkingLot(small, medium, large, clock=time.time)`, where the first three numbers are how many spots of each size the lot has. `clock` is a function that returns the current time **in seconds**. Tests pass in a fake clock, so use `clock()` everywhere you need the time, never `time.time()` directly.

**Vehicles** are named by a kind, and each kind fits certain sizes:

| kind | fits |
|---|---|
| `"motorcycle"` | small, medium or large |
| `"car"` | medium or large |
| `"truck"` | large only |

A vehicle takes the **smallest** size that fits and has a free spot.

**Methods**

- `park(plate, kind)` parks the vehicle and returns a **ticket id**: `1, 2, 3, ...` in the order of **successful** parks (a failed attempt does not use up an id). Raise `ValueError` with exactly this message, checking in this order, and change nothing:
  1. `"Unknown vehicle"`: the kind is not in the table;
  2. `"Already parked"`: this plate is already in the lot;
  3. `"Lot full"`: no spot that fits is free.
- `unpark(ticket_id)` removes the vehicle, frees its spot (and its plate, which may park again) and returns the **fee in cents**: **200 cents for each hour started, and at least one hour**. Parking for 0 seconds, 1 second or exactly 3600 seconds costs 200; 3601 seconds costs 400. An unknown or already used ticket raises `ValueError("Unknown ticket")`.
- `available()` returns how many spots are free, as `{"small": n, "medium": n, "large": n}`. It is a **new dictionary on every call**: changing the one you got must not change the lot.

**Example**

```
lot = ParkingLot(1, 1, 1, clock=my_clock)
lot.park("KA-01", "motorcycle")     # 1   takes the small spot
lot.park("KA-02", "motorcycle")     # 2   small is taken, so medium
lot.park("KA-03", "car")            # 3   medium is taken, so large
lot.available()                     # {"small": 0, "medium": 0, "large": 0}
```
tests:
many = ParkingLot(200, 200, 200, clock=clock)
tickets = [many.park("P-%d" % i, "motorcycle") for i in range(600)]
hints: Keep a count of free spots for each size, and a dictionary from ticket id to what you need later: the plate, the size taken and the time it arrived (from `clock()`).

To pick the spot, walk the sizes a vehicle fits **in order from smallest** and take the first with a free spot. Write the table of what fits what as data (a dictionary), not as a chain of `if`s: step 2 and step 3 will be easier.
Hours started is `ceil(seconds / 3600)`, with a minimum of 1. Check your three refusals in the order the statement gives, and only change anything after all three have passed.
lld-parking-lot-1.explanation:
**The idea.** There is no clever algorithm here: the work is modelling. A lot has spots of three sizes, vehicles of three kinds, a ticket per parked vehicle, and a fee. The solution keeps exactly that and nothing more.

```mermaid
classDiagram
    class ParkingLot {
        +park()
        +unpark()
        +available()
    }
    class Ticket {
        plate
        size
        started
    }
    ParkingLot "1" o-- "*" Ticket
```

**Two decisions worth saying out loud.**

- **The clock is an argument.** `ParkingLot(..., clock=time.time)` instead of calling `time.time()` inside. That one parameter is what makes fees testable at all: the tests move a fake clock to exactly 3600 or 3601 seconds. This is *dependency injection* in its smallest form, and it is the first thing interviewers look for when they ask "how would you test this?".
- **What fits what is data.** `FITS` is a dictionary from kind to sizes in preference order. The park logic is one loop over it. If the table were a nest of `if kind == "car"` branches, adding a vehicle kind would mean editing the algorithm.

**Validate, then change.** The three refusals happen before any counter moves, in a fixed order, so a refused `park` leaves the lot exactly as it was.

**Complexity.** All operations are O(1) (a few dictionary and set operations).

**What comes next.** The fee is the weakest part of this design: 200 cents is written into `unpark`. Step 2 is about to ask for different prices per vehicle, and you will see why hard-coding it was the problem.

lld-parking-lot-2.title: Parking Lot, Step 2: Swap the Pricing
lld-parking-lot-2.description: Step 2 of 3: the owner wants prices per vehicle and the freedom to change the rules; pull pricing out of the lot.
lld-parking-lot-2.statement:
This is **step 2 of 3**. The editor already holds a working step 1; change it. Every rule of step 1 still holds (kinds and sizes, the refusals and their order, ticket ids, `available()`, the injected `clock`) **except how the fee is worked out**.

**The change request.** The owner wants

1. a different price for each kind of vehicle, and
2. to change how fees work (flat day rate, a surcharge, happy hour) **without anyone editing `ParkingLot`**.

**A pricing** is any object with a method `fee(kind, minutes)` that returns the fee in cents. `minutes` is the time parked, in **whole minutes, rounded up**: 0 seconds is `0`, 1 second is `1`, 3600 seconds is `60`, 3601 seconds is `61`.

**What to write**

- `ParkingLot(small, medium, large, clock=time.time, pricing=None)`: `unpark` returns `pricing.fee(kind, minutes)` for the kind of the vehicle that is leaving. It calls `fee` **exactly once per `unpark`** and never in `park`. `pricing=None` means `HourlyPricing()`.
- `HourlyPricing(rates=None)` with `fee(kind, minutes)`: the fee is the rate for that kind **times the hours started** (`ceil(minutes / 60)`), with a minimum of one hour. `rates` maps a kind to cents per hour; the default is `{"motorcycle": 100, "car": 200, "truck": 500}`.

**The tests plug in pricing classes you have never seen**, including one that wraps an `HourlyPricing` and adds to its fee. `ParkingLot` must work through `fee(kind, minutes)` alone.

**Example**

```
class DayRate:
    def fee(self, kind, minutes):
        return 1500

lot = ParkingLot(1, 1, 1, clock=my_clock, pricing=DayRate())
lot.unpark(lot.park("KA-01", "car"))     # 1500, whatever the time
```
tests:
priced = ParkingLot(2, 2, 2, clock=clock, pricing=HourlyPricing(rates))
clock.now = 0
ticket = priced.park("P-1", "car")
clock.now = 60 * 61

class Spy:
    def __init__(self):
        self.calls = []
    def fee(self, kind, minutes):
        self.calls.append((kind, minutes))
        return 7
spy = Spy()
watched = ParkingLot(2, 2, 2, clock=clock, pricing=spy)
clock.now = 100
car = watched.park("S-1", "car")
bike = watched.park("S-2", "motorcycle")
hints: The fee is a rule about *money*, not about *parking*. Move it out of `ParkingLot` into its own small class with one method, `fee(kind, minutes)`, and have `unpark` ask it. That class is the "pricing" the owner wants to swap.

`ParkingLot` needs the vehicle's **kind** when it leaves, so remember it in the ticket (step 1 only stored the size). Work out whole minutes rounded up with `math.ceil(seconds / 60)` and hand them over.
Default to `HourlyPricing()` when no pricing is given, and make sure `park` never calls the pricing: the tests check that it is called once per `unpark`, with the right kind and minutes.
lld-parking-lot-2.explanation:
**What changed, and why it hurt.** In step 1 the fee was `hours * 200` inside `unpark`. A per-vehicle price list would have meant editing `unpark`, and so would a flat day rate, and so would a happy-hour discount. A class that has to be reopened for every new business rule violates the **Open/Closed principle**, and a class that does parking *and* pricing violates the **Single Responsibility principle**. Both are the same smell seen from two sides.

**The fix is the same move as the discounts problem.** Pull the changing part out behind a one-method interface and let the caller choose it (**Strategy**). `ParkingLot` now knows only "a pricing has `fee(kind, minutes)`".

```mermaid
classDiagram
    class ParkingLot {
        +park()
        +unpark()
    }
    class Pricing {
        <<interface>>
        +fee()
    }
    ParkingLot --> Pricing : asks once per unpark
    Pricing <|.. HourlyPricing
    Pricing <|.. DayRate
    Pricing <|.. WithSurcharge
    WithSurcharge o-- Pricing : wraps
```

**Decorating pricing.** The `WithSurcharge` test wraps one pricing in another and still looks like a pricing to the lot. That is the **Decorator** pattern, and it only works because the lot depends on the interface and not on `HourlyPricing`.

**What you hand over matters.** The lot gives pricing `kind` and `minutes`: the smallest facts a price could depend on. It does not hand over the lot, the plate, or the ticket. The narrower the interface, the more kinds of pricing can implement it, and the fewer things a pricing can break.

**Keeping step 1 working.** The first dozen tests are step 1's, with the new default rates. Changing a design under existing tests is the real skill here: the old behaviour (ids, refusals, availability) must not move.

**Complexity.** Unchanged: O(1) per operation.

**What comes next.** Pricing is now swappable, but *where a vehicle parks* is still decided inside `park`. Step 3 changes that.

lld-parking-lot-3.title: Parking Lot, Step 3: Choose the Spot
lld-parking-lot-3.description: Step 3 of 3: name the individual spots, report where a vehicle is, and let the owner plug in how a spot is chosen.
lld-parking-lot-3.statement:
This is **step 3 of 3**. The editor holds a working step 2; change it. Every rule of step 2 still holds (kinds, refusals and their order, ticket ids, `available()`, the injected `clock`, and `pricing` with `HourlyPricing` as the default).

**The change request.** The owner wants to know *which spot* each vehicle is in, and wants to change the rule for choosing a spot (nearest the exit, spread out, keep the large ones for trucks) without editing `ParkingLot`.

**Spots have names.** The small spots are `"S1"`, `"S2"`, ... the medium ones `"M1"`, `"M2"`, ... and the large ones `"L1"`, `"L2"`, ... numbered from 1 in each size.

**An allocator** is any function `allocator(candidates)` that returns the name of the spot to use. `candidates` is a list of the spots that are **free and fit the vehicle**, ordered **smallest size first, then by number**: for a car in a fresh lot with 2 medium and 1 large spot it is `["M1", "M2", "L1"]`.

**What to write**

- `ParkingLot(small, medium, large, clock=time.time, pricing=None, allocator=None)`. With `allocator=None` the lot takes the **first** candidate (which is the step 2 behaviour, now with a named spot).
- `park(plate, kind)` works out the candidates, and:
  - if there are none, raises `ValueError("Lot full")` (the allocator is **not** called);
  - otherwise calls `allocator(candidates)` and parks the vehicle in the spot it returns. If the allocator returns a name that is **not in the candidates**, raise `ValueError("Bad allocation")` and change **nothing**: no spot taken, no ticket id used, the plate not recorded.
  - The existing refusals keep their order: `"Unknown vehicle"`, then `"Already parked"`, then the above.
- `spot_of(ticket_id)` returns the spot name of a vehicle that is parked, or raises `ValueError("Unknown ticket")`.
- `unpark` frees that particular spot, so it appears among the candidates of the next vehicle.

**The tests plug in allocators you have never seen**, including one that records what it was given.

**Example**

```
lot = ParkingLot(1, 2, 1, clock=my_clock)
t = lot.park("KA-01", "car")
lot.spot_of(t)                    # "M1"

last = ParkingLot(1, 2, 1, clock=my_clock, allocator=lambda c: c[-1])
last.spot_of(last.park("KA-02", "car"))     # "L1"   candidates were ["M1", "M2", "L1"]
```
tests: last = ParkingLot(1, 2, 1, clock=clock, allocator=lambda candidates: candidates[-1])

class Spy:
    def __init__(self):
        self.calls = []
    def __call__(self, candidates):
        self.calls.append(list(candidates))
        return candidates[0]
spy = Spy()
watched = ParkingLot(1, 1, 1, clock=clock, allocator=spy)
a = watched.park("W-1", "motorcycle")
b = watched.park("W-2", "truck")
c = watched.park("W-3", "car")

taken = ParkingLot(1, 1, 0, clock=clock, allocator=lambda candidates: "M1")
taken.park("Y-1", "car")

priced = ParkingLot(1, 1, 1, clock=clock)
clock.now = 0
ticket = priced.park("Q-1", "car")
clock.now = 3601

big = ParkingLot(300, 300, 300, clock=clock)
spots = [big.spot_of(big.park("P-%d" % i, "motorcycle")) for i in range(900)]
assert spots[0] == "S1" and spots[299] == "S300" and spots[300] == "M1" and spots[899] == "L300"
hints: Give every spot a name when the lot is built (`"S1"` ... `"M1"` ... `"L1"` ...) and keep the set of **taken** names. A spot is free when its name is not in that set; `available()` just counts the free ones per size.

In `park`, build the list of candidates first (the free spots that fit, smallest size first, then by number). Hand `allocator` a **copy** of that list, then check that what it returns is really one of the candidates before you change anything.

The default allocator is just "take the first candidate", so it is a one-line function you pass in your own constructor, not a special case inside `park`. Keep the order of your checks: unknown vehicle, already parked, lot full, then the allocator.
lld-parking-lot-3.explanation:
**What changed.** Step 2 stopped `ParkingLot` from deciding *the price*. Step 3 stops it from deciding *the spot*. It is the same refactor a third time, which is the point of the ladder: once you see the pattern ("the part that varies goes behind a one-method interface; the caller chooses it") you apply it in minutes.

```mermaid
classDiagram
    class ParkingLot {
        +park()
        +unpark()
        +spot_of()
        +available()
    }
    class Pricing {
        <<interface>>
        +fee()
    }
    class Allocator {
        <<interface>>
        +call() spot
    }
    ParkingLot --> Pricing
    ParkingLot --> Allocator
```

**The interesting design choice is what the allocator receives.** It is given a **list of the spots that are free and fit**, not the lot. That has three consequences, and they are the whole lesson:

1. The allocator cannot return a spot that does not fit, *unless it ignores its input*, so the lot still verifies the answer (`"Bad allocation"`) rather than trusting a plug-in.
2. The allocator never needs to know about sizes, plates or tickets, so a new rule (nearest the exit, spread the load, reserve large spots for trucks) is a few lines that only look at names.
3. The lot passes a **copy**, so an allocator that reorders or empties its list cannot damage the lot's own bookkeeping. Trust is a design decision: hand out the least you can.

**Failing safely.** `park` checks the allocator's answer *before* it touches the taken set, the plate set or the ticket counter. A bad allocation therefore leaves the lot exactly as it was and uses no ticket id. When an operation can fail halfway, order it so that every check comes before the first change.

**Why the order of candidates is part of the interface.** The default behaviour ("first candidate") equals step 2's "smallest size that fits, then lowest number" only because the candidates are ordered that way. A documented order is a contract; an undocumented one is a bug waiting for someone to depend on it.

**Complexity.** `park` is O(spots) because it builds the candidate list; `unpark` and `spot_of` are O(1). A lot with thousands of spots would keep a free list per size instead, at the cost of making the allocator's interface harder to explain.

**Looking back at the ladder.** Step 1 was a model, step 2 pulled out pricing, step 3 pulled out allocation. A fourth request (reservations, multiple floors, EV chargers) would, with this shape, be a new class and a constructor argument. That is what "designed for change" looks like from the outside.

lld-payment-adapters.title: Payment Gateway Adapters
lld-payment-adapters.description: Wrap two incompatible payment SDKs behind one interface and try gateways in order until one accepts (Adapter).
lld-payment-adapters.statement:
You must put two third-party payment SDKs, which you cannot change, behind **one** interface, and write a processor that falls back from one gateway to the next.

**The two SDKs** (the tests provide fakes with exactly these methods)

- Stripe-like: `sdk.create_charge(source=<token>, amount=<cents>, currency=<lowercase code>)` returns a dict `{"status": "succeeded" or "failed", "id": "<ref>"}`.
- PayPal-like: `sdk.execute_payment(<token>, <amount as a string such as "12.34">, <UPPERCASE code>)` returns a tuple `(code, ref)` where `code` is `"APPROVED"` or `"DECLINED"`.

**The interface you define.** A **gateway** is any object with `charge(amount_cents, currency, token)` that returns a `Receipt`.

**What to write**

- `Receipt(ok, ref)`: a value with those two attributes; two receipts with the same `ok` and `ref` are equal.
- `StripeAdapter(sdk)` and `PayPalAdapter(sdk)`: gateways that call their SDK as above and turn the answer into a `Receipt` (`ok` is `True` for `"succeeded"` / `"APPROVED"`). Turn cents into the PayPal amount string with integer arithmetic (`1234` becomes `"12.34"`, `5` becomes `"0.05"`, `1200` becomes `"12.00"`); `currency` is passed in any case, so lower-case it for Stripe and upper-case it for PayPal.
- `PaymentFailed` is an exception class (a subclass of `Exception`) with an attribute `attempts`.
- `PaymentProcessor(gateways)` with `pay(amount_cents, currency, token)`:
  - `amount_cents` must be a whole number above 0, otherwise `ValueError("Bad amount")` before any gateway is touched.
  - It tries the gateways **in order**. The first `Receipt` with `ok=True` is returned and **no later gateway is called**.
  - A gateway that returns `ok=False` is recorded as `"declined"`. A gateway that **raises** an exception is recorded as `"error: <message>"` and the next one is tried.
  - If none succeeds, raise `PaymentFailed("All gateways failed")` whose `attempts` is the list of those records, one per gateway, in order.

**Your processor is tested with gateways you have never seen**: the tests write their own adapter class with a `charge` method and add it.

**Example**

```
processor = PaymentProcessor([StripeAdapter(stripe), PayPalAdapter(paypal)])
processor.pay(1234, "usd", "tok_1")     # Receipt(True, "ch_1") if Stripe accepts, else tries PayPal
```
tests:
first, second = FakeStripe(), FakePayPal()
processor = PaymentProcessor([StripeAdapter(first), PayPalAdapter(second)])

declined = FakeStripe("failed")
backup = FakePayPal()
chain = PaymentProcessor([StripeAdapter(declined), PayPalAdapter(backup)])

broken = FakePayPal(fail=RuntimeError("timeout"))
survivor = FakeStripe()
after_error = PaymentProcessor([PayPalAdapter(broken), StripeAdapter(survivor)])
hints: An **adapter** translates one interface into another. Each adapter holds an SDK object and has the *one* method your processor expects, `charge(amount_cents, currency, token)`. All the ugliness (argument names, lower-case vs upper-case currency, strings instead of cents) stays inside the adapter.

Make the PayPal amount with integer arithmetic: `cents // 100` for the whole part and `cents % 100` formatted with two digits (`:02d`) for the rest. Never divide by 100.0: floats print `0.05` as `0.050000000000000003` in some cases.

The processor must only call `gateway.charge(...)` and read `receipt.ok`. Catch `Exception` around each call so one gateway's crash is recorded and the next is tried, and stop at the first success so later gateways are never touched.
lld-payment-adapters.explanation:
**The idea.** The **Adapter** pattern makes an incompatible interface look like the one your code expects. You cannot edit Stripe's or PayPal's SDK, so you write thin classes that speak *your* interface (`charge(...) -> Receipt`) on the outside and *theirs* on the inside.

```mermaid
classDiagram
    class Gateway {
        <<interface>>
        +charge() Receipt
    }
    class PaymentProcessor
    PaymentProcessor o-- Gateway
    Gateway <|.. StripeAdapter
    Gateway <|.. PayPalAdapter
    StripeAdapter --> StripeSDK : adapts
    PayPalAdapter --> PayPalSDK : adapts
```

**What each adapter hides.** Stripe wants a lower-case currency and a source token; PayPal wants an upper-case code and the amount as a decimal *string*. Those conversions live in one place each, so the rest of the system never sees them, and replacing PayPal means writing one new adapter.

**The processor is a Chain of Responsibility.** It tries gateways in order and stops at the first success. It depends only on `charge` and `Receipt.ok`; the test's own `BraintreeAdapter` and `Refusing` classes work because nothing in the processor names a concrete gateway.

**Failure handling is policy.** A *decline* (the bank said no) and an *error* (the network failed) are both "this gateway did not work", but you record them differently so that an operator can tell them apart in `attempts`. Whether to retry the same gateway on an error is a separate decision; this design moves on.

**Money detail.** Integer cents all the way, formatted only at the very edge, for the PayPal string.

**Complexity.** O(number of gateways) per payment.

**Going further.** Charging twice is the worst failure here: a timeout does not mean the first gateway did *not* charge. What would you add so a retry elsewhere cannot double-charge (hint: an idempotency key passed to every gateway)?

lld-poll-voting.title: Poll Voting
lld-poll-voting.description: Build a polling system with single and multiple choice, changed votes, retraction, closing and tie-aware results.
lld-poll-voting.statement:
Write a class `PollBox` that holds many polls, each identified by an id.

**Methods**

- `create(poll_id, options, max_choices=1)` makes a poll. Checks in order: id already used `"Poll already exists"`; fewer than two options `"Need at least two options"`; repeated options `"Options must be unique"`; `max_choices` not an `int` between 1 and the number of options `"Bad max choices"`.
- `vote(poll_id, voter, choices)` records a vote; `choices` is a list of options. A voter who votes again **replaces** their earlier vote. Checks in order: `"Unknown poll"`, `"Poll is closed"`, `"Choose at least one"`, `"Too many choices"` (more than `max_choices`), `"Duplicate choice"`, then the first option in `choices` that does not exist `"Unknown option: <option>"`. A refused vote changes nothing, including a voter's earlier vote.
- `retract(poll_id, voter)` removes a voter's vote. Checks: `"Unknown poll"`, `"Poll is closed"`, `"No vote to retract"`.
- `close(poll_id)` closes a poll for good (closing again is fine).
- `results(poll_id)` is a list of `(option, votes)`, **most votes first, ties in the order the options were created**. A voter who picked several options counts once for each.
- `winners(poll_id)` is the list of options with the most votes, in creation order; an empty list when nobody has voted.
- `choices_of(poll_id, voter)` is the voter's current choices (a new list) or `None`; `turnout(poll_id)` is how many voters have a vote.

Results and the other questions work on closed polls too; an unknown poll is always `"Unknown poll"`.
tests: assert error_of(box.create, "p", ["a"]) == "ValueError: Need at least two options"
assert error_of(box.create, "p", []) == "ValueError: Need at least two options"
assert error_of(box.create, "p", ["a", "a"]) == "ValueError: Options must be unique"
assert error_of(box.create, "p", ["a", "b"], True) == "ValueError: Bad max choices"
assert box.winners("lunch") == [] and box.turnout("lunch") == 0 and box.choices_of("lunch", "ann") is None
assert error_of(box.vote, "lunch", "dan", []) == "ValueError: Choose at least one"
assert error_of(box.retract, "langs", "zed") == "ValueError: No vote to retract"
assert box.turnout("langs") == 2 and box.choices_of("langs", "b") is None
hints: Store each poll as a dict: its options in creation order, `max_choices`, a `votes` dict from voter to their list of choices, and a closed flag. Replacing a vote is then just `votes[voter] = choices`.
Never keep a running tally you must also undo when a vote is replaced or retracted. Count from the votes each time you need results: it is slower, but it cannot get out of step.
`sorted` is stable, so sorting `(option, count)` pairs by `-count` alone keeps ties in the order the options were created, because the tally dict was built in that order.
lld-poll-voting.explanation:
**The idea.** A poll is options plus a map from voter to their current choices. Results are *derived*: count the map. Because there is no stored tally, changing or retracting a vote cannot leave a wrong count behind.

**Validate completely, then store.** A vote is refused for one of six reasons, in a fixed order, and a refused vote must not disturb the voter's previous one. Building the new list first and assigning it last is the whole trick.

**Stable sort for tie-breaking.** Python's sort keeps equal items in their original order. Building the tally in option order and sorting by count alone gives "ties in creation order" with no extra key.

**Closed means closed.** The closed check comes right after the poll lookup, before looking at the vote. Otherwise an empty vote on a closed poll would report "Choose at least one" instead of the real problem.

**Complexity.** `vote` is O(options) in the worst case; `results` is O(votes x choices + options log options).

**Going further.** Add a *ranked-choice* poll: each vote is an ordered list, and the winner is found by eliminating the last-place option round by round. What data does `results` need to return?

lld-polynomial.title: Polynomial with Operators
lld-polynomial.description: Build an immutable Polynomial that supports +, -, *, calling it like a function, equality and a readable text form.
lld-polynomial.statement:
Write a class `Polynomial` for a polynomial with whole-number coefficients.

**Creating one:** `Polynomial(coefficients)`, given **lowest power first**: `Polynomial([-1, 0, 3])` is `3x^2 - 1`. Trailing zeros (the highest powers) are dropped, so `Polynomial([1, 2, 0, 0])` equals `Polynomial([1, 2])`. The zero polynomial has no coefficients at all. It is **immutable** (assigning to an attribute raises `AttributeError`) and it must not keep a reference to the list it was given.

**Reading it**

- `coefficients` is a tuple, lowest power first, with no trailing zeros (`()` for the zero polynomial).
- `degree` is the highest power, and `-1` for the zero polynomial.

**Operators**

- `p + q`, `p - q`, `-p`.
- `p * q` multiplies two polynomials; `p * 3` and `3 * p` multiply every coefficient by an `int`.
- `p + 1` and `1 + p` add an `int` as a constant.
- `p(x)` evaluates the polynomial at `x`.
- Equal polynomials are `==` and have the same hash; comparing with a non-polynomial is `False`.
- `p.derivative()` is the derivative as a new polynomial.

**Text form.** `str(p)` lists terms from the highest power to the lowest, skipping zero terms, joined with `" + "` and `" - "`. A coefficient of `1` or `-1` is written without the number (`x`, `-x`) except for the constant term; the power `1` is written `x`, not `x^1`. The zero polynomial is `"0"`.

```
str(Polynomial([-1, 0, 3]))     # "3x^2 - 1"
str(Polynomial([0, -1, 1]))     # "x^2 - x"
str(Polynomial([5]))            # "5"
str(Polynomial([1, 1]))         # "x + 1"
```
tests: assert Polynomial([1, 2]) == Polynomial([1, 2, 0]) and Polynomial([1, 2]) != Polynomial([2, 1]) and Polynomial([5]) != 5
assert p(2) == 11 and p(0) == -1 and p(-1) == 2 and Polynomial([])(7) == 0
hints: Normalise in `__init__`: copy into a list, pop trailing zeros, and store a tuple. Then equality and hashing are just equality and hashing of that tuple.

Return `NotImplemented` (not an exception) from `__add__` and `__mul__` when the other side is a type you do not know; Python then tries the reflected method. `__radd__ = __add__` is enough for `1 + p`.
Evaluate with Horner's rule (`value = value * x + c` from the highest power down). For the text, build each term from the highest power down, and handle the sign separately from the magnitude.
lld-polynomial.explanation:
**The idea.** Python lets your class behave like a built-in number: `+`, `*`, `-`, `==`, calling, `str`. Each operator is a method (`__add__`, `__mul__`, `__neg__`, `__call__`, `__str__`) that Python looks up for you. The skill is making them agree.

**One canonical form.** Trailing zeros are removed once, in `__init__`. After that `Polynomial([1, 2, 0])` and `Polynomial([1, 2])` are literally the same data, so equality, hashing, `degree` and `str` all work without special cases. Normalise on the way in and everything downstream gets simpler.

**Reflected operators.** `2 * p` first asks `int.__mul__(2, p)`, which answers `NotImplemented`; Python then calls `p.__rmul__(2)`. Returning `NotImplemented` instead of raising is what allows that hand-off.

**Horner's rule.** `3x^2 + 0x - 1` at `x` is `(3x + 0)x - 1`: one multiplication and one addition per coefficient, no powers.

**Complexity.** Addition and evaluation are O(n); multiplication is O(n x m).

**Going further.** Add `__divmod__` by a degree-1 polynomial, or `compose(other)` so that `p.compose(q)(x) == p(q(x))`.

lld-product-filters.title: Product Filters (Specification)
lld-product-filters.description: Build composable filter rules that combine with &, | and ~, describe themselves in words, short-circuit and accept custom rules.
lld-product-filters.statement:
Write a small **specification** library for filtering dictionaries (products, users, anything).

**`Spec`** is the base class of every rule. A subclass must implement `is_satisfied_by(item)`, which returns a bool. `Spec` itself provides:

- `a & b` is a rule that holds when **both** hold; `a | b` when **either** holds; `~a` when `a` does **not** hold. They return new rules and change neither operand.
- `a.filter(items)` returns the list of items (in order) that satisfy the rule.
- `a.describe()` returns the rule as text, see below.

`And` and `Or` are **short-circuiting**: `a & b` does not ask `b` when `a` already failed; `a | b` does not ask `b` when `a` already held.

**`where(field, op, value)`** returns a rule about one field. The operators are `"=="`, `"!="`, `"<"`, `"<="`, `">"`, `">="`, `"in"` (the item's value is in the collection `value`) and `"contains"` (`value` is in the item's value). Any other operator raises `ValueError("Unknown operator")` **when `where` is called**.

- An item **without** that field does not satisfy the rule (for every operator, `"!="` included).
- A comparison Python cannot make (a string compared with `<` to a number, say) simply does not hold, instead of raising.

**Describing.** A single `where` is `field op value` with the value shown by `repr`: `price < 50`, `color == 'red'`. `a & b` is `(<a> and <b>)`, `a | b` is `(<a> or <b>)`, and `~a` is `not <a>`. Custom rules describe themselves with the class name, `ClassName()`, unless they override `describe()`.

**Example**

```
cheap_red = where("price", "<", 50) & where("color", "==", "red")
cheap_red.describe()     # "(price < 50 and color == 'red')"
(~cheap_red).describe()  # "not (price < 50 and color == 'red')"
```
tests: assert names(cheap & red) == ["pen"] and names(cheap | red) == ["pen", "lamp", "mug"]
assert names(~(cheap | red)) == ["desk"] and names(~~cheap) == names(cheap)
assert ((cheap | red) & ~where("name", "in", ["pen"])).describe() == "((price < 50 or color == 'red') and not name in ['pen'])"
assert names(in_stock) == ["pen", "desk"] and names(in_stock & cheap) == ["pen"] and names(~in_stock) == ["lamp", "mug"]
assert (Probe("a", False) & Probe("b", True)).is_satisfied_by({}) is False and calls == ["a"]
assert (Probe("a", True) | Probe("b", False)).is_satisfied_by({}) is True and calls == ["a"]
assert (Probe("a", True) & Probe("b", True)).is_satisfied_by({}) is True and calls == ["a", "b"]
assert (Probe("a", False) | Probe("b", True)).is_satisfied_by({}) is True and calls == ["a", "b"]
assert names(cheap) == ["pen", "mug"] and names(red) == ["pen", "lamp"] and names(combined) == ["pen"]
hints: Three small combinator classes (`And`, `Or`, `Not`) hold their operands and implement `is_satisfied_by` by asking them. Python's `and` / `or` already short-circuit, so use them directly instead of computing both sides first.
Put the operators in a dictionary from the symbol to a small function. `where` checks the symbol is in the dictionary immediately (so the error comes from `where`, not from a later `filter`).

A leaf rule returns `False` for a missing field *before* trying the operator, and catches `TypeError` around the comparison. `describe` is built from the children's `describe`, so nested rules print themselves with no extra code.
lld-product-filters.explanation:
**The idea.** The Specification pattern turns a business rule ("cheap and red") into an **object** you can combine, test, print and pass around. Instead of one function with a growing pile of `if` flags, you build rules from small ones.

```mermaid
classDiagram
    class Spec {
        is_satisfied_by(item)
        describe()
        filter(items)
    }
    Spec <|-- Where
    Spec <|-- And
    Spec <|-- Or
    Spec <|-- Not
    And o-- Spec
    Or o-- Spec
    Not o-- Spec
```

**Composite in disguise.** `And`, `Or` and `Not` are *composites*: they are `Spec`s that contain `Spec`s. Because every rule has the same two methods, a rule built from rules is used exactly like a simple one. The same trick appears in expression trees, file systems and UI widgets.

**Operator overloading.** `&`, `|` and `~` map to `__and__`, `__or__` and `__invert__`, so `where(...) & ~where(...)` reads like the sentence it means. (Python's `and` / `or` / `not` cannot be overloaded, which is why symbols are used.)

**Open for extension.** The test defines `InStock`, a rule the library has never heard of, and combines it with the built-in ones. That is the Open/Closed principle: new behaviour is a new subclass, with no edits to existing code.

**Self-description.** A rule that can describe itself is easy to log ("why was this product hidden?") and to test. It costs one method per class and falls out of the structure.

**Short-circuiting** matters when a rule is expensive (a database call): `cheap & expensive_check` only runs the expensive part for cheap items.

**Going further.** Translate a `Spec` tree into a SQL `WHERE` clause. Which classes need a new method, and what must `InStock` do to take part?

lld-prototype-document.title: Prototype Registry
lld-prototype-document.description: Create new documents by cloning registered templates, with deep copies so that no two documents share mutable state.
lld-prototype-document.statement:
Write two classes, `Document` and `DocumentRegistry`, using the *Prototype* pattern: new objects are made by copying a ready-made one instead of building from scratch.

**Document.** `Document(title, body="", tags=None, meta=None)`.

- `title` must be a non-blank string, else `ValueError("Title required")`.
- It stores its own **copies** of `tags` (a list, default empty) and `meta` (a dict, default empty), so later changes to what the caller passed in do not affect it. Nested values inside `meta` count: copy **deeply**.
- Attributes `title`, `body`, `tags`, `meta` can be changed freely, and `id` starts as `None`.
- `clone(**changes)` returns a new document with the same values and `id` `None`. Everything mutable is copied **deeply**, so changing the clone's `tags` or `meta` (at any depth) never changes the original, and the other way round. `changes` may name `title`, `body`, `tags` or `meta` and replaces that field (also stored as a deep copy); any other name is `ValueError("Unknown field: <name>")` and nothing is made.
- Two documents are equal (`==`) when their `title`, `body`, `tags` and `meta` are equal; the `id` is ignored.

**DocumentRegistry.**

- `register(key, document)` stores a **deep copy** of the document as a prototype; a key already used is `ValueError("Prototype already registered: <key>")`.
- `create(key, **changes)` returns a clone of that prototype with `changes` applied (same rules as `clone`) and an `id` of `1` for the first document the registry creates, `2` for the next, and so on. An unknown key is `ValueError("Unknown prototype: <key>")`. A refused `create` (unknown key or field) does **not** use up an id.
- `keys()` is the sorted list of keys.

Changing the document you registered, or any document you created, must never change the stored prototype.
tests: assert doc.title == "Report" and doc.body == "body" and doc.tags == ["a"] and doc.meta == meta and doc.id is None
assert blank.body == "" and blank.tags == [] and blank.meta == {}
assert twin == doc and twin is not doc and twin.id is None
assert doc.clone().id is None and doc.clone() == doc
assert changed.title == "Other" and changed.tags == ["z"] and changed.body == "body" and changed.meta == doc.meta
assert error_of(doc.clone, color="red") == "ValueError: Unknown field: color"
assert error_of(doc.clone, title="x", color="red") == "ValueError: Unknown field: color"
assert Document("A", "b") == Document("A", "b") and Document("A", "b") != Document("A", "c") and Document("A", tags=["x"]) != Document("A")
assert Document("A", meta={"k": 1}) != Document("A", meta={"k": 2}) and Document("A", meta={"k": 1}) == Document("A", meta={"k": 1})

template = Document("Invoice", "Dear customer", ["finance"], {"fields": {"due": 30}})
reg.register("memo", Document("Memo"))
reg.register("invoice", template)
assert error_of(reg.register, "invoice", Document("X")) == "ValueError: Prototype already registered: invoice"
assert first.tags == ["finance"] and first.meta == {"fields": {"due": 30}} and first.id == 1 and first.title == "Invoice"

first.tags.append("changed")
first.meta["fields"]["due"] = 1
second = reg.create("invoice", title="Invoice 2", body="Hi")
assert second.id == 2 and second.title == "Invoice 2" and second.body == "Hi" and second.tags == ["finance"] and second.meta == {"fields": {"due": 30}}
assert error_of(reg.create, "invoice", color="red") == "ValueError: Unknown field: color"
assert third.id == 3 and third.title == "Memo" and third is not reg.create("memo")
hints: `copy.deepcopy` is the whole mechanism: it copies a list of dicts of lists all the way down. Use it in the constructor (so the document owns its data), in `clone`, and in `register`.
Validate the field names of `clone` **before** copying or changing anything. In `create`, take the next id only after the clone succeeded, so a refused call does not burn a number.
A clone starts from a deep copy of the original and then has `id` reset to `None`. Replacement values from `changes` are deep-copied too, otherwise the clone would share a list with the caller.
lld-prototype-document.explanation:
**The idea.** When building an object is complicated (many fields, nested settings) it is easier to keep a few ready-made examples and copy them. The registry is a catalogue of such templates: "invoice", "memo", "report".

**Deep versus shallow.** `dict(meta)` copies only the top level: the inner dict is still shared, so editing a clone's `meta["owner"]["roles"]` secretly edits the template and every other clone. That is the classic Prototype bug, and the test goes three levels down on purpose.

**Copy at every boundary.** Data enters (constructor, `register`, `changes`) and leaves (`clone`, `create`). Copying in both directions is what makes the registry safe against a caller who keeps a reference and changes it later.

**Identity is not value.** `==` ignores the id: two documents with the same content are equal, and the id says "which one". `__hash__ = None` makes that honest: a mutable value object should not be a dictionary key.

**Complexity.** Cloning costs time proportional to the size of the document.

**Going further.** `copy.deepcopy` calls `__deepcopy__` if you define it. When would you want a document to copy its `tags` but *share* a large attachment?

lld-pubsub-broker.title: Publish-Subscribe Broker
lld-pubsub-broker.description: Build a message broker where subscribers pull messages at their own pace and the broker forgets what everyone has already read.
lld-pubsub-broker.statement:
Write a class `Broker` that moves messages from publishers to subscribers through named **topics**.

**Methods**

- `create_topic(name)` makes a topic. A name that exists raises `ValueError("Topic exists")`.
- `subscribe(topic, subscriber)` starts a subscription. The subscriber receives only the messages published **after** this call. Subscribing twice raises `ValueError("Already subscribed")`.
- `unsubscribe(topic, subscriber)` ends it (`ValueError("Not subscribed")` if there is none). Subscribing again later starts fresh: old messages are not replayed.
- `publish(topic, message)` adds a message and returns its **sequence number** in that topic (`1, 2, 3, ...`, never reused).
- `poll(topic, subscriber, limit=10)` returns the subscriber's next undelivered messages, **oldest first**, at most `limit`, and marks them delivered (they are not returned again). `ValueError("Not subscribed")` if there is no subscription.
- `backlog(topic, subscriber)` is how many messages that subscriber has not yet polled.
- `retained(topic)` is how many messages the broker is still **storing**: a message is kept only while at least one subscriber has not polled it. With no subscribers nothing is kept.

An unknown topic raises `ValueError("Unknown topic")` in every method except `create_topic`. Check the topic **before** the subscription.

**Example**

```
broker = Broker()
broker.create_topic("news")
broker.subscribe("news", "ann")
broker.publish("news", "hello")        # 1
broker.subscribe("news", "bob")        # bob does not see "hello"
broker.publish("news", "world")        # 2
broker.poll("news", "bob")             # ["world"]
broker.poll("news", "ann", limit=1)    # ["hello"]
broker.retained("news")                # 1   only "world" is still needed (ann has not read it)
```
tests:
slow = Broker()
slow.create_topic("t")
slow.subscribe("t", "fast")
slow.subscribe("t", "slow")
for i in range(1000):
    slow.publish("t", i)
    assert slow.poll("t", "fast") == [i]
hints: Per topic keep one list of messages, the sequence number of its first element, and for each subscriber the sequence number of the **next** message they have not read. One shared list, many cursors: no copy of a message per subscriber.
`subscribe` sets the cursor to the topic's *next* sequence number, which is exactly "only messages published after now". `backlog` is `next - cursor`.

After every change to a cursor or to the subscribers, drop messages that every cursor has passed: delete the list prefix up to `min(cursors)` (or everything when there are no subscribers) and advance the first-sequence number. Slice with `cursor - first` because the list no longer starts at 1.
lld-pubsub-broker.explanation:
**The idea.** A broker decouples senders from receivers. The design question is *where messages wait*. This solution uses one log per topic and one **cursor per subscriber**, the same shape as Kafka.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    P[publish] --> L["topic log: m4 m5 m6 m7"]
    L --> A["ann cursor at m6"]
    L --> B["bob cursor at m5"]
    A -. polls .-> L
    B -. polls .-> L
```

**Pull instead of push.** Subscribers call `poll` when they are ready, so a slow consumer never blocks a fast one and the broker needs no callbacks, threads or queues per subscriber. Back-pressure is simply `backlog`.

**One copy of each message.** The alternative is a private queue per subscriber, which copies every message once per reader. A shared log plus offsets stores each message once; the price is deciding when it can be **dropped**, which is what `retained` tests.

**Trimming.** A message may go once every cursor is past it. The slowest subscriber therefore decides how much memory the topic uses, and with no subscribers nothing is kept at all. Because the list shrinks from the front, positions are `sequence - first`, not the sequence itself; getting that offset right is the part to test carefully.

**Complexity.** `publish` is O(1) amortised (the trim deletes a prefix, amortised); `poll` is O(batch size).

**Going further.** Real brokers add *acknowledgements*: a message is redelivered if the subscriber crashes before acking. What would `poll` have to return, and what would the cursor mean?

lld-read-write-lock.title: Read-Write Lock
lld-read-write-lock.description: Design the state machine of a fair read-write lock: shared readers, an exclusive writer, a FIFO queue and no starvation.
lld-read-write-lock.statement:
Threads are hard to test, but the *rules* of a lock are plain state. Write a class `ReadWriteLock` that decides who holds a lock and who waits, without any real threads or blocking: calls return what happened.

**Rules.** Any number of **readers** may hold the lock together, or **one writer** alone. Requests are served **fairly, first come first served**: a request is granted at once only if **nobody is queued** and it is compatible with the current holders; otherwise it joins the queue. (So a waiting writer stops *new* readers from slipping in and starving it.)

**Methods**

- `acquire_read(owner)` and `acquire_write(owner)` return `"granted"` or `"queued"`. An owner that already holds the lock or is queued is `ValueError("Already holding or waiting: <owner>")` (a lock is not re-entrant).
- `release(owner)` releases what the owner holds and returns the **list of owners granted as a result**, in the order they were granted. Releasing without holding (including when only queued) is `ValueError("Not holding: <owner>")`.
- `cancel(owner)` removes a **queued** request and returns the owners granted as a result (the removal may unblock readers behind a writer). Not queued: `ValueError("Not waiting: <owner>")`.
- `state` is `("read", [owners])` (in the order granted), `("write", [owner])` or `(None, [])`; `waiting` is a **new list** of `(owner, "read" or "write")`, oldest first.

**Granting after a release or cancel.** Look at the **head of the queue** only. If it is a **writer**: grant it only when nobody holds the lock (then stop). If it is a **reader**: grant it and keep granting the readers that follow it in the queue, until the next writer, as long as no writer holds the lock.
tests: assert lock.state == ("read", ["r1", "r2"]) and lock.state[1].append("junk") is None and lock.state == ("read", ["r1", "r2"])
assert error_of(lock.acquire_read, "r1") == "ValueError: Already holding or waiting: r1" and error_of(lock.acquire_write, "r2") == "ValueError: Already holding or waiting: r2"
assert error_of(lock.acquire_write, "w1") == "ValueError: Already holding or waiting: w1" and error_of(lock.acquire_read, "r3") == "ValueError: Already holding or waiting: r3"
assert error_of(lock.release, "zed") == "ValueError: Not holding: zed" and error_of(lock.release, "w1") == "ValueError: Not holding: w1"
assert lock.release("r1") == [] and lock.state == ("read", ["r2"]) and lock.waiting == [("w1", "write"), ("r3", "read")]
assert lock.release("r2") == ["w1"] and lock.state == ("write", ["w1"]) and lock.waiting == [("r3", "read")]
assert lock.release("w1") == ["r3", "r4"] and lock.state == ("read", ["r3", "r4"]) and lock.waiting == [("w2", "write")]
assert lock.release("r3") == [] and lock.release("r4") == ["w2"] and lock.state == ("write", ["w2"]) and lock.waiting == []
assert w.acquire_read("a") == "queued" and w.acquire_read("b") == "queued" and w.acquire_write("w1") == "queued" and w.acquire_read("c") == "queued"
assert w.release("w0") == ["a", "b"] and w.state == ("read", ["a", "b"]) and w.waiting == [("w1", "write"), ("c", "read")]
assert w.release("a") == [] and w.release("b") == ["w1"] and w.release("w1") == ["c"] and w.state == ("read", ["c"])
assert w.cancel("w2") == ["d"] and w.state == ("read", ["c", "d"]) and w.waiting == []
assert error_of(w.cancel, "w2") == "ValueError: Not waiting: w2" and error_of(w.cancel, "c") == "ValueError: Not waiting: c" and error_of(w.cancel, "zed") == "ValueError: Not waiting: zed"

x = ReadWriteLock()
x.acquire_read("r1")
x.acquire_write("w1")
x.acquire_write("w2")
x.acquire_read("r2")

z = ReadWriteLock()
z.acquire_read("r1")
z.acquire_read("r2")
z.acquire_write("w")
z.acquire_read("r3")
assert z.waiting == [] and z.state[1].append("junk") is None and z.state == ("write", ["w"])
assert s.acquire_write("w") == "granted" and s.acquire_write("w2") == "queued" and s.acquire_read("r") == "queued"
assert s.cancel("w2") == [] and s.waiting == [("r", "read")] and s.state == ("write", ["w"])
hints: State is three things: the list of readers holding, the writer holding (or `None`), and one queue of `(owner, mode)`. A new request is **granted only if the queue is empty** and it fits; otherwise it joins the queue. That one rule is the fairness.

Write one `_grant()` and call it after every release **and** every cancel. It looks at the queue head only: a writer needs an empty lock (then stop), a reader is granted unless a writer holds, and then the loop continues so the readers behind it are granted too.

A queued owner does not hold anything, so `release` must refuse it (`Not holding`). Removing a writer from the head of the queue (`cancel`) can free the readers behind it, which is why `cancel` also calls `_grant()` and returns who was granted.
lld-read-write-lock.explanation:
**The idea.** A lock is a tiny state machine: who holds it (readers, a writer or nobody) and who waits. Real threads add blocking and wake-ups on top of this machine; the *design* question (who is allowed in, in what order) can be answered and tested without any thread.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A[request] --> B{queue empty and compatible?}
    B -- yes --> C[granted]
    B -- no --> D[queued]
    E[release or cancel] --> F{head of queue}
    F -- writer --> G[grant only if lock is empty, then stop]
    F -- reader --> H[grant it and the readers after it, until a writer]
```

**Fairness is a choice.** If new readers could join whenever the current holders are readers, a steady stream of readers would keep a writer waiting for ever (*starvation*). Making every request wait behind the queue costs some read throughput and buys a bound on how long anyone waits.

**Batching readers.** After a writer finishes, all the readers at the head of the queue can run together. That is the point of a read-write lock; stopping at the first writer keeps the order fair.

**Return what changed.** `release` returns who was granted so that the caller (a scheduler, a thread pool) knows whom to wake. A lock that only returned `None` would force the caller to poll.

**Complexity.** Each call is O(queue) at worst.

**Going further.** Add *upgrade* (a reader asks to become the writer). Why is this the classic source of deadlocks, and what would you refuse?

lld-report-template.title: Report Template Method
lld-report-template.description: Build a base Report that fixes the order of the steps and let a text report, a CSV report and your own subclasses fill in the details.
lld-report-template.statement:
Write a base class `Report` whose method `generate(rows)` is a **template method**: it fixes the order of the steps, and subclasses fill in the steps. Then write two subclasses.

**`Report.generate(rows)`** takes a list of dictionaries and returns one string. Anything that is not a `list` raises `ValueError("Rows must be a list")`. Then, in this order:

1. call `self.header(rows)`;
2. if there are rows, call `self.format_row(row)` for each, in order; if there are none, call `self.empty_message()` instead (once);
3. call `self.footer(rows)`;
4. leave out every part that is the empty string, and return `self.join(parts)`.

**The steps (what subclasses may override)**

| method | in `Report` |
|---|---|
| `header(rows)` | must be overridden: raises `NotImplementedError` |
| `format_row(row)` | must be overridden: raises `NotImplementedError` |
| `empty_message()` | returns `"(no data)"` |
| `footer(rows)` | returns `""` |
| `join(parts)` | returns the parts joined by `"\n"` |

**`TextReport(title)`**: header `"== <title> =="`; each row is `"- "` followed by `key=value` pairs sorted by key and joined by `", "`; footer is `"<n> rows"`, or `"1 row"` for exactly one.

**`CsvReport(columns)`**: header is the column names joined by `","`; each row is that row's value for each column (missing: empty), joined by `","`. A value containing a comma, a double quote or a line break is wrapped in double quotes, with inner quotes doubled. With no rows there is **no** message (the report is just the header).

**Example**

```
TextReport("Sales").generate([{"item": "pen", "qty": 3}])
# "== Sales ==\n- item=pen, qty=3\n1 row"
```
tests: assert text.generate([{"item": "pen", "qty": 3}]) == "== Sales ==\n- item=pen, qty=3\n1 row"

assert text.generate([{"b": 2, "a": 1}, {"a": 9}]) == "== Sales ==
- a=1, b=2
- a=9
2 rows"
assert error_of(text.generate, "rows") == "ValueError: Rows must be a list"
assert error_of(text.generate, ({"a": 1},)) == "ValueError: Rows must be a list"
assert error_of(csv.generate, None) == "ValueError: Rows must be a list"
assert issubclass(TextReport, Report) and issubclass(CsvReport, Report)
assert "generate" not in TextReport.__dict__ and "generate" not in CsvReport.__dict__
hints: `generate` is the only method with logic: build a list of parts by calling the step methods in order, drop the empty ones, and hand the list to `join`. It must call the steps through `self`, so a subclass's version is the one that runs.

The base class steps `header` and `format_row` are *abstract*: raise `NotImplementedError`. `empty_message`, `footer` and `join` are *hooks* with sensible defaults that a subclass may override or ignore.
In the subclasses write only the steps, never `generate`. For CSV, check each cell for a comma, a quote or a line break; if there is one, double the quotes and wrap the cell in quotes.
lld-report-template.explanation:
**The idea.** The Template Method pattern puts an algorithm's *skeleton* in a base class and lets subclasses supply the *steps*. The skeleton here is "header, then the rows (or a message), then a footer, drop blanks, join". Every report has that shape; only the details differ.

```mermaid
classDiagram
    class Report {
        generate(rows)
        header(rows)*
        format_row(row)*
        empty_message()
        footer(rows)
        join(parts)
    }
    Report <|-- TextReport
    Report <|-- CsvReport
```

**Inversion of control.** Normally your code calls a library. Here the base class calls *your* methods: "don't call us, we'll call you" (the Hollywood principle). That is why `generate` must call `self.header(...)` and not a fixed function: a subclass that overrides `header` changes the result without touching `generate`.

**Abstract steps and hooks.** `header` and `format_row` have no sensible default, so the base refuses to run without them. `empty_message`, `footer` and `join` have defaults, so subclasses only override them when they need to; the CSV report overrides `empty_message` to say nothing, and a test subclass overrides `join` to use pipes.
