assert run(compose([tracer("a"), lambda request, next: "403", tracer("b")], handler)) == ("403", ["a in", "a out"])
assert run(compose([tracer("outer"), catch_errors, tracer("inner")], failing)) == ("500 boom", ["outer in", "inner in", "handler", "caught", "outer out"])
assert escapes(compose([tracer("a"), tracer("b")], failing)) == ("ValueError", ["a in", "b in", "handler"])
assert run(compose([retry, tracer("inner")], flaky)) == ("ok", ["inner in", "retry 0", "inner in", "retry 1", "inner in", "inner out"])
assert run(compose([twice, tracer("inner")], handler)) == (["handled r", "handled r"], ["inner in", "handler", "inner out", "inner in", "handler", "inner out"])

scenario = "one app, two requests"
layers = [tracer("a"), tracer("b")]
app = compose(layers, handler)
trace = ["a in", "b in", "handler", "b out", "a out"]
assert [run(app, "one"), run(app, "two")] == [("handled one", trace), ("handled two", trace)]
assert len(layers) == 2, "compose must not remove middlewares from the list it was given"
hints: Think of the chain as nested calls: layer 1 calls layer 2, which calls layer 3, and the last one calls the handler. What should `next` be for layer `i`?

`next` for layer `i` is a function of the request that runs layer `i + 1` with its own `next`; after the last layer it calls `handler`. A small recursive function of the position does it, or you can wrap the handler from the last layer outwards.
Keep the position inside each `next` closure, not in a variable shared by the whole `app`: otherwise a layer that calls `next` twice, or a second request, finds the position already moved.
middleware-pipeline.explanation:
**The idea.** Each middleware wraps everything after it. Seen from the inside out: the last layer wraps `handler`, the layer before it wraps that, and so on, and `app` is the outermost wrapper. Calling `next(request)` inside layer `i` just calls the wrapper for layer `i + 1`. That is the "onion": the code before `next` runs on the way in (first layer first), the code after it on the way out (first layer last).

**Short-circuits and errors come for free.** `next` is an ordinary function call. A layer that returns without calling it ends the chain early. If a later layer raises, Python unwinds the stack through each `next(...)` call, so a `try/except` around it in an earlier layer can catch the error. That is how error-handling middleware works, which is why it goes near the front of the list.

**The trap.** If you track "where are we" in a variable that all calls share (a counter each `next` increments), then a layer that calls `next` twice, or a second request, finds it already moved. Keep the position in each closure, as the recursion on `position + 1` does, or build the wrapped functions once, from the inside out.

**Follow-up.** Koa and Express do the same with async functions; Koa's `compose` also raises an error if one layer calls `next()` twice. Django's `get_response` and WSGI middleware are the same pattern.

min-stack.title: Min Stack
min-stack.description: Design a stack that also returns its smallest element in constant time.
min-stack.statement:
Design a stack that supports `push`, `pop`, `top` and `get_min`, each in **O(1)** time.

- `push(x)` adds `x` on top.
- `pop()` removes the top element and returns it.
- `top()` returns the top element without removing it.
- `get_min()` returns the smallest element currently in the stack.
- You will never call `pop`, `top` or `get_min` on an empty stack.

**Example**

```python
s = MinStack()
s.push(5); s.push(2); s.push(7)
s.get_min()    # 2
s.pop()        # 7
s.pop()        # 2
s.get_min()    # 5, the minimum goes back up when the 2 is removed
```
tests: assert t.get_min() == 1, "a duplicate minimum must survive one pop"
hints: Scanning the stack for the minimum is O(n). What could you store *when you push* so that the answer is already known later?
With each element, store the smallest value in the stack up to and including that element.
When you pop, the minimum goes back to what it was before that push. Because it was stored with the element below, you do not have to recompute anything.
min-stack.explanation:
**The idea.** Scanning for the minimum is O(n). Instead, store the answer next to each element: when you push `x`, also record the smallest value in the stack *at that moment*. The minimum of the whole stack is then always the one recorded on the top element, and popping simply discards it, which restores the previous minimum automatically.

**Two ways to store it.** A tuple `(value, minimum_so_far)` per element, as here, or a second stack that only gets a value pushed when it is `<=` the current minimum. The second uses less memory when the minimum rarely changes; note the `<=` (not `<`), or duplicates of the minimum break it.

**Complexity.** Every operation is O(1). Space is O(n).

minimum-size-subarray-sum.title: Minimum Size Subarray Sum
minimum-size-subarray-sum.description: Find the shortest run of positive numbers whose sum reaches a target.
minimum-size-subarray-sum.statement:
Given a positive integer `target` and a list `nums` of positive integers, return the length of the shortest contiguous subarray whose sum is **at least** `target`.

- If no subarray reaches `target` (even the whole list does not), or `nums` is empty, return `0`.
- A subarray is a non-empty run of neighbouring items. All the numbers are positive, so adding an item always raises a sum.

**Examples**

```python
min_subarray_len(7, [2, 3, 1, 2, 4, 3])   # 2: the subarray [4, 3]
min_subarray_len(4, [1, 4, 4])            # 1: the single 4
min_subarray_len(11, [1, 1, 1, 1])        # 0: even all of it sums to only 4
```

Aim for O(n): the last tests have 100,000 numbers, too many to sum every subarray.
tests: assert min_subarray_len(50_000, [1] * 100_000) == 50_000, "too slow or wrong on 100,000 numbers; summing every subarray is O(n^2)"
assert min_subarray_len(100_000, [1] * 99_999 + [100_000]) == 1, "too slow or wrong on 100,000 numbers; summing every subarray is O(n^2)"
assert min_subarray_len(1_000_000_000, list(range(1, 50_001))) == 27_639, "too slow or wrong on 50,000 numbers"   # the 27,639 largest numbers are the first to reach it
hints: Every number is positive, so a longer subarray always has a bigger sum. Picture a window from `left` to `right`: when is it worth moving `right`, and when `left`?
Move `right` forward, adding numbers, until the window sum reaches `target`. Then move `left` forward while the sum still reaches `target`, noting the shortest length you see.
Shrink with a `while` loop, not an `if`. And return `0` (not infinity) when no window ever reached the target.
minimum-size-subarray-sum.solution:
def min_subarray_len(target, nums):
    none_found = len(nums) + 1                  # longer than any real window
    best = none_found
    total = left = 0
    for right, x in enumerate(nums):
        total += x
        while total >= target:                  # long enough: shrink it from the left as far as it can go
            best = min(best, right - left + 1)
            total -= nums[left]
            left += 1
    return 0 if best == none_found else best
minimum-size-subarray-sum.explanation:
**The idea.** Grow a window `nums[left : right + 1]` on the right, adding numbers until its sum reaches `target`. Then shrink it from the left for as long as the sum still reaches `target`, recording the length each time. This works because every number is positive: adding makes the sum bigger and removing makes it smaller, so a window that is long enough can only stop being long enough by losing numbers, and `left` never needs to move backwards.

**Why a `while`, not an `if`.** One large new number can let you drop several old ones at once.

**Complexity.** O(n) time, because `left` and `right` only move forward, and O(1) space. Summing every subarray is O(n²).

**If negative numbers were allowed** this breaks, since removing a number could raise the sum. You would use prefix sums with a monotonic deque instead.

minimum-window-substring.title: Minimum Window Substring
minimum-window-substring.description: Find the shortest substring of a text that contains every required character, counts included.
minimum-window-substring.statement:
Write `min_window(text, needed)` that returns the shortest substring of `text` that contains every character of `needed`, repeats included: if `needed` has two `"a"`, the window must contain at least two `"a"`.

- Extra characters inside the window are fine, and their order does not matter.
- If no window works, or `needed` is empty, return `""`.
- If several windows have the minimum length, return the leftmost one: the one that starts first.
- Comparison is case-sensitive.

**Examples**

```python
min_window("aabdec", "abc")   # "abdec"
min_window("xabyba", "ab")    # "ab"   ("ba" is as short, but "ab" starts first)
min_window("ab", "aa")        # ""     (the text has only one "a")
```

Aim for O(len(text)): trying every start and every end is far too slow.
hints: Any window is defined by its two ends. Think of the right end as moving forward and the left end as chasing it: when is it worth moving each of them?

Count how many required characters (repeats included) the window still misses. Move the right end until nothing is missing; then move the left end as far as you can while nothing becomes missing, and record the window every time it is valid.

A character the window has in surplus can be dropped from the left for free, so keep counts that are allowed to go negative. Only record a window when it is strictly shorter than the best one, so that ties keep the leftmost.
minimum-window-substring.solution:
from collections import Counter


def min_window(text, needed):
    if not needed or len(needed) > len(text):
        return ""

    lacking = Counter(needed)         # lacking[c]: how many more copies of c the window needs (negative: a surplus)
    missing = len(needed)             # characters still missing in total, repeats counted
    best_start, best_length = 0, len(text) + 1
    left = 0
    for right, char in enumerate(text):
        if lacking[char] > 0:
            missing -= 1
        lacking[char] -= 1
        while missing == 0:                          # [left, right] covers `needed`: shrink it as far as it stays valid
            if right - left + 1 < best_length:       # strictly shorter, so on a tie the leftmost window is kept
                best_start, best_length = left, right - left + 1
            lacking[text[left]] += 1
            if lacking[text[left]] > 0:
                missing += 1
            left += 1
    return text[best_start:best_start + best_length] if best_length <= len(text) else ""
minimum-window-substring.explanation:
**The idea.** Two ends, `left` and `right`, bound the window. Move `right` forward one character at a time and keep count of how many required characters (repeats included) the window still lacks. When nothing is lacking, the window is valid: record it if it is the shortest so far, then move `left` forward to shrink it for as long as it stays valid. Then move `right` again.

**Why it finds the minimum.** Any shortest window becomes valid at some moment while `right` sweeps, and by then the shrinking loop has pushed `left` as far as validity allows. Both ends only ever move forward, so nothing is missed and nothing is revisited.

**Counts may go negative.** `lacking[c]` is how many more copies of `c` are needed; a negative number is a surplus, which is exactly what lets `left` drop a character for free. Characters that are not in `needed` just drift below zero and are never counted as missing.

**Complexity.** O(len(text) + len(needed)): each character enters the window once and leaves it at most once.

**Usual mistakes.** Counting distinct characters instead of copies (then `"aa"` would be satisfied by one `"a"`), shrinking only once instead of while the window stays valid, and recording the window on ties, which returns the rightmost instead of the leftmost.

**Follow-up.** When `needed` is small and the text is long, list only the positions of the needed characters and slide over that list; each step then skips the irrelevant characters.

missing-number.title: Missing Number
missing-number.description: Find the one number from 0 to n that is missing from a list of n distinct numbers.
missing-number.statement:
Write `missing_number(nums)`. The list `nums` holds `n` **different** integers (`n` is `len(nums)`), every one of them in the range `0` to `n` inclusive. That range has `n + 1` numbers, so exactly one of them is missing. Return it.

- The items are in no particular order.
- The missing number can be `0` or `n` itself.
- An empty list has `n = 0`, so the only number in its range, `0`, is the missing one.

**Examples**

```python
missing_number([3, 0, 1])                    # 2
missing_number([0, 1])                       # 2, the missing number is n itself
missing_number([9, 6, 4, 2, 3, 5, 7, 0, 1])  # 8
```

Checking `i in nums` for every `i` from 0 to `n` is O(n²) and too slow for a long list. Aim for O(n) time.
tests: assert missing_number([v for v in scrambled if v != 73_219]) == 73_219, "wrong or too slow for 100,000 numbers in a scrambled order"
hints: You know exactly which numbers the complete set `0 … n` contains, even though nobody gave it to you. How could you compare "everything" with "what I have" without searching for each number?
The sum of `0 … n` has a closed form. Compare it with the sum of the list. (Another route: XOR all the numbers `0 … n` together with all the items, so that every present number cancels itself.)
`n` is `len(nums)`, not the largest item: when the missing number is `n` itself, the largest item in the list is `n - 1`.
missing-number.explanation:
**The idea.** You know exactly what the complete set `0, 1, …, n` adds up to: `n * (n + 1) / 2`. The list has the same numbers minus one, so its sum is smaller by exactly the missing number. Subtract and you are done: one pass, no extra memory.

**The XOR way.** `a ^ a == 0` and `a ^ 0 == a`, so if you XOR together every index `0 … n` and every item of the list, each number that is present appears twice and cancels out; what is left is the missing number. The sum can get large in languages with fixed-size integers (it overflows), and XOR never does; in Python integers do not overflow, so either works.

**Details to get right.** `n` is `len(nums)`, not `max(nums)` or `len(nums) - 1`: when the missing number is the largest one (`n` itself), the biggest item in the list is only `n - 1`.

**Complexity.** O(n) time, O(1) extra space. A set of the items, or a sorted copy, also works at the cost of O(n) space or O(n log n) time.

**Follow-up.** What if two numbers are missing? The sum alone no longer identifies them; the sum and the sum of squares do, or you can split the range around the XOR of the two.

mlp-forward-pass.title: Forward Pass of a Neural Network
mlp-forward-pass.description: Run an input through a small multi-layer network, layer by layer: weights, bias, activation.
mlp-forward-pass.statement:
A neural network is layers of the same operation. Write `forward(x, layers)`, which sends the input vector `x` (a list of numbers) through each layer in turn and returns the output vector.

A layer is a tuple `(weights, biases, activation)`:

- `weights` is a list of rows, one per output unit; each row has one number per input.
- `biases` has one number per output unit.
- Output unit `j` is `activation(sum(weights[j][i] * input[i]) + biases[j])`.
- `activation` is one of `"relu"` (`max(0, z)`), `"tanh"`, `"sigmoid"` (`1 / (1 + exp(-z))`) or `"linear"` (`z`). Anything else raises `ValueError`.

The output of each layer is the input of the next. With no layers, the output is `x` itself.

```python
layers = [([[1, 1], [1, -1]], [0, 0], "relu"),    # 2 inputs -> 2 units
          ([[1, 1]], [0], "linear")]              # 2 inputs -> 1 unit
forward([3, 1], layers)   # [6]    (hidden: relu([4, 2]) = [4, 2]; output: 4 + 2)
```
mlp-forward-pass.starter:
import math


def forward(x, layers):
    """Return the output of the network for the input vector x."""
    ...
tests: assert forward([1, 2], [([[1, 0], [0, -1]], [0, 0], "relu")]) == [1, 0], "relu clips the negative unit to 0"
assert forward([5, 6], []) == [5, 6], "no layers: the input comes back"
assert forward([2], [([[3], [-1]], [1, 1], "linear")]) == [7, -1], "weights times input, plus the bias, for each unit"
assert forward([1000], [([[1]], [0], "sigmoid")]) == [1.0], "a very large input must not overflow"
assert forward([-1000], [([[1]], [0], "sigmoid")]) == [0.0], "nor a very negative one"
assert [forward(list(p), xor)[0] for p in [(0, 0), (0, 1), (1, 0), (1, 1)]] == [0, 1, 1, 0], "two layers can compute XOR, which one layer cannot"
hints: One layer: for each row of `weights` take the dot product with the input, add that unit's bias. Write that as a list comprehension producing the layer's output.
Put the activation functions in a dict keyed by name, and look the name up once per layer so an unknown name raises `ValueError`.

The output list of one layer becomes the input list of the next, so reassign `x` inside the loop. A sigmoid computed as `1 / (1 + exp(-z))` overflows for very negative `z`: use the other form for negative numbers.
mlp-forward-pass.explanation:
**The idea.** One layer is a matrix-vector product plus a bias, then a non-linear function applied to every number. A network is that, repeated. Training (backpropagation) is the same computation run backwards to find how to change each weight; the forward pass is what runs when you serve predictions.

**Why the non-linearity matters.** Without it, two layers collapse into one (a matrix times a matrix is a matrix), and the network could only draw straight lines. The last test is XOR, the classic function that no single layer can compute; with a `relu` in between, two layers can.

**Complexity.** O(total number of weights).

**Usual mistakes.** Applying the activation before adding the bias; confusing which axis of `weights` is the input and which the output; letting `exp` overflow in the sigmoid; applying `relu` to the output layer of a regression model.

**Follow-up.** In practice this is one `numpy` or `torch` call per layer (`x @ W.T + b`), vectorised over a whole batch. Writing it once by hand is the way to see what those libraries do.

month-over-month-growth.title: Month-over-Month Revenue Growth
month-over-month-growth.description: Compare each month's revenue with the month before it using LAG.
month-over-month-growth.statement:
Revenue is `quantity * unit_price` summed over the items of `paid` and `shipped` orders.

Return one row for each **month with revenue**: `month` (as `YYYY-MM`), `revenue` (rounded to 2 places) and `growth_pct`: the change from the previous month **in the result**, as a percentage rounded to 1 decimal place (`(this - previous) / previous * 100`). The first month has no previous one: `NULL`. Oldest first.
month-over-month-growth.starter:
SELECT ordered_at AS month
FROM orders;
variants: UPDATE orders SET status = 'cancelled' WHERE ordered_at LIKE '2025-03-%'
hints: Get one row per month first. Then you want, on each row, the value from the row before.
`LAG(revenue) OVER (ORDER BY month)` is the previous month's revenue.
Multiply by `100.0` (not `100`) so the division is not an integer division, and round the final percentage.
month-over-month-growth.solution:
WITH monthly AS (
  SELECT substr(o.ordered_at, 1, 7) AS month, SUM(i.quantity * i.unit_price) AS revenue
  FROM orders AS o
  JOIN order_items AS i ON i.order_id = o.id
  WHERE o.status IN ('paid', 'shipped')
  GROUP BY substr(o.ordered_at, 1, 7)
)
SELECT month,
       ROUND(revenue, 2) AS revenue,
       ROUND((revenue - LAG(revenue) OVER (ORDER BY month)) * 100.0 / LAG(revenue) OVER (ORDER BY month), 1) AS growth_pct
FROM monthly
ORDER BY month;
month-over-month-growth.explanation:
**The idea.** `LAG(x) OVER (ORDER BY month)` is the value of `x` in the previous row of the window, and `NULL` for the first row, so the first month gets a `NULL` growth with no special case. After grouping to one row per month, "previous month" is just "previous row".

**Details that matter.** `* 100.0` makes the division decimal (`7 / 2` is `3` in integer arithmetic, `7 / 2.0` is `3.5`); round at the end; compute the growth from the *unrounded* revenues, not from the rounded ones shown. Months are cut from the date text with `substr(date, 1, 7)` (or `strftime('%Y-%m', date)`).

**A note.** A month with no revenue at all would not be a row, so the "previous" month would be the one before the gap. For a calendar-exact comparison you would generate every month first and join to it.

move-zeroes.title: Move Zeroes
move-zeroes.description: Move all zeros to the end of a list in place, keeping the order of everything else.
move-zeroes.statement:
Write `move_zeroes(nums)`, which moves every `0` in the list `nums` to the end of the list, **in place**, and keeps all the other items in the order they had.

- Change the list you are given instead of building a new one. The caller looks at `nums` afterwards; the return value is ignored.
- The list keeps its length. An empty list, or one with no zeros, is fine too.
- The other items may be negative or repeated; only the value `0` moves.

**Examples**

```python
nums = [0, 1, 0, 3, 12]
move_zeroes(nums)
nums                     # [1, 3, 12, 0, 0]

nums = [4, 2, 4]
move_zeroes(nums)
nums                     # [4, 2, 4]
```

Taking the zeros out one at a time with `remove` or `pop` is O(n²) on a long list. Aim for one pass: O(n).
tests:
def moved(values):
    # Runs move_zeroes on a fresh copy of the list and returns that same list, which is what the caller would see afterwards.
    nums = list(values)
    returned = move_zeroes(nums)
    if returned is not None and returned != nums:
        raise AssertionError(f"move_zeroes must change the list it is given, but nums is still {nums!r}: it looks like you returned a new list instead")
    return nums
long_list = [0] * 100_000 + [0 if i % 3 else i + 1 for i in range(300_000)]
assert moved(long_list) == [v for v in long_list if v != 0] + [0] * long_list.count(0), "wrong result, or too slow, for 400,000 items"
hints: Imagine two fingers on the list: one reads every item in turn, the other points at the slot where the next non-zero item should go.
Walk the list with the reader. Each time it sees a non-zero item, put that item where the second finger is and move that finger one step. Whatever is left after the second finger must be zeros.
Do not remove or insert items while you walk (the positions shift under you), and do not build a new list: the caller's list has to be the one that changes.
move-zeroes.explanation:
**The idea (two pointers).** One pointer, `i`, reads every item. The other, `next_slot`, marks where the next non-zero item belongs. Whenever the reader finds a non-zero item it is swapped into `next_slot`, and `next_slot` moves one step on. The non-zero items arrive in `next_slot` in the order the reader met them, which is why their order is kept, and the zeros are pushed behind the writer without ever being moved on purpose.

**Complexity.** One pass: O(n) time and O(1) extra space.

**Fewer writes.** The swap writes two slots even when `next_slot == i` (no zero has been skipped yet). Skipping the swap in that case, or copying the non-zero items forward and then filling the tail with zeros, writes less. The tests do not care, but it matters when writes are expensive (flash memory, a database).

**Mistakes to avoid.** Calling `remove(0)` or `pop(i)` while walking the list: every call shifts the rest, so it is O(n²), and removing during a `for` loop makes you skip the item after each removal. Building a new list and returning it: the caller's list stays as it was.

**Follow-up.** The same writer-and-reader pattern removes duplicates from a sorted list in place, or removes every occurrence of a given value.

movie-ticket-booking.title: Movie Ticket Booking
movie-ticket-booking.description: Write a Movie class that remembers its seats, books tickets and reports its status.
movie-ticket-booking.statement:
Write a class `Movie` for a cinema's booking desk.

**Attributes** (set in `__init__(self, movie_name, total_seats, ticket_price)`):

- `movie_name`: the name of the movie
- `total_seats`: how many seats the theatre has
- `ticket_price`: the price of one ticket
- `booked_seats`: how many seats are booked so far. It starts at `0`.

**Methods**

- `book_ticket(num_tickets)` books that many tickets if enough seats are still free, and **prints** one line:
  - enough seats: `Booked 3 ticket(s). Total to pay: 750`, with your number of tickets and the amount `num_tickets * ticket_price`, written the way Python prints it (a price of `99.5` for 2 tickets gives `199.0`). The seats become booked.
  - not enough seats: `Sorry, not enough seats available`. Nothing is booked.
- `show_status()` **prints** three lines, in this order: `Movie: <name>`, `Seats available: <free seats>`, `Seats booked: <booked seats>`.

Rules: `num_tickets` is a positive whole number. Booking exactly the seats that are left is allowed. Two `Movie` objects are independent: booking one does not touch the other.

**Example**

```
movie = Movie("Dune", 50, 250)
movie.book_ticket(3)      # prints: Booked 3 ticket(s). Total to pay: 750
movie.book_ticket(48)     # prints: Sorry, not enough seats available   (only 47 are free)
movie.show_status()       # prints: Movie: Dune
                          #         Seats available: 47
                          #         Seats booked: 3
```
tests:
import contextlib
import io
def printed(action, *args):
    """The lines a call prints."""
    out = io.StringIO()
    with contextlib.redirect_stdout(out):
        action(*args)
    return out.getvalue().strip().split("\n")
movie = Movie("Dune", 50, 250)
assert printed(movie.book_ticket, 3) == ["Booked 3 ticket(s). Total to pay: 750"]
assert printed(movie.book_ticket, 48) == ["Sorry, not enough seats available"]
assert printed(movie.book_ticket, 47) == ["Booked 47 ticket(s). Total to pay: 11750"]
assert printed(movie.book_ticket, 1) == ["Sorry, not enough seats available"]
assert printed(other.book_ticket, 2) == ["Booked 2 ticket(s). Total to pay: 199.0"]
hints: `__init__` runs when the object is created. `self.movie_name = movie_name` is how the object remembers the value for its other methods, and `self.booked_seats = 0` is the starting value.
Do not store the free seats: work them out with `total_seats - booked_seats` whenever you need them, so they can never disagree with the booked count.
Compare first, change second: only when `num_tickets` fits in the free seats do you add to `booked_seats` and print the total. Otherwise print the sorry line and touch nothing.
movie-ticket-booking.explanation:
**The idea.** A class is a template, and each object made from it remembers its own facts. `__init__` runs when you write `Movie("Dune", 50, 250)`, and `self.movie_name = ...` is how an object keeps something for later. Because the facts live on `self`, a second `Movie` has its own `booked_seats`: booking one never touches the other.

**What to store and what to work out.** The free seats are not stored. They are always `total_seats - booked_seats`, so computing them when needed means they can never disagree with the booked count. Storing both is a classic source of bugs: you update one and forget the other.

**The check comes first.** `book_ticket` compares the request with the free seats *before* changing anything. Only a booking that fits adds to `booked_seats`, so a refused booking leaves the object exactly as it was. Note `<=`: booking exactly the seats that are left is fine.

**Going further.** What should happen for `book_ticket(0)` or a negative number? Real code would refuse them (usually by raising `ValueError`), which is the next step in the Bank Account exercise.

mvcc-tuple-visibility.title: MVCC Snapshot Isolation Tuple Visibility
mvcc-tuple-visibility.description: Determine PostgreSQL-style multi-version concurrency control (MVCC) tuple visibility under snapshot isolation.
mvcc-tuple-visibility.statement:
Relational databases like PostgreSQL implement **Multi-Version Concurrency Control (MVCC)** to permit concurrent reads and writes without read-write locking. When a query begins under Snapshot Isolation, it acquires a transaction snapshot:
- `snapshot.xmin`: Lowest transaction ID that was active when snapshot was taken.
- `snapshot.xmax`: Highest transaction ID assigned $+ 1$.
- `snapshot.active_txns`: Set of transaction IDs currently in progress when snapshot was created.

Every physical row tuple carries two transaction headers:
- `xmin`: Transaction ID that inserted/created the tuple.
- `xmax`: Transaction ID that deleted or updated the tuple (`None` if never deleted).

### Visibility Rules

1. **Creator (`xmin`) check:**
   - If `xmin >= snapshot.xmax`: Tuple was created in the future $\rightarrow$ **Invisible**.
   - If `xmin in snapshot.active_txns`: Tuple was created by an uncommitted in-flight transaction $\rightarrow$ **Invisible**.
   - If `xmin not in committed_txns`: Tuple was aborted $\rightarrow$ **Invisible**.
   - (If `xmin < snapshot.xmin` or `xmin` is committed and not in `active_txns`, the creation is visible).

2. **Deleter (`xmax`) check:**
   - If `xmax is None`: Tuple was never deleted $\rightarrow$ **Visible**.
   - If `xmax >= snapshot.xmax`: Deleted in the future $\rightarrow$ Deletion invisible $\rightarrow$ Tuple **Visible**.
   - If `xmax in snapshot.active_txns`: Deletion is in-flight $\rightarrow$ Deletion invisible $\rightarrow$ Tuple **Visible**.
   - If `xmax not in committed_txns`: Deleting transaction aborted $\rightarrow$ Deletion rolled back $\rightarrow$ Tuple **Visible**.
   - Otherwise, `xmax` committed before the snapshot $\rightarrow$ Tuple was deleted $\rightarrow$ **Invisible**.

### Your Task
Implement `is_tuple_visible(tuple_hdr: dict, snapshot: dict, committed_txns: set[int]) -> bool` in Python.

tests.name: tuple created and committed before snapshot is visible
tuple created by in-flight active transaction is invisible
tuple deleted in the future remains visible to older snapshot
tuple deleted before snapshot is invisible

hints: First evaluate `xmin`: if `xmin >= snapshot.xmax`, `xmin in snapshot.active_txns`, or `xmin not in committed_txns`, return `False` immediately.
Then evaluate `xmax`: if `xmax is None`, return `True`.
If `xmax >= snapshot.xmax`, `xmax in snapshot.active_txns`, or `xmax not in committed_txns`, the deletion has not taken effect for this snapshot, so return `True`.
mvcc-tuple-visibility.explanation: **Why MVCC?** In traditional 2-Phase Locking, reading rows acquires shared locks that block writers. In MVCC, readers never block writers, and writers never block readers. Every query evaluates tuple visibility headers against its transaction snapshot.

ndcg-at-k.title: NDCG@k for Ranking
ndcg-at-k.description: Score a ranked list of results against the best possible order, rewarding relevant results near the top.
ndcg-at-k.statement:
Search and recommendation systems are judged on how good the **top** of a ranked list is. Write `ndcg_at_k(relevances, k)`, where `relevances[i]` is the graded relevance (0, 1, 2, 3, ...) of the result the system put at position `i` (best guess first).

- **DCG@k** is the sum, over the first `k` positions, of `relevance / log2(position + 1)` with positions counted from 1: the first result is divided by `log2(2) = 1`, the second by `log2(3)`, and so on. (So a relevant result counts for less the further down it is.)
- **IDCG@k** is the DCG@k of the best possible order of the **same** relevances (sorted from highest to lowest, over all the results, not only the first `k`).
- The result is `DCG@k / IDCG@k`, a number from 0 to 1. If IDCG@k is 0 (nothing is relevant), return `0.0`.
- If `k` is larger than the list, use the whole list. Raise `ValueError` if `k < 1`.

```python
ndcg_at_k([3, 2, 3, 0, 1, 2], 6)   # 0.9608
ndcg_at_k([0, 3, 0, 3], 2)         # 0.3869
```
ndcg-at-k.starter:
import math


def ndcg_at_k(relevances, k):
    """Return DCG@k divided by the DCG@k of the ideal ordering of the same relevances."""
    ...
tests: assert round(ndcg_at_k([0, 3, 0, 3], 2), 4) == 0.3869, "the ideal list is [3, 3] even though the system ranked a 0 first"
assert ndcg_at_k([3, 3, 2, 1, 0], 5) == 1.0, "already in the best order"
assert ndcg_at_k([3, 2, 1], 1) == 1.0, "at k = 1 only the first result counts, and it is the best one"
assert ndcg_at_k([0, 0, 0], 3) == 0.0, "nothing is relevant: 0.0, not a division by zero"
assert ndcg_at_k([0, 0, 3], 2) == 0.0, "the only relevant result is below the cut-off"
assert round(ndcg_at_k([1, 2], 10), 4) == round(ndcg_at_k([1, 2], 2), 4), "k beyond the list is the whole list"
hints: Write a small function `dcg(values)` first. The first position's discount is `log2(2)`: what is the discount of position `i` (counting from 0)?
The ideal ranking is the same relevances sorted from highest to lowest; compute `dcg` on that.
Truncate to `k` inside `dcg` (after sorting, for the ideal list), and return `0.0` when the ideal DCG is `0`.
ndcg-at-k.explanation:
**The idea.** *Gain* is the relevance of a result; *discount* shrinks it by `log2(position + 1)` because users rarely look far down; *cumulative* adds up the first `k`. The raw DCG depends on how relevant the results available for that query are, so you cannot compare two queries. Dividing by the DCG of the best possible ordering **normalises** it to 0 to 1.

**What "ideal" means.** The best list is built from all the results that exist for the query, not just the ones the system returned in its top `k`; the second test shows why: a system that put a 0 first and missed one of the 3s scores low.

**Where it is used.** It is the standard offline metric for search ranking and recommender systems, and for judging the retrieval step of a RAG pipeline when relevance has grades. Binary relevance (relevant or not) gives MRR, hit rate and precision@k, which are simpler but ignore how good a result is.

**Complexity.** O(n log n) for the sort.

**Usual mistakes.** Counting positions from 0 in the logarithm (`log2(0)` fails; the first position divides by `log2(2)`); computing the ideal from only the first `k` returned items; the exponential-gain variant `2 ** rel - 1` (also common, but it is not the one asked for here).

normalize-url-path.title: Normalize a URL Path
normalize-url-path.description: Resolve dot segments and duplicate slashes in a URL path without ever climbing above the root.
normalize-url-path.statement:
A static-file server must clean the requested path before it looks for a file, so that `/../../etc/passwd` cannot climb out of the web root. Write `normalize_path(path)` for an absolute URL path: it always starts with `/` and has no query string.

- Repeated slashes count as one: `//a///b` is `/a/b`.
- A `.` segment means "here" and disappears. A `..` segment removes the segment before it.
- `..` at the root has nothing to remove and is ignored, so the result never goes above `/`.
- The result ends with `/` only if the input ended with `/` (and the result is not just `/`): `/a/b/..` gives `/a`, but `/a/b/../` gives `/a/`.
- Names such as `...` or `.hidden` are ordinary names. Nothing is decoded.

**Examples**

```python
normalize_path("/a/b/../c")      # "/a/c"
normalize_path("//a///b/./c/")   # "/a/b/c/"
normalize_path("/../../a")       # "/a"
normalize_path("/a/..")          # "/"
```
hints: Read the path one segment at a time, from the root. What do you need to remember about the segments you have already accepted, so that `..` can undo the last one?
Split on `/`: skip empty segments and `.`; for `..` remove the last accepted segment if there is one; add anything else. Join what is left with `/`.
Two details: `..` when nothing has been accepted yet must not fail or go below the root, and the trailing slash comes from the original path but must never turn the root into `//`.
normalize-url-path.explanation:
**The idea.** Treat the path as a stack of names. Read the segments left to right: skip empty ones (repeated slashes) and `.`; for `..` pop the last name if there is one; push anything else. Joining the stack with `/` gives the clean path, and an empty stack is the root.

**Why this is a security fix.** The classic path traversal attack requests `/static/../../etc/passwd`. If the server joins that onto its web root without resolving it, the file system happily climbs out of the directory. Resolving `..` against an empty stack and ignoring it means a request can never leave the root. In production, resolve the path *before* checking permissions, and compare the final real path with the root again.

**The trailing slash** comes from the original string: `/docs/` names a directory and `/docs` a file, so the distinction is kept, except that the root is always just `/`.

**Complexity.** O(n) time and space. Repeatedly replacing `/x/../` pairs inside the string is O(n²) on a deeply nested path.

**Usual mistakes.** Popping from an empty list, treating `...` or `.hidden` as dot segments, and returning `//` for the root.

**Follow-up.** Real servers also decode `%2e%2e` and `%2f` before resolving, and treat backslashes as slashes on Windows. Decoding after the safety check, or decoding twice, are famous vulnerabilities.

number-of-islands.title: Number of Islands
number-of-islands.description: Count the islands, the groups of connected land cells, in a grid of land and water.
number-of-islands.statement:
Count the islands in a grid. `grid` is a list of rows, and each cell is `1` (land) or `0` (water). An island is a group of land cells connected **horizontally or vertically**. Cells that touch only at a corner are not connected, and neither are cells on opposite edges of the grid.

- An empty grid (`[]`) has `0` islands.
- The grid is rectangular, but it need not be square.
- The tests give your function a fresh grid on every call, so you may change the grid if you like.

**Examples**

```python
num_islands([[1, 1, 0],
             [1, 0, 0],
             [0, 0, 1]])     # 2
num_islands([[1, 0, 1],
             [0, 1, 0]])     # 3, the cells only touch at corners
num_islands([])              # 0
```

In the tests a grid is written as strings of `0` and `1`, one string per row.
tests:
def count(*rows):
    """Count the islands of a grid written as strings, such as count("110", "001"). A fresh list of lists is built on every call."""
    return num_islands([[int(cell) for cell in row] for row in rows])
snake = ["11111", "10000", "11111", "00001", "11111"]
checkerboard = ["".join("1" if (r + c) % 2 == 0 else "0" for c in range(200)) for r in range(200)]
stripes = ["1" * 100 if r % 2 == 0 else "0" * 100 for r in range(40)]
full = ["1" * 20 for _ in range(15)]
hints: Each island is one connected blob. When you find one land cell, how can you visit every other cell of the same island so that it is never counted twice?

Scan the grid. At a land cell that has not been visited, add one to the count, then explore everything connected to it (up, down, left, right) with a stack, a queue or recursion, marking each cell as visited.

Check the bounds before you read a neighbour: in Python `grid[r][-1]` does not fail, it wraps around to the last column. Mark a cell visited when you add it to the stack or queue, and remember that diagonal neighbours do not count.
number-of-islands.explanation:
**The idea.** Scan the grid. Each time you meet a land cell that no earlier island has reached, you have found a new island: count it, then **flood** it, visiting every land cell connected to this one so that none of them is counted again.

**Flooding.** Keep a stack (or a queue) of cells still to visit. Take a cell, look at its four neighbours, and for each one that is inside the grid, is land and has not been seen, mark it as seen and add it. Marking a cell when you add it, not when you take it out, stops it from entering the stack twice.

**Python details.** Check the bounds yourself: a neighbour index of `-1` does not raise an error in Python, it wraps around to the other edge of the grid, and would silently join islands that are not connected. A stack also avoids the recursion limit on a big island, though plain recursion is fine for the grids in these tests.

**Complexity.** O(rows × cols) time and space: each cell is looked at a constant number of times. If you may modify the grid, overwriting visited land with `0` replaces the `seen` set.

**Follow-up.** Return the size of the biggest island, or let diagonal neighbours connect.

observer-event-bus.title: Publish-Subscribe Event Bus
observer-event-bus.description: Decouple domain events with an in-memory event bus, subscription tracking, and isolated handler dispatch.
observer-event-bus.statement:
Implement an in-memory `EventBus` to facilitate low-level decoupling between components.

- `subscribe(event_name, handler)`: Registers a callable `handler` for `event_name` (a string). A handler can be registered multiple times or once per distinct function. Return a callable unsubscription function that, when called with no arguments, removes that specific registration.
- `unsubscribe(event_name, handler)`: Removes the first registered instance of `handler` for `event_name` if present. If not found, do nothing.
- `publish(event_name, *args, **kwargs)`: Sequentially calls all handlers registered for `event_name` with `*args` and `**kwargs`. Handlers must execute in insertion order. Return the count of handlers invoked.

**Example**

```python
bus = EventBus()
log = []
def on_login(user_id):
    log.append(f"login:{user_id}")

unsub = bus.subscribe("user_login", on_login)
bus.publish("user_login", 42)    # calls on_login(42), returns 1
unsub()                          # unregisters handler
bus.publish("user_login", 42)    # returns 0, log unchanged
```
tests:
bus = EventBus()
log = []
def h1(x):
    log.append(f"h1:{x}")
def h2(x):
    log.append(f"h2:{x}")

unsub1 = bus.subscribe("order_placed", h1)
bus.subscribe("order_placed", h2)

scenario = "Unsubscribe via bus method"
bus.unsubscribe("order_placed", h2)

scenario = "Multiple arguments and keyword arguments forwarded intact"
kwargs_log = []
def handler_with_kw(a, b, status="pending"):
    kwargs_log.append((a, b, status))

bus.subscribe("txn", handler_with_kw)
bus.publish("txn", 1, 2, status="completed")
hints: Store handlers in a dictionary mapping event_name strings to lists of callables: self._handlers = defaultdict(list).
When subscribe() is called, append the handler to the list and return a closure lambda: self.unsubscribe(event_name, handler).
To prevent mutation issues if a handler unsubscribes during publish(), iterate over a shallow copy of the handler list: list(self._handlers.get(event_name, [])).
observer-event-bus.explanation:
**Shallow copy during dispatch.** If a subscriber unsubscribes itself or registers a new listener during the execution of `publish()`, mutating the underlying list while iterating over it causes skipped callbacks or runtime modification errors. Iterating over `list(handlers)` avoids this hazard.

**Return unsubscription tokens.** Returning a simple parameterless cancellation callback (`unsub()`) gives callers ergonomic lifecycle management without forcing them to retain the original event name and handler reference.

oop-abstract-payment.title: Abstract Payment Methods
oop-abstract-payment.description: An abstract base class with an abstract method: it cannot be created, and every child must supply pay().
oop-abstract-payment.statement:
Use Python's `abc` module (`ABC`, `abstractmethod`).

Create an **abstract class** `Payment`.

- It has an **abstract method** `pay(amount)`.
- It has a normal (concrete) method `describe()` that returns the **class name** of the object, for example `"UPI"`.
- Trying to create a `Payment` directly raises `TypeError`, and so does creating a subclass that has not implemented `pay`.

Create these concrete payment classes:

- `CreditCard(number)`: `pay(amount)` prints `Paid <amount> by credit card ending <last 4 digits of number>`
- `UPI(upi_id)`: `pay(amount)` prints `Paid <amount> using UPI <upi_id>`
- `Wallet(balance)`: if `amount` is more than the balance it prints `Insufficient wallet balance` and changes nothing; otherwise it reduces `balance` and prints `Paid <amount> from wallet. Balance left: <balance>`

Write `checkout(payment, amount)` that calls `payment.pay(amount)`. It works for every kind of payment.
tests: assert error_of(Payment) is not None and error_of(Payment).startswith("TypeError")

card = CreditCard("1234567812345678")
upi = UPI("asha@bank")
wallet = Wallet(500)
assert isinstance(card, Payment) and isinstance(upi, Payment) and isinstance(wallet, Payment)
assert out(card.pay, 250) == ["Paid 250 by credit card ending 5678"] and out(upi.pay, 99) == ["Paid 99 using UPI asha@bank"]
assert out(wallet.pay, 200) == ["Paid 200 from wallet. Balance left: 300"] and wallet.balance == 300
assert out(wallet.pay, 301) == ["Insufficient wallet balance"] and wallet.balance == 300
assert out(wallet.pay, 300) == ["Paid 300 from wallet. Balance left: 0"] and wallet.balance == 0
assert out(checkout, card, 10) == ["Paid 10 by credit card ending 5678"] and out(checkout, upi, 5) == ["Paid 5 using UPI asha@bank"]
hints: Write `class Payment(ABC):` and put `@abstractmethod` above `def pay(self, amount):`. The body can be just a docstring: it is never meant to run.
`describe()` is a normal method written once in `Payment`; `type(self).__name__` gives the name of the real class, so every child gets the right answer for free.
Python refuses to create an object whose class still has an unimplemented abstract method, and the error is a `TypeError`. You do not write that check yourself.
oop-abstract-payment.explanation:
**Abstract class versus abstract method.** An *abstract method* is a promise with no body: "every payment can `pay`, but only a concrete one knows how". An *abstract class* is a class that has at least one abstract method (or is marked that way), so it **cannot be instantiated**. The abstract class can still contain normal methods such as `describe()`.

| | Abstract method | Abstract class |
|---|---|---|
| What it is | a method declared without a body | a class you cannot create objects from |
| Who fills it in | each concrete subclass | it is extended, never created |
| Enforced by | `@abstractmethod` + `ABC` | the same: `TypeError` on creation |

**Why bother?** It turns a forgotten method into an error at once (`TypeError: Can't instantiate abstract class`), instead of a crash deep inside a program. And `checkout` can rely on "everything I am given can `pay`".

**Plain Python alternative.** Many programmers just write `raise NotImplementedError` in the base method. It works, but the error appears only when `pay` is *called*, not when the object is created.

oop-abstract-report.title: Abstract Class With Shared Code
oop-abstract-report.description: An abstract class that mixes finished code (render) with holes the children must fill (title, body).
oop-abstract-report.statement:
Create an abstract class `Report` (use `ABC` and `abstractmethod`).

- Abstract methods: `title()` and `body()`, each returns a string.
- A concrete method `render()` returns the finished text: the line `=== <title> ===`, then a new line, then the body. For example `"=== Sales ===\nTotal: 500"`.
- A concrete method `print_report()` prints `render()`.
- `Report` itself cannot be created (`TypeError`).

Create two concrete reports:

- `SalesReport(total)`: title `Sales`, body `Total: <total>`
- `AttendanceReport(present, total)`: title `Attendance`, body `Present: <present>/<total> (<percent>%)` where `percent` is `present * 100 / total` rounded to **1 decimal place** (`0.0` when `total` is 0).

`render` and `print_report` are written **once**, in `Report`.
tests: assert sales.title() == "Sales" and sales.body() == "Total: 500" and sales.render() == "=== Sales ===\nTotal: 500"
assert att.title() == "Attendance" and att.body() == "Present: 45/60 (75.0%)" and att.render() == "=== Attendance ===\nPresent: 45/60 (75.0%)"
assert out(sales.print_report) == ["=== Sales ===", "Total: 500"] and out(att.print_report) == ["=== Attendance ===", "Present: 45/60 (75.0%)"]
assert "render" not in SalesReport.__dict__ and "render" not in AttendanceReport.__dict__ and "print_report" not in SalesReport.__dict__
assert isinstance(sales, Report) and isinstance(att, Report)
assert c.render() == "=== Mine ===\nline one\nline two" and out(c.print_report) == ["=== Mine ===", "line one", "line two"]
assert getattr(Report.title, "__isabstractmethod__", False) and getattr(Report.body, "__isabstractmethod__", False) and not getattr(Report.render, "__isabstractmethod__", False)
hints: Mark `title` and `body` with `@abstractmethod`; leave `render` and `print_report` as ordinary methods.
`render` calls `self.title()` and `self.body()`. In the base class they have no real code, but at run time `self` is a `SalesReport` or an `AttendanceReport`, so their versions run.
For the percentage use `round(x, 1)`; guard against `total == 0` before dividing.
oop-abstract-report.explanation:
**An abstract class is not "empty".** `Report` holds finished code (`render`, `print_report`) *and* two blanks (`title`, `body`) that each child must fill in. The common layout is written once; only what differs is left to the children. This shape is called the **template method** pattern.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    A[render in Report] --> B[title in the child]
    A --> C[body in the child]
```

**Abstract method versus abstract class, again.** The *methods* are the blanks; the *class* is abstract because it has blanks, so you cannot make a `Report()` that would print half a report. Python enforces both.

**Extending it.** A new report only writes `title` and `body` and gets `render` and `print_report` for free: the test defines `Custom` to prove it.

oop-animal-sounds.title: Animal Sounds
oop-animal-sounds.description: Runtime polymorphism: one loop makes every animal speak in its own way, including animals added later.
oop-animal-sounds.statement:
Create a class `Animal` with `Animal(name)`.

- `speak()` prints `<name> makes a sound`.

Create subclasses that **override** `speak()`:

- `Dog` prints `<name> says Woof`
- `Cat` prints `<name> says Meow`
- `Cow` prints `<name> says Moo`

Write a function `make_all_speak(animals)` that calls `speak()` on every animal in the list, in order. It must not check which kind of animal each one is.

**Example**

```
make_all_speak([Dog("Rex"), Cat("Tom"), Animal("Thing")])
# Rex says Woof
# Tom says Meow
# Thing makes a sound
```
tests: assert out(Dog("Rex").speak) == ["Rex says Woof"] and out(Cat("Tom").speak) == ["Tom says Meow"] and out(Cow("Bella").speak) == ["Bella says Moo"]
assert issubclass(Dog, Animal) and issubclass(Cat, Animal) and issubclass(Cow, Animal) and Dog("Rex").name == "Rex"
assert out(make_all_speak, herd) == ["Rex says Woof", "Tom says Meow", "Bella says Moo", "Thing makes a sound"]
assert out(make_all_speak, [Duck("Don"), Dog("Rex")]) == ["Don says Quack", "Rex says Woof"]
assert out(make_all_speak, [Cat("A"), Cat("B")]) == ["A says Meow", "B says Meow"]
hints: Only `Animal` needs an `__init__`; the children inherit it. They only override `speak`.
`make_all_speak` is a three-line loop: `for animal in animals: animal.speak()`. There is no `if isinstance(...)` anywhere.
A subclass that does not override `speak` (the tests define one called `Silent`) simply falls back to the parent's version.
oop-animal-sounds.explanation:
**Polymorphism** means "many forms": the *same call* (`animal.speak()`) does *different things* depending on the object. The caller only needs to know that every animal can `speak`.

**It runs at run time.** Python decides which `speak` to run when the line executes, by looking at the object's class (and then its parents). This is called *dynamic dispatch* or *late binding*.

**Why it matters.** `make_all_speak` never changes when you add a `Duck`. Without polymorphism you would have a growing `if/elif` chain that has to be edited every time. That is the *open/closed* idea: open for new animals, closed for edits.

**Duck typing.** Python does not even require `Duck` to inherit from `Animal`: any object with a `speak()` method works. Inheritance is one way to get polymorphism, not the only one.

oop-class-vs-instance-attributes.title: Class vs Instance Attributes
oop-class-vs-instance-attributes.description: Tell shared (class) data from per-object (instance) data: a school name for everyone, a roll number for each student.
oop-class-vs-instance-attributes.statement:
Create a class `Student` with `Student(name)`.

- **Class attributes** (shared by all students): `school`, which starts as `"Green Valley"`, and `count`, the number of students created so far, which starts at `0`.
- **Instance attributes** (one per student): `name` and `roll_no`. The first student created gets roll number 1, the next 2, and so on; creating a student adds 1 to `count`.
- `info()` prints `<roll_no>: <name> (<school>)`.
- `rename_school(new_name)` is a **class method**: it changes `school` for the class, so every student who has not set their own school sees it.
- `total()` is a **class method** that returns `count`.

Assigning `student.school = "X"` on one student creates an instance attribute that affects **only that student**.
tests: assert Student.school == "Green Valley" and Student.count == 0 and Student.total() == 0

a = Student("Asha")
b = Student("Ben")
c = Student("Cy")
assert Student.count == 3 and Student.total() == 3 and a.count == 3 and a.total() == 3
assert out(a.info) == ["1: Asha (Green Valley)"] and out(c.info) == ["3: Cy (Green Valley)"]
assert Student.rename_school("Blue Hill") is None and Student.school == "Blue Hill"
assert out(a.info) == ["1: Asha (Blue Hill)"] and out(b.info) == ["2: Ben (Blue Hill)"]
assert out(b.info) == ["2: Ben (Private Tutor)"] and out(a.info) == ["1: Asha (Blue Hill)"] and Student.school == "Blue Hill"
assert out(a.info) == ["1: Asha (Red Oak)"] and out(b.info) == ["2: Ben (Private Tutor)"]
assert Student.count == 3 and Student.total() == 3 and b.count == 3
assert d.roll_no == 4 and Student.count == 4 and Student.total() == 4
assert "school" in Student.__dict__ and "count" in Student.__dict__ and "name" not in Student.__dict__ and "roll_no" not in Student.__dict__
assert "name" in a.__dict__ and "roll_no" in a.__dict__ and "school" not in c.__dict__
hints: Anything written directly inside the class body (`school = ...`, `count = 0`) belongs to the **class** and is shared. Anything set on `self` in `__init__` belongs to **one object**.
To change the shared counter write `Student.count += 1`. Writing `self.count += 1` would create a new instance attribute and leave the class counter alone.
A class method receives the class (`cls`) instead of an object: `cls.school = new_name` changes the shared attribute for everybody.
oop-class-vs-instance-attributes.explanation:
**Two places for data.** Class attributes live on the class; instance attributes live on each object. When you read `student.school`, Python looks on the object first and then on the class. That is why one student can have a private `school` while the others follow the class.

**The classic trap.** `self.count += 1` reads the class value, adds one and stores the result *on the object*: the shared counter never moves. The test `a.count = 99` shows that setting through an instance never changes the class.

**Class method versus instance method.** An instance method works on one object (`self`). A class method works on the class (`cls`): counters, alternative constructors, settings shared by everyone.

oop-discount-polymorphism.title: Discounts and Polymorphism
oop-discount-polymorphism.description: A shop applies a list of different discounts to a price; one function works for every kind, even new ones.
oop-discount-polymorphism.statement:
Create a class `Discount` whose `apply(price)` returns the price **unchanged**. Prices are whole numbers (rupees).

Create two subclasses that **override** `apply`:

- `PercentDiscount(percent)` takes `percent` off: `price - price * percent // 100`. A percent outside 0 to 100 is `ValueError("Percent must be between 0 and 100")`.
- `FlatDiscount(amount)` takes a fixed `amount` off but never goes below 0: `max(0, price - amount)`. A negative amount is `ValueError("Amount cannot be negative")`.

Write `final_price(price, discounts)` that applies the discounts **in the order given** (each one to the result of the previous) and returns the final price. It must not check what kind of discount each one is.

**Example:** `final_price(1000, [PercentDiscount(10), FlatDiscount(50)])` is `850`.
tests: assert isinstance(p, Discount) and isinstance(f, Discount)
assert p.apply(1000) == 900 and p.apply(99) == 90 and PercentDiscount(0).apply(80) == 80 and PercentDiscount(100).apply(80) == 0
assert f.apply(1000) == 950 and f.apply(30) == 0 and FlatDiscount(0).apply(30) == 30
assert error_of(PercentDiscount, -1) == "ValueError: Percent must be between 0 and 100" and error_of(PercentDiscount, 101) == "ValueError: Percent must be between 0 and 100"
assert error_of(FlatDiscount, -5) == "ValueError: Amount cannot be negative"
assert final_price(1000, [p, f]) == 850 and final_price(1000, [f, p]) == 855
assert final_price(100, [Festival(), PercentDiscount(50)]) == 47 and final_price(100, [Discount(), Festival()]) == 93
hints: Each subclass keeps its own setting (`percent`, `amount`) in `__init__` and overrides only `apply`.
`final_price` is a loop that feeds the price through every discount: `price = discount.apply(price)`.
The tests define a new `Festival` discount that your function has never seen. If `final_price` works for it without any change, you have used polymorphism correctly.
oop-discount-polymorphism.explanation:
**Run-time polymorphism for beginners.** `discount.apply(price)` looks the same for every discount, but each class does its own sum. The *caller* (`final_price`) knows nothing about percentages or flat amounts.

**Open for extension.** Adding "Buy one get one free" means writing one new class. Nothing that already works is edited: no `if kind == ...` anywhere.

**Order matters.** `final_price(1000, [10%, 50 off])` is 850 but the other way round is 855, because each discount applies to the result of the previous one. Say that out loud in a real shop.

oop-employee-payroll.title: Employees and Payroll
oop-employee-payroll.description: Inheritance plus overriding: three kinds of employee are paid differently, and one payroll function works for all of them.
oop-employee-payroll.statement:
Create a class `Employee` with `Employee(name, base_salary)`.

- Attributes `name` and `base_salary`.
- `calculate_pay()` returns the base salary.
- `show()` prints `<name> earns <pay>` where `<pay>` is what `calculate_pay()` returns **for that kind of employee** (write `show` once, in `Employee`).

Create two subclasses that override `calculate_pay()`:

- `Manager(name, base_salary)` has a `team` (an empty list at first) and `add_member(employee)` which appends to it. Pay is the base salary plus **1000 for every team member**.
- `Developer(name, base_salary, overtime_hours=0)` has `overtime_hours`. Pay is the base salary plus **200 for every overtime hour**.

Finally write a plain function `total_payroll(employees)` that returns the sum of every employee's pay. It must **not** check which kind of employee each one is.
tests: assert boss.team == [] and boss.calculate_pay() == 50000 and isinstance(boss, Employee)
assert (dev.overtime_hours, other_dev.overtime_hours) == (10, 0) and dev.calculate_pay() == 42000 and other_dev.calculate_pay() == 45000 and isinstance(dev, Employee)
assert boss.add_member(dev) is None and boss.add_member(other_dev) is None and boss.team == [dev, other_dev]
assert out(boss.show) == ["Ben earns 52000"] and out(dev.show) == ["Cy earns 42000"]
assert total_payroll([Intern("Kim", 1), clerk]) == 35000 and out(Intern("Kim", 1).show) == ["Kim earns 5000"]
hints: Each subclass overrides **one** method, `calculate_pay`. `show` is written once in `Employee` and calls `self.calculate_pay()`: `self` is the real object, so Python picks the right version.
Give `Manager` its own list in `__init__` (`self.team = []`). A list written at class level would be shared by every manager.

`total_payroll` just loops and calls `employee.calculate_pay()`. No `isinstance`, no `if`: that is the whole point of polymorphism, and the tests add a new `Intern` class that your function has never heard of.
oop-employee-payroll.explanation:
**Runtime polymorphism in one example.** `total_payroll` is written once and works for every kind of employee, including ones that do not exist yet. Which `calculate_pay` runs is decided **when the program runs**, by the real class of each object. That is *dynamic dispatch*.

**The same for `show`.** It sits in the parent but calls `self.calculate_pay()`, so a `Manager` prints a manager's pay. Code in a base class can call methods that only the children define.

**What to avoid.** `if type(e) is Manager: ... elif ...` inside `total_payroll` would break every time a new kind is added. Let the objects decide.

**Going further.** What if every employee needs a tax? Where would you add `tax()` so that all subclasses get it for free, and one can still change it?

oop-library-books.title: Library Book Desk
oop-library-books.description: A small library that lends and takes back copies and prints a clear message for every case.
oop-library-books.statement:
Create a class `Library` with no arguments. It keeps books by title.

- `add_book(title, author, copies=1)` adds copies. A known title gets more copies (same author kept). `copies` below 1 is `ValueError("Copies must be at least 1")`.
- `checkout(title)` **prints**:
  - `We do not have <title>` for an unknown title
  - `Sorry, <title> is not available` when every copy is out
  - otherwise it lends one copy and prints `You borrowed <title>`
- `return_book(title)` **prints**:
  - `We do not have <title>` for an unknown title
  - `All copies are already here` when no copy is out (nothing changes)
  - otherwise it takes one copy back and prints `Thanks for returning <title>`
- `show_catalog()` prints one line per book, **sorted by title**: `<title> by <author>: <available>/<total> available`. An empty library prints `The library is empty`.
tests: assert out(lib.checkout, "Dune") == ["We do not have Dune"] and out(lib.return_book, "Dune") == ["We do not have Dune"]
assert lib.add_book("Dune", "Herbert", 2) is None and lib.add_book("Emma", "Austen") is None
assert error_of(lib.add_book, "X", "Y", 0) == "ValueError: Copies must be at least 1" and error_of(lib.add_book, "Dune", "Z", -1) == "ValueError: Copies must be at least 1"
assert out(lib.show_catalog) == ["Dune by Herbert: 2/2 available", "Emma by Austen: 1/1 available"]
assert out(lib.checkout, "Dune") == ["You borrowed Dune"] and out(lib.checkout, "Dune") == ["You borrowed Dune"] and out(lib.checkout, "Dune") == ["Sorry, Dune is not available"]
assert out(lib.show_catalog) == ["Dune by Herbert: 0/2 available", "Emma by Austen: 1/1 available"]
assert out(lib.return_book, "Dune") == ["Thanks for returning Dune"] and out(lib.show_catalog)[0] == "Dune by Herbert: 1/2 available"
assert out(lib.return_book, "Emma") == ["All copies are already here"] and out(lib.show_catalog)[1] == "Emma by Austen: 1/1 available"
assert out(lib.show_catalog) == ["Alice by Carroll: 1/1 available", "Dune by Herbert: 2/3 available", "Emma by Austen: 1/1 available"]
assert out(lib.checkout, "dune") == ["We do not have dune"]
hints: One dictionary from title to a small record (`author`, `total`, `available`) is enough. Create it in `__init__` so each library has its own.
Handle the cases in the order of the statement: unknown, none left (or none out), otherwise the normal path. Each branch prints exactly one line.
`sorted(self._books)` gives the titles in alphabetical order for the catalogue.
oop-library-books.explanation:
**The idea.** The class owns a small table and exposes a few actions. Callers never touch the numbers directly, so the rules ("never lend a copy that is not there", "never take back more than were lent") live in one place.

**Every path says something.** A good beginner class never fails silently: each of the three outcomes of `checkout` and of `return_book` has its own message, and the tests check every one.

**Why a dictionary per library.** `self._books = {}` is created in `__init__`, so two libraries never share books (the last test checks it). Writing `_books = {}` in the class body would share it.

oop-money-operators.title: Money With Operators
oop-money-operators.description: Operator overloading: make + - * == < and str() work on a Money class, including sum().
oop-money-operators.statement:
Create a class `Money` that stores whole **cents**: `Money(cents)`. `cents` must be an `int` of 0 or more (not a `bool`), otherwise `ValueError("Cents must be a non-negative integer")`. The attribute is `cents`.

Make it behave like a number by writing these **special methods**:

- `Money + Money` gives a new `Money`; `sum([m1, m2, m3])` must work too (`sum` starts from the integer `0`).
- `Money - Money` gives a new `Money`; if the result would be negative raise `ValueError("Result would be negative")`.
- `Money * n` and `n * Money` with an `int` of 0 or more give a new `Money`.
- `==`, `<`, `<=`, `>`, `>=` compare the cents. Equal amounts have the same `hash`. Comparing with a plain number is not equal.
- `str(money)` is `"$<dollars>.<cents with 2 digits>"`, for example `"$12.50"` and `"$0.05"`; `repr(money)` is `Money(1250)`.

Anything unsupported (`Money + 5`, `Money * 1.5`, `Money < 5`) must raise `TypeError`: return `NotImplemented` from your method and Python does the rest.
tests: assert a.cents == 1250 and str(a) == "$12.50" and str(Money(5)) == "$0.05" and str(Money(0)) == "$0.00" and str(Money(100)) == "$1.00" and repr(a) == "Money(1250)"

for bad in (-1, 1.5, True, "5", None):
    assert error_of(Money, bad) == "ValueError: Cents must be a non-negative integer"
assert (a + b).cents == 1550 and isinstance(a + b, Money) and a.cents == 1250
assert (a - b).cents == 950 and (a - a).cents == 0 and error_of(lambda: b - a) == "ValueError: Result would be negative"
assert sum([Money(100), Money(250), Money(5)]).cents == 355 and sum([]) == 0
assert a == Money(1250) and a != b and not (a == 1250) and a != 1250
assert b < a and a > b and b <= b and a >= a and not a < b and sorted([a, b, Money(1)]) == [Money(1), b, a] and max(a, b) is a
assert hash(Money(7)) == hash(Money(7)) and len({Money(7), Money(7), Money(8)}) == 2 and {Money(5): "x"}[Money(5)] == "x"

assert kind_of(lambda: a + 5) == "TypeError" and kind_of(lambda: 5 + a) == "TypeError" and kind_of(lambda: a * 1.5) == "TypeError" and kind_of(lambda: a * -1) == "TypeError" and kind_of(lambda: a < 5) == "TypeError" and kind_of(lambda: a - 1) == "TypeError"
hints: `a + b` is Python's shorthand for `a.__add__(b)`. Return a **new** `Money`; do not change either operand.

When the other side is not a `Money`, `return NotImplemented` (not `raise`). Python then tries the other operand and finally raises `TypeError` for you. `sum()` starts with `0 + money`, which is why `__radd__` exists.
`functools.total_ordering` fills in `<=`, `>` and `>=` once you write `__eq__` and `__lt__`. Objects that are equal must have equal hashes, so base `__hash__` on `cents`.
oop-money-operators.explanation:
**Operator overloading is compile-time-style polymorphism done with special methods.** In C++ and C# it is a language feature; in Python the operators *are* method calls (`a + b` calls `a.__add__(b)`), so `Money` can define them. It is "the same operator, different behaviour per type".

**Why `NotImplemented`.** `Money + 5` should not be Money's decision to reject: returning `NotImplemented` lets Python try `int.__radd__`, and only then raise `TypeError`. That also makes `5 + money` and `sum()` work through `__radd__`.

**Money is a value object.** Whole cents in an `int`, never a float (`0.1 + 0.2` is not `0.3`), operations return *new* objects, and equal amounts compare and hash equal.

oop-movie-ticket-counter.title: Movie Ticket Counter
oop-movie-ticket-counter.description: Write a Movie class that books tickets, refuses a booking when the seats run out, and prints its status.
oop-movie-ticket-counter.statement:
Create a class `Movie`.

**Attributes**

- `movie_name`: the name of the movie
- `total_seats`: total seats in the theatre
- `ticket_price`: price of one ticket
- `booked_seats`: starts at `0`

Create it with `Movie(movie_name, total_seats, ticket_price)`.

**Methods**

- `book_ticket(num_tickets)` books the given number of tickets. The method **prints** its answer (it returns nothing):
  - fewer than 1 ticket: `Please book at least 1 ticket`
  - enough seats left: the booking is confirmed (`booked_seats` goes up) and it prints `Booked <num_tickets> ticket(s). Total amount: <amount>` where `amount = num_tickets * ticket_price`
  - not enough seats left: it prints `Sorry, not enough seats available` and **changes nothing**
- `show_status()` prints three lines: `Movie: <movie_name>`, `Seats available: <seats left>` and `Seats booked: <booked_seats>`.

**Example**

```
movie = Movie("Leo", 5, 150)
movie.book_ticket(2)    # Booked 2 ticket(s). Total amount: 300
movie.book_ticket(4)    # Sorry, not enough seats available
movie.show_status()     # Movie: Leo / Seats available: 3 / Seats booked: 2
```
tests: assert out(movie.book_ticket, 2) == ["Booked 2 ticket(s). Total amount: 300"] and movie.booked_seats == 2
assert out(movie.book_ticket, 4) == ["Sorry, not enough seats available"] and movie.booked_seats == 2
assert out(movie.book_ticket, 3) == ["Booked 3 ticket(s). Total amount: 450"] and movie.booked_seats == 5
assert out(movie.book_ticket, 1) == ["Sorry, not enough seats available"]
assert out(other.book_ticket, 0) == ["Please book at least 1 ticket"] and out(other.book_ticket, -2) == ["Please book at least 1 ticket"] and other.booked_seats == 0
assert out(other.book_ticket, 1) == ["Booked 1 ticket(s). Total amount: 200"] and movie.booked_seats == 5 and other.booked_seats == 1
hints: `__init__` just stores the three arguments on `self` and sets `self.booked_seats = 0`. Every object gets its own copy of each attribute.
Seats left is not stored: it is `self.total_seats - self.booked_seats`. Check the bad-input case first, then "enough seats", and put the "sorry" message in the `else`.
Only the *successful* branch changes `booked_seats`. A refused booking must leave the object exactly as it was.
oop-movie-ticket-counter.explanation:
**The idea.** A class bundles data (`booked_seats`) with the actions that are allowed to change it (`book_ticket`). The rule "never sell more seats than exist" lives in *one* method, so no caller can forget it.

**Derive, do not store.** Seats left is `total_seats - booked_seats`. Storing it as a fourth attribute would mean two numbers that must always agree.

**Print versus return.** These methods *print* because the exercise is about what the user sees. In real code you would return a value (or raise an error) and let the caller decide how to show it; that is easier to test and to reuse.

**Going further.** What should happen if `num_tickets` is `2.5`? Where would you put that check?

oop-multilevel-inheritance.title: Multilevel Inheritance
oop-multilevel-inheritance.description: A chain Animal, Mammal, Dog: each level adds behaviour, and the bottom class has all of it.
oop-multilevel-inheritance.statement:
Build three classes in a **chain** (multilevel inheritance).

- `Animal(name)`: `eat()` prints `<name> eats`. `lineage()` returns the list of the class names of the object's own class and all its parents, **nearest first, leaving out `object`**, for example `["Dog", "Mammal", "Animal"]`.
- `Mammal(Animal)`: `feed_milk()` prints `<name> feeds milk`.
- `Dog(Mammal)`: `bark()` prints `<name> barks`.

A `Dog` must be able to use all three methods without defining `eat` or `feed_milk` itself. A plain `Animal` has only `eat` and `lineage`.
tests: assert rex.name == "Rex" and out(rex.eat) == ["Rex eats"] and out(rex.feed_milk) == ["Rex feeds milk"] and out(rex.bark) == ["Rex barks"]
assert out(cow.eat) == ["Bella eats"] and out(cow.feed_milk) == ["Bella feeds milk"] and not hasattr(cow, "bark")
assert out(fish.eat) == ["Nemo eats"] and not hasattr(fish, "feed_milk") and not hasattr(fish, "bark")
assert issubclass(Dog, Mammal) and issubclass(Dog, Animal) and issubclass(Mammal, Animal) and not issubclass(Animal, Mammal)
assert rex.lineage() == ["Dog", "Mammal", "Animal"] and cow.lineage() == ["Mammal", "Animal"] and fish.lineage() == ["Animal"]
assert "eat" not in Dog.__dict__ and "feed_milk" not in Dog.__dict__ and "eat" not in Mammal.__dict__
assert Puppy("Bit").lineage() == ["Puppy", "Dog", "Mammal", "Animal"] and out(Puppy("Bit").feed_milk) == ["Bit feeds milk"]
assert isinstance(rex, Animal) and isinstance(rex, Mammal) and isinstance(rex, Dog) and not isinstance(fish, Dog)
hints: Only `Animal` needs `__init__`. `Mammal` and `Dog` inherit it, so `Dog("Rex")` works without any constructor of its own.
`type(self)` is the real class of the object. Every class has `__mro__`, the tuple of the class and its parents in the order Python searches them.
Filter out `object` (the invisible parent of every class) so the list matches the statement.

oop-multiple-inheritance-mro.title: Multiple Inheritance and MRO
oop-multiple-inheritance-mro.description: A class with two parents: use cooperative super() so every ability is collected once, in method resolution order.
oop-multiple-inheritance-mro.statement:
Create a base class `Animal` with `Animal(name)`.

- `abilities()` returns a list of ability names; for a plain `Animal` it is `[]`.
- `describe()` prints `<name> can <abilities joined with ", ">`, or `<name> has no special abilities` when the list is empty.

Create three **mixin-style** subclasses of `Animal`. Each one's `abilities()` returns **its own ability first** and then whatever `super().abilities()` returns:

- `Flyer`: `"fly"`
- `Swimmer`: `"swim"`
- `Runner`: `"run"`

Create these classes with **several parents**, and write **no** `abilities` method in them (the parents are enough):

- `Duck(Flyer, Swimmer, Runner)`
- `Otter(Swimmer, Runner)`

Write `mro_names(cls)` that returns the names of the classes in `cls.__mro__` (method resolution order), including `object`.
tests: assert a.name == "Thing" and a.abilities() == [] and out(a.describe) == ["Thing has no special abilities"]
assert Flyer("Eagle").abilities() == ["fly"] and Swimmer("Fish").abilities() == ["swim"] and Runner("Dog").abilities() == ["run"]
assert duck.name == "Don" and duck.abilities() == ["fly", "swim", "run"] and otter.abilities() == ["swim", "run"]
assert out(duck.describe) == ["Don can fly, swim, run"] and out(otter.describe) == ["Ollie can swim, run"]
assert isinstance(duck, Flyer) and isinstance(duck, Swimmer) and isinstance(duck, Runner) and isinstance(duck, Animal) and not isinstance(otter, Flyer)
assert "abilities" not in Duck.__dict__ and "abilities" not in Otter.__dict__

assert mro_names(Duck) == ["Duck", "Flyer", "Swimmer", "Runner", "Animal", "object"] and mro_names(Otter) == ["Otter", "Swimmer", "Runner", "Animal", "object"] and mro_names(Animal) == ["Animal", "object"]
assert Robot("R2").abilities() == ["charge", "run", "fly", "swim"] and out(Robot("R2").describe) == ["R2 can charge, run, fly, swim"]
assert Duck.__bases__ == (Flyer, Swimmer, Runner) and Otter.__bases__ == (Swimmer, Runner)
hints: Each mixin writes `return ["fly"] + super().abilities()`. `super()` does **not** mean "the parent": it means "the next class in the method resolution order", which for a `Duck` after `Flyer` is `Swimmer`.

`class Duck(Flyer, Swimmer, Runner): pass` is the whole class. Python builds the order `Duck, Flyer, Swimmer, Runner, Animal, object` (see `Duck.__mro__`) so `Animal.abilities` is reached **once**, at the end.
Because every class in the chain calls `super()`, adding a new ability class never needs the others to change.
oop-multiple-inheritance-mro.explanation:
**Multiple inheritance** means a class has more than one parent. The danger is the *diamond*: `Flyer` and `Swimmer` both inherit `Animal`, so which `Animal` code runs, and how many times?

```mermaid
classDiagram
    Animal <|-- Flyer
    Animal <|-- Swimmer
    Animal <|-- Runner
    Flyer <|-- Duck
    Swimmer <|-- Duck
    Runner <|-- Duck
```

**Python's answer is the MRO** (method resolution order, computed by the *C3 linearisation*): a single list in which every class appears once and every class comes before its parents. `super()` follows that list, so with cooperative `super()` calls each ability is added exactly once.

**Order of the parents matters.** `Penguin(Swimmer, Flyer)` gives `["swim", "fly"]`, while `Duck(Flyer, Swimmer)` gives `["fly", "swim"]`. The test shows both.

**Use with care.** Small *mixins* (one ability each) are a good use. Big trees of multiple inheritance are hard to read; prefer composition when in doubt. Java and C# avoid the problem by allowing only one parent class (plus many interfaces).

oop-overloading-in-python.title: Overloading in Python
oop-overloading-in-python.description: Python has no compile-time overloading: write one method that behaves differently for different arguments (default values, *args, type checks).
oop-overloading-in-python.statement:
Java and C# let you write several methods with the same name and different parameters (*method overloading*, "compile-time polymorphism"). In Python a second `def` with the same name simply **replaces** the first, so one method has to handle every case itself.

Write a class `Greeter` with:

- `greet(name=None, title=None)` **returns** a string:
  - `greet()` gives `"Hello!"`
  - `greet("Ravi")` gives `"Hello, Ravi!"`
  - `greet("Ravi", "Dr.")` gives `"Hello, Dr. Ravi!"`
  - a `title` without a `name` is `ValueError("A title needs a name")`

Write a class `Calculator` with:

- `add(*numbers)` returns the sum of **any number** of arguments (`0` for none).
- `describe(value)` returns, depending on the **type** of `value` (check in this order): a `bool` gives `"Boolean <value>"`; an `int` gives `"Integer <value>"`; a `float` gives `"Decimal <value>"`; a `str` gives `"Text '<value>'"`; a `list` or `tuple` gives `"Collection of <n> items"`; anything else gives `"Something else"`.
tests: assert g.greet() == "Hello!" and g.greet("Ravi") == "Hello, Ravi!" and g.greet("Ravi", "Dr.") == "Hello, Dr. Ravi!"
assert g.greet(name="Asha") == "Hello, Asha!" and g.greet(title="Prof.", name="Kim") == "Hello, Prof. Kim!"
assert error_of(g.greet, None, "Dr.") == "ValueError: A title needs a name" and error_of(g.greet, title="Dr.") == "ValueError: A title needs a name"
assert c.add() == 0 and c.add(5) == 5 and c.add(1, 2) == 3 and c.add(1, 2, 3, 4, 5) == 15 and c.add(1.5, 2.5) == 4.0
assert c.describe(True) == "Boolean True" and c.describe(False) == "Boolean False"
assert c.describe(5) == "Integer 5" and c.describe(0) == "Integer 0" and c.describe(2.5) == "Decimal 2.5"
assert c.describe([1, 2, 3]) == "Collection of 3 items" and c.describe((1,)) == "Collection of 1 items" and c.describe([]) == "Collection of 0 items"
assert c.describe(None) == "Something else" and c.describe({"a": 1}) == "Something else" and c.describe({1}) == "Something else"
